Teachers described comparing their own claims with AI suggestions, reflecting on their reasoning process, and using the tool in ways analogous to Socratic questioning, indicating perceived gains in metacognition and critical thinking rather than measured skill gains.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of higher-order thinking, reasoning, reflection, and self-directed learning during AI-assisted scientific writing

finding.finding_summary: Teachers expressed positive reactions such as surprise, interest, and motivation when using the system, noting that it made the writing process engaging. However, they also reported skepticism and anxiety about AI adoption, especially concerns over changing teacher roles and uncertainty about AI outputs, so the affective response was not uniformly positive.
finding.measure: Teacher interview comments about perceived engagement, interest, anxiety, and receptiveness to AI use

finding.finding_summary: Teachers valued the system’s immediate feedback and rapid generation of text, describing the support as individualized and timely compared with typical classroom feedback constraints. They also noted that such tools might reduce repetitive instructional burden, although the study did not measure teacher workload quantitatively.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of immediacy, individualized feedback, and instructional efficiency

paper_profiles.title: Facilitating student engagement through the flipped learning approach in K-12: A systematic review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the question of how flipped learning affects student engagement in K-12 settings, and what technologies are being used to implement flipped learning in schools. The author conducted a narrative systematic review of empirical studies published in English between 2012 and 2018 across seven databases, synthesizing 107 articles, book chapters, dissertations, conference papers, and grey literature.

The review conceptualizes flipped learning as an approach in which students access instructional content outside class and use class time for active, collaborative work. Across the corpus, the most common technologies were teacher-made videos, self-assessment quizzes, and learning management systems such as Edmodo, Google Classroom, and Moodle. The review found that flipped learning was generally associated with increased behavioral, affective, and cognitive engagement, especially peer interaction, enjoyment, participation, teacher interaction, and confidence, although the evidence base was heterogeneous and often methodologically weak.

Most studies came from the United States and from secondary/high school contexts; STEM subjects dominated, especially mathematics. The paper emphasizes that many studies lacked clear definitions of engagement, theoretical grounding, or detailed reporting of intervention design, which limits reproducibility and interpretation. The overall conclusion is that flipped learning often appears to support engagement in K-12, but stronger, more transparent research designs are needed to understand which implementation features matter most and under what conditions.

finding.finding_summary: Across 107 K-12 flipped-learning studies, 79 studies (74%) reported affective engagement indicators and 87 studies (81%) reported behavioral engagement indicators. The review concludes that flipped learning overwhelmingly supported engagement-related outcomes such as enjoyment, interest, confidence, participation, and increased interaction with peers and teachers, although many individual studies did not report effect sizes.
finding.measure: Student engagement indicators from surveys, interviews, observations, and focus groups

finding.finding_summary: The review found repeated evidence that flipped learning supported collaboration, communication, responsibility, self-regulation, and interaction with peers. The most common behavioral indicator was increased interaction with peers (50 studies; 47%), and several studies reported students taking greater ownership of learning, asking more questions, and engaging in collaborative classroom and out-of-class activities.
finding.measure: Observed and self-reported collaboration, self-regulation, responsibility, participation, and peer interaction

finding.finding_summary: Mathematics was the most frequently studied subject area in the corpus (38.3%, n=41), and the review reports that flipped learning in these studies was often associated with improved engagement and active learning in math classrooms. However, the paper focuses on engagement rather than direct math achievement, so the evidence for numeracy outcomes is indirect.
finding.measure: Engagement and participation in mathematics flipped-learning studies

paper_profiles.title: AutoTutor and Family: A Review of 17 Years of Natural Language Tutoring
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review synthesizes 17 years of research on AutoTutor and related natural-language tutoring systems. The paper asks how conversational tutoring can approximate some of the benefits of human tutoring, and which design features of dialogue-based intelligent tutoring systems actually support learning, motivation, and metacognition.

The review focuses on the development of AutoTutor’s core dialogue architecture, including human-inspired tutoring strategies, deep reasoning questions, expectation/misconception handling, pedagogical agents, and supporting technologies such as latent semantic analysis, affect detection, and web-based delivery platforms. It summarizes evidence from multiple domains, including computer literacy, physics, biology, critical thinking, reading comprehension, and self-regulated learning, drawing on laboratory and field studies with undergraduate students, college students, and some middle-school learners in reading-comprehension research.

Across the studies reviewed, AutoTutor and its descendants generally produced positive learning gains relative to static materials or minimal-instruction controls, with effects often around 0.5σ to 0.8σ depending on domain and test type. The paper concludes that deep-reasoning dialogue, collaborative scaffolding, and well-implemented pedagogical supports can yield meaningful learning benefits, but that effects vary by domain, learner knowledge, and the specific interaction strategy used. It also notes open questions about when to emphasize affect support, macro-adaptivity, collaborative lecturing, and metacognitive training versus direct domain tutoring.

finding.finding_summary: Across the physics and scientific-inquiry studies reviewed, AutoTutor-style deep reasoning dialogue produced substantial learning gains over comparison conditions. The review reports gains around 0.5σ in early computer literacy work, 0.61σ over a control and 1.22σ over reading a textbook in a physics study, and 0.79σ in a small DeepTutor evaluation (n=30) when macro-adaptivity was added.
finding.measure: Physics conceptual understanding and scientific reasoning tests; essay questions, multiple-choice items, and posttests on conceptual physics/scientific inquiry
finding.study_size: varies_by_study; e.g., n=30 for DeepTutor evaluation

finding.finding_summary: The review includes reading-comprehension tutoring systems such as iSTART, which improved comprehension differently for skilled and less-skilled readers, including middle-schoolers. Less-skilled readers improved more on single-sentence content questions, while more skilled readers improved on bridging questions that require integrating information across sentences; exact effect sizes are not reported in the paper excerpt.
finding.measure: Reading comprehension performance on sentence-content and bridging questions

finding.finding_summary: The review reports gains for critical-thinking and metacognitive tutoring systems such as SEEK, Operation ARIES/ARA, and MetaTutor, though results vary by intervention. Operation ARA showed a 1.4σ gain on a scientific research-skills test versus no-instruction controls, and MetaTutor research reported higher learning efficiency when prompts and feedback supported self-regulated learning during hypermedia exploration.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, scientific inquiry, metacognitive self-regulation, and learning efficiency measures
finding.study_size: varies_by_study; exact n not reported in excerpt

finding.finding_summary: Affect-sensitive tutoring improved outcomes for some learners but not others. Supportive AutoTutor produced a 0.71σ posttest gain for low-knowledge students compared with standard AutoTutor, but benefits appeared mainly in a second session and high-knowledge students did not benefit, sometimes learning less when emotional support was added. GazeTutor also increased attention and produced 0.26σ overall gains and 0.45σ gains on deep learning, though the overall effect was not statistically significant.
finding.measure: Posttest learning, attention/disengagement, and affective state responses
finding.confidence_interval: p<.178 for overall GazeTutor gain; p<.035 for deep learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that AutoTutor’s authoring and delivery tools, as well as related platforms, were developed to make web-based tutoring more accessible and reusable. However, the excerpt provides limited direct empirical evidence on workload or productivity outcomes, so this is a weaker assignment based on the implementation discussion rather than a dedicated efficiency study.
finding.measure: Implementation/accessibility features of tutoring delivery and authoring platforms

paper_profiles.title: Why lockdown and distance learning during the COVID-19 pandemic are likely to increase the social class achievement gap
paper_profiles.population: Elementary (PreK-5th), Middle School, High School, Undergraduate
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review article asks why COVID-19 school closures and the rapid shift to distance learning are likely to widen academic inequalities by social class. Rather than evaluating a single intervention, it synthesizes multidisciplinary evidence on digital access, digital skills, family cultural resources, autonomy/self-regulation, and unequal school support during lockdown.

The paper focuses primarily on K-12 and higher-education learners in France, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, the United States, and other countries, with especially relevant implications for elementary and secondary students. It argues that school closures increased reliance on digital tools and family support, both of which are distributed unequally, thereby disadvantaging working-class and other marginalized students. The authors also review early pandemic evidence showing widened achievement gaps and propose practical recommendations for teachers, schools, and policymakers.

Key recommendations include improving teacher awareness of barriers faced by working-class families, providing individualized homework feedback, training families in digital technology, prioritizing in-person learning when possible, concentrating resources on the most deprived students, and funding remedial programs. Overall, the article concludes that school closures and distance learning are structurally likely to amplify existing social class achievement gaps, even though the paper itself is a narrative review rather than an empirical test of a specific AI tool or intervention.

finding.finding_summary: The review synthesizes evidence that school closures and distance learning can worsen overall academic achievement, but the magnitude and direction vary by context. It cites early pandemic studies showing larger learning losses for disadvantaged students, including a Dutch analysis where working-class children experienced losses 40% greater than upper/middle-class children (n not reported in the review for that comparison).
finding.measure: National assessments, achievement tests, and comparisons of progress in reading, mathematics, and language during school closures

finding.finding_summary: The review reports evidence that mathematics learning declined during lockdown and that losses were larger for working-class students. In the Netherlands, a comparison of progress before and after closures found general learning loss in mathematics/arithmetic, with losses for working-class children about 40% greater than for upper/middle-class children (8% of the sample were working-class, but the underlying study size is not reported in the review).
finding.measure: Mathematics/arithmetic progress and national assessment scores

finding.finding_summary: The paper reviews evidence of literacy-related learning loss during school closures, including spelling, reading comprehension, and oral reading. It notes that oral reading development slowed significantly in more than 100 U.S. school districts between spring and autumn 2020, with the slowdown more pronounced in lower-achieving districts; it also cites increased gaps in French language-related assessments and greater losses for disadvantaged students.
finding.measure: Reading comprehension, spelling, oral reading assessments, and language scores

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that distance learning can reduce self-efficacy, engagement, and persistence, especially for working-class students and parents who feel less able to support schoolwork. It synthesizes survey evidence that upper/middle-class families felt better able to support children in distance learning than working-class families, suggesting differential impacts on confidence and engagement rather than a single experimental effect size.
finding.measure: Self-efficacy, perceived ability to support learning, engagement in learning activities

finding.finding_summary: The article discusses implementation differences in how schools organized remote teaching, including posting work on platforms, emailing assignments, live sessions, and providing feedback. It suggests that individualized monitoring, regular calls, and homework feedback may improve continuity, but it does not provide a single quantitative estimate of operational efficiency effects.
finding.measure: Remote teaching practices, homework feedback, and individualized monitoring

finding.finding_summary: The core claim is that school closures and unequal access to digital resources, school support, and family capital systematically amplify social class and racial inequalities. The review cites survey evidence that support from schools, online teaching, and technical assistance were more available to advantaged households and schools, and it argues these structural patterns contribute to widening achievement gaps during lockdown.
finding.measure: Access to online teaching, school support, technical support, and differential learning opportunities by social class/race

paper_profiles.title: Differentiated Instruction in Secondary Education: A Systematic Review of Research Evidence
paper_profiles.population: Secondary education (middle school and high school)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This systematic review examines the empirical evidence on within-class differentiated instruction in secondary education and asks both how the approach is operationalized and how effective it is for student achievement. The authors focus on planned classroom adaptations to content, process, product, learning environment, or learning time, and they explicitly exclude between-class tracking, tutoring outside class, and fully computerized adaptive programs that cannot be directly controlled by teachers.

Using a best-evidence synthesis, the review identified 14 papers representing 12 unique studies published between 2006 and 2016. The included studies covered several forms of differentiation, including teacher training in adaptive instruction, ability grouping and tiering, individualized reading conferences, mastery-like approaches, and remediation within flipped classrooms. The evidence base was mixed but generally positive: most studies reported small to moderate gains in academic achievement, though effects varied by implementation and context, and several findings were not statistically significant.

The review also highlights implementation features that matter for differentiated instruction, such as pre-assessment, teacher coaching or professional development, careful lesson planning, and the use of student readiness, interest, or learning profiles to guide adaptations. Overall, the authors conclude that differentiated instruction shows promise in secondary settings, but the evidence is still limited, heterogeneous, and not strong enough for firm conclusions about which specific approaches work best.

finding.finding_summary: One included U.S. study (Little et al., 2014) evaluated individualized reading instruction with self-selected challenging books and teacher-student conferences. Reading outcomes were mostly null to small positive: combined effects were d = 0.030 to 0.266 depending on site, with standardized reading comprehension and fluency measures across roughly n=3,000 student observations across sites.
finding.measure: Standardized reading comprehension test and fluency test
finding.confidence_interval: varied by site; overall CIs reported as site-specific in table, not fully reported here

finding.finding_summary: Several studies focused on differentiated mathematics instruction and found generally positive effects. Effects ranged from very large in one Turkey study of project-based differentiated math instruction (combined d = 4.504, n=144 across grades 6–7) to moderate in ability-grouping and tiering studies such as Bal (2016) (d = 1.085, n=57) and Bikić et al. (2016) (overall d = 0.539, n=165), with some smaller or mixed subgroup effects in flipped-classroom remediation (Bhagat et al., 2016; combined d = 0.376, n=82).
finding.measure: Researcher-made mathematics achievement tests / algebra tests / trigonometry achievement tests

finding.finding_summary: The review includes a U.S. science study using peer tutoring plus tiered materials for grade 8 science (Mastropieri et al., 2006). The intervention improved science achievement on both a unit test and a high-stakes end-of-year test, with a combined effect of d = 0.386 (n=213, including 44 students with disabilities).
finding.measure: Science achievement unit test and high-stakes end-of-year science test

finding.finding_summary: The review includes one U.S. study of alcohol, tobacco, and other drug (ATOD) prevention education (Huber et al., 2009), which is not a core academic subject but was treated as an achievement-like outcome in the review. The adaptive-teaching/PALS intervention produced a large positive effect on the researcher-made ATOD survey, d = 1.374 (n=1,170 students across conditions).
finding.measure: Alcohol, tobacco and other drug survey (researcher-made)

finding.finding_summary: Several interventions explicitly used student readiness, interest, or learning profiles to tailor tasks and supports, and the paper notes improvements in engagement-related processes such as motivation and adaptive implementation in some studies. However, the review’s main synthesis target was achievement rather than direct social-emotional measures, so evidence here is indirect and secondary.
finding.measure: Student interest/readiness inventories and teacher-reported adaptive implementation; indirect engagement-related indicators

paper_profiles.title: A meta systematic review of artificial intelligence in higher education: a call for increased ethics, collaboration, and rigour
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a tertiary review (review of reviews) that maps the scope, methods, and main findings of artificial intelligence in higher education (AIHEd) evidence syntheses published from January 2018 to July 2023. The authors ask what kinds of evidence syntheses exist, where they are published, who conducts them, what tools and methods are used, how good the reviews are, and what AI application areas dominate the literature.

The review included 66 AIHEd reviews out of 307 AI evidence syntheses identified across education levels. It finds that most reviews are systematic literature reviews, with broad 'general AI' topics most common, followed by profiling/prediction and adaptive systems/personalisation; fewer reviews focus on assessment/evaluation or intelligent tutoring systems. Across the corpus, the authors report generally moderate methodological quality, substantial under-reporting of key review methods, and a need for stronger rigor, transparency, ethics, and interdisciplinary collaboration.

The paper is not an intervention study and does not estimate causal effects of AI tools on student outcomes. Instead, it synthesizes secondary research to show that AI in higher education is most often discussed in relation to personalized/adaptive learning, chatbots, learning analytics, and prediction, while also highlighting gaps such as limited quality appraisal, limited use of review software, and uneven reporting of search and screening procedures.

finding.finding_summary: This review does not directly test AI tools for scientific reasoning, but it does identify adjacent higher-education evidence syntheses in STEM and AI-supported learning contexts. The paper reports that adaptive systems/personalisation, chatbots, and intelligent tutoring systems are prominent AI applications, but it does not provide pooled effects for scientific reasoning outcomes, so any relevance to scientific reasoning is indirect and descriptive rather than causal.
finding.measure: Narrative coding of review topics and findings across included AIHEd evidence syntheses

paper_profiles.title: Teacher’s Perceptions of Using an Artificial Intelligence-Based Educational Tool for Scientific Writing
paper_profiles.population: K-12 teachers in STEM-related disciplines (primarily elementary, middle, and high school educators in the United States)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how STEM teachers perceive an artificial intelligence-enhanced scaffolding system for scientific writing, with attention to both perceived benefits and concerns about using AI in classrooms. The study was motivated by the broader challenge of implementing educational technology in ways teachers will actually adopt, especially in STEM instruction where students need support for complex writing, reasoning, and evidence-based argumentation.

The researchers developed an AI-based scaffolding system (AISS) using GPT-2 to generate expert-model text and individualized prompts for an ill-structured scientific writing task about U.S. air quality. Nine in-service K-12 STEM teachers in the United States, enrolled in a doctoral course, used the system, completed a writing task, and then participated in brief interviews; log files and thematic analysis were used to interpret their experiences. Teachers generally viewed the tool positively as a source of superior scaffolding, noting its immediate, individualized feedback, expert modeling, and potential to support argumentation, reasoning, and scientific writing for middle and high school students. They also raised concerns about transparency, reliability, and the possibility that AI could reduce the teacher’s role in instruction.

Because the study is qualitative and focused on teacher perceptions rather than student outcomes, it does not provide direct causal evidence that AI improves scientific reasoning or writing achievement. Its main contribution is descriptive: it identifies how teachers believe AI scaffolding may support STEM learning, implementation conditions that matter, and limitations that should be addressed before classroom adoption.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers judged the AI-enhanced scaffolding system to be useful for supporting scientific writing processes tied to reasoning, evidence selection, and argumentation. They described it as an expert model that helped users justify claims with evidence and think more logically and systematically, but this was based on teacher perceptions rather than student outcome data (n=9 teachers).
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of AI-supported scientific writing, argumentation, and reasoning potential

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the AI system generated well-written sentences and paragraphs and could help students improve sentence structure, sequencing, and scientific essay writing. The system was viewed as a useful model for writing support, especially for middle and high school learners, but the study did not measure student writing outcomes directly (n=9 teachers).
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of AI-supported scientific writing quality, sentence structure, and paragraph sequencing

finding.finding_summary: Teachers believed the AI tool could foster higher-order thinking skills such as reasoning, problem solving, metacognition, and self-directed learning. Interview responses emphasized reflection on AI feedback and comparing/justifying claims, but these were perceived benefits rather than measured learner gains (n=9 teachers).
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of higher-order thinking, reasoning, and self-directed learning support

paper_profiles.title: AutoTutor and Family: A Review of 17 Years of Natural Language Tutoring
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review synthesizes 17 years of research on AutoTutor and related natural-language tutoring systems. The paper asks what design features of conversational tutors help learning, how those features evolved across the AutoTutor family, and what outcomes were observed across domains such as computer literacy, physics, biology, critical thinking, reading comprehension, and self-regulated learning.

The approach is a narrative review of major AutoTutor-family projects rather than a single new experiment. It covers core design elements including the 5-step tutoring frame, deep-reasoning questions, expectation-misconception dialogue, collaborative lecturing, macro-adaptive learning progressions, affect-sensitive tutoring, gaze-based disengagement detection, and pedagogical agents. The review summarizes evidence from prior studies comparing these systems with textbook study, classroom instruction, non-expert human tutors, and control conditions.

Overall, the paper concludes that natural-language tutoring can produce meaningful learning gains, often outperforming static materials and sometimes matching human tutoring in certain contexts. It also finds that benefits depend on design choices and learner characteristics: deep reasoning and collaborative explanation tend to help, affective support benefits low-knowledge learners, collaborative lecturing can be effective in biology, and macro-adaptive tutoring can improve learning in small-scale evaluations. However, the evidence is uneven across domains and outcomes, and the review notes limitations such as short training durations in some studies, difficulty detecting misconceptions, and the need for more research on when particular tutor strategies are most effective.

finding.finding_summary: Across the AutoTutor family, natural-language tutoring on science concepts produced learning gains relative to static instructional materials and sometimes compared favorably to human tutors. In the physics studies summarized here, WHY2/AutoTutor produced learning gains of about 0.5σ over textbook study for equivalent time, with one study reporting 0.61σ over a no-materials control and 1.22σ over a textbook-reading condition; normalized gains were 0.32σ for AutoTutor versus 0.04σ for textbook reading. The review also reports a small-scale DeepTutor evaluation (n=30) with 0.79σ pretest-posttest gain over 1 hour when macro-adaptivity was included, versus very little learning when dialogs were not dynamically selected.
finding.measure: Physics concept tests; essay questions and multiple-choice questions adapted in part from the Force Concept Inventory; pretest-posttest learning outcomes on scientific concepts
finding.study_size: various_studies; one cited DeepTutor study n=30

finding.finding_summary: The review summarizes evidence that affect-sensitive tutoring can improve outcomes for low-knowledge learners, but not for high-knowledge learners. In the Supportive AutoTutor comparison, low-knowledge students showed a 0.71σ gain on posttest scores relative to standard AutoTutor, with benefits emerging mainly in a second session when difficulty was greater; high-knowledge students did not benefit and sometimes learned less with emotional support. A related gaze-sensitive tutor increased attention and produced 0.26σ overall learning gain (p<.178) and 0.45σ gain on deep learning (p<.035), suggesting engagement/disengagement adaptation can matter even when broad gains are modest.
finding.measure: Posttest learning scores; attention to tutor; deep-learning posttest measures

finding.finding_summary: A major portion of the review concerns critical thinking, metacognition, and scientific inquiry skills. SEEK was designed to improve critical thinking and scientific inquiry processes, but did not significantly improve students’ ability to find relevant information after a short 1-hour training. In contrast, Operation ARA reported learning gains of 1.4σ on a test of scientific research skills compared with no-instruction controls after 8–12 hours of use, and the review also notes that iSTART improved reading-comprehension strategy use differently for skilled versus less-skilled readers, indicating meaningful effects on higher-order skills.
finding.measure: Critical-thinking/scientific inquiry tests; information-finding performance; reading-comprehension strategy outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The review summarizes adjacent evidence from reading and writing tutors in the AutoTutor family. iSTART improved reading comprehension for both college students and middle-schoolers, with less-skilled readers improving on single-sentence content questions and more skilled readers improving on bridging questions that require integrating information across sentences. Writing-Pal is described as a writing tutor for argument essays that uses automated essay assessment and feedback, though the excerpted paper does not report a new effect size for writing outcomes.
finding.measure: Reading-comprehension questions; reading strategy performance; automated essay feedback outcomes

paper_profiles.title: AI Grand Challenges for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article is a vision and agenda piece outlining five long-term grand challenges for artificial intelligence in education: mentors for every learner, 21st century skills, interaction data for learning, universal access to global classrooms, and lifelong/lifewide learning. Rather than testing a specific intervention, it argues that AI can address persistent problems in education by enabling personalized tutoring, adaptive feedback, richer modeling of learner knowledge and affect, and new forms of collaborative and inquiry-based learning.

The paper discusses broad application areas such as intelligent tutoring systems, learning analytics, educational data mining, collaborative tools, and AI-based agents. It emphasizes that these systems could support students in science learning, problem solving, collaboration, and self-regulated learning, while also helping teachers and researchers use fine-grained learning data to improve instruction. The article is largely conceptual and synthesizes prior work and examples from existing systems, but does not present original empirical evidence or evaluate outcomes for a specific population.

Because the piece is a high-level perspective rather than an empirical study, it does not provide direct effect estimates for middle school U.S. students or for scientific reasoning outcomes. Its relevance to the user’s question is indirect: it identifies scientific reasoning as an intended target for AI mentoring systems and cites the need for technology-supported inquiry and science practices, but it does not compare AI tools against standard instruction or non-AI supports.

finding.finding_summary: The article does not report an empirical test of AI tools on scientific reasoning. It only argues conceptually that AI mentors, inquiry systems, and Learning by Design tools could help students learn science practices and scientific reasoning, but provides no effect size, sample, or outcome data.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively discusses durable skills such as critical thinking, collaboration, metacognition, communication, and self-direction as goals for AI in education, but it does not evaluate any intervention on these outcomes. No quantitative findings are reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The article describes AI systems as potentially supporting engagement, motivation, affect, and self-efficacy, and mentions emotional self-regulation as an area for future systems. However, it presents no empirical evidence, sample size, or measured effect on social-emotional outcomes.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses heavily on system-level implications for education policy, data infrastructures, global classrooms, and teacher professional development, but these are presented as a vision rather than measured institutional effects. No empirical results are reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Example-Tracing Tutors: Intelligent Tutor Development for Non-programmers
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.population: Elementary (PreK-5th), Middle School, High School, Undergraduate
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews the example-tracing tutor paradigm and the Cognitive Tutor Authoring Tools (CTAT), with the goal of showing that non-programmers can build effective intelligent tutoring systems. The authors argue that CTAT and its Tutorshop deployment environment lower the barrier to building ITS by supporting drag-and-drop interface authoring, behavior-graph creation without programming, Bayesian Knowledge Tracing-based student modeling, adaptive problem selection, logging, and deployment across web and LMS platforms.

The paper is primarily a synthesis of prior work and a review of 18 example-tracing tutors built since 2009, many of which were used in real classrooms or other authentic educational settings. Across these tutors, the authors highlight evidence that example-tracing tutors can support learning in mathematics, chemistry, genetics, and related domains, often with sizable pre/post gains or favorable comparisons to alternative instructional conditions. The paper also explains where the approach works well, such as step-based problem solving and worked-example instruction, and where it is limited, such as open-ended domains, natural-language tutoring, and very large solution spaces.

The review is not a single primary efficacy study, but rather a design-and-evidence paper that makes the case that CTAT is a mature, practical ITS authoring environment. It concludes that example-tracing tutors can be effective, cost-efficient to build, and adaptable to a range of instructional formats, while also noting unresolved limitations around richer student modeling, open-ended problem types, and integration with broader learning platforms.

finding.finding_summary: Multiple CTAT-built tutors in mathematics showed positive learning effects in real educational settings. The review reports, for example, that the Fractions Tutor was used in five classroom studies with over 3,000 students and produced gains of d=.40 on an immediate post-test and d=.60 on a delayed post-test, while the Lynnette equation-solving tutor showed medium to large pre/post gains in four classroom studies with 487 grades 6-8 students (d=.69, d=1.65, d=1.17; one study was not significant due to a ceiling effect).
finding.measure: Mathematics learning outcomes, including pre/post tests and immediate and delayed post-tests

finding.finding_summary: The paper summarizes positive evidence from science-oriented tutors, especially the Genetics Tutor and the Stoichiometry Tutor. The Genetics Tutor was evaluated in 45 single-unit in-course studies across 15 colleges/universities and 4 high schools, with average pretest-to-posttest gains of about 18 percentage points; the Stoichiometry Tutor studies found that worked and erroneous examples produced learning outcomes comparable to tutored and untutored problems, while being more efficient in time (d ranging from 1.76 to 3.31) and mental effort (d ranging from 0.89 to 1.04).
finding.measure: Genetics reasoning/problem-solving assessments; stoichiometry learning outcomes; pre/post tests; time and mental effort
finding.study_size: n=45 single-unit evaluations for Genetics Tutor; n=295 across Stoichiometry Tutor classroom studies
finding.effect_size: about 18 percentage points gain; d=1.76 to 3.31 (time), d=0.89 to 1.04 (mental effort)

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes evidence for self-explanation and related metacognitive supports within example-tracing tutors, but these are secondary to the main content-focused outcomes. For instance, tutors using worked or erroneous examples prompted explanation and reflection, and the authors argue these features support adaptive learning behaviors and deeper reasoning, though the review does not isolate a single durable-skills effect estimate across studies.
finding.measure: Self-explanation, reflection, and adaptive reasoning processes embedded in tutors

paper_profiles.title: Promises and challenges of generative artificial intelligence for human learning
paper_profiles.population: Not directly studied; conceptual across learners and educators, with examples spanning K-12, higher education, and adult learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This perspective paper examines the emerging role of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in human learning, arguing that these systems could transform learning support, resource creation, feedback, and assessment. The paper is not an intervention study; instead, it synthesizes early empirical findings and conceptual arguments from learning sciences, educational technology, and human-computer interaction to outline where GenAI may help and where it may harm learning.

The authors organize the discussion around four promises of GenAI: scalable personalized tutoring, faster creation of learning resources, timely feedback, and more adaptive/authentic assessment. Across these areas, the paper emphasizes that GenAI can augment instruction when paired with human oversight and pedagogical design, but that evidence remains limited and mixed. The paper repeatedly notes concerns about hallucinations, transparency, privacy, bias, and overreliance, and argues that stronger evidence is needed before broad educational adoption.

No single population or setting is studied empirically in this article. Instead, it draws on examples from writing, programming, language learning, STEAM, and assessment contexts across secondary and higher education, including some K-12 references. The overall conclusion is that GenAI has promise as a learning tool, but its benefits are contingent on careful implementation, AI literacy, and rigorous future research, especially longitudinal and randomized studies on learning outcomes and human-AI interaction.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not report a primary empirical study of academic achievement, but it synthesizes early evidence that GenAI can support learning across subjects. It highlights examples where GenAI-generated resources and tutoring may improve performance, while also noting a preliminary study with no significant differences in learning gains between GenAI-generated videos with synthetic instructors and traditional recorded instructor videos.
finding.measure: Learning gains, performance, and task outcomes across varied educational contexts

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that GenAI may enhance motivation, engagement, and positive learning experiences, but evidence is inconsistent. It cites studies where AI-generated feedback increased secondary students’ motivation and positive emotions, while also noting cases where GenAI support reduced engagement and that removing support lowered performance, suggesting complex effects on student agency and engagement.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, positive emotions, and student agency

finding.finding_summary: A central theme is that GenAI may foster or undermine durable skills such as critical thinking, problem-solving, self-regulation, and metacognition. The paper cites evidence that guided tutoring and inquiry-oriented use may support deep conceptual understanding, but warns that overreliance can reduce agency and create a performance illusion, and that some AI-assisted performance gains disappear when support is removed.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, self-regulation, metacognition, and learner agency

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that GenAI can improve efficiency by scaling personalized support, generating resources, and producing faster feedback. It cites studies suggesting ChatGPT-generated feedback is more in-depth and fluent than human feedback, and that AI systems can reduce the labor required for formative feedback and content creation, though accuracy and validation remain concerns.
finding.measure: Feedback quality, feedback generation efficiency, and resource creation workload

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes broader institutional implications including transparency, privacy, equity, accountability, and assessment validity. It argues that GenAI adoption may widen digital divides and complicate assessment systems, while also calling for policy, governance, and methodological standards to support responsible deployment.
finding.measure: Transparency, privacy, equality, beneficence, and assessment integrity

paper_profiles.title: Proactive and reactive engagement of artificial intelligence methods for education: a review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a broad review of how artificial intelligence, machine learning, and deep learning have been used across the full education pipeline. The authors organize prior work into two large phases: proactive engagement, which includes admissions logistics, curriculum/content design, scheduling, and content generation; and reactive engagement, which includes intelligent tutoring, performance assessment, and student outcome prediction.

The review is based on 195 original research articles published from 2003–2022. Rather than testing a single intervention, it synthesizes design patterns, data sources, and algorithm choices across subareas such as admissions, question generation, tutoring systems, knowledge tracing, and teacher/learner analytics. The paper emphasizes that AI in education has expanded rapidly, with especially mature work in tutoring aids and assessment, while also noting infrastructural, ethical, fairness, and privacy concerns that affect adoption.

For the specific question of whether AI improves scientific reasoning for U.S. middle school students, this paper does not provide direct evidence. It does mention K-12 uses in general, including mathematical word problem generation and intelligent tutoring, but it does not report a study focused on U.S. middle school scientific reasoning outcomes or comparative effect estimates against standard instruction or non-AI supports. As a result, it is best treated as an organizing review that points to adjacent AIEd evidence rather than as outcome evidence for scientific reasoning.

finding.finding_summary: The review finds substantial evidence that AI can improve operational efficiency in education by reducing human workload and accelerating administrative or instructional processes. Examples include admissions screening systems such as GRADE, which reduced the number of full application reviews and review time per application, and AI-based content generation and tutoring tools that automate question generation, scheduling, and feedback support.
finding.measure: Task efficiency / review time / automation of administrative and instructional workflows

finding.finding_summary: The review summarizes multiple lines of work suggesting that AI-supported tutoring can improve engagement, motivation, and self-regulated learning. It cites interactive tutoring aids, conversational systems, and motivational prompt systems as approaches intended to keep students engaged longer and support persistence during learning tasks.
finding.measure: Engagement, motivation, and self-regulated learning indicators

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses AI systems designed to support durable skills such as metacognition, reflection, and collaboration, especially through conversational tutoring and partial-solution guidance. However, the paper is a review and does not provide a single pooled estimate; instead, it reports that these systems are intended to help learners reflect on lessons learned and progress toward self-regulated learning.
finding.measure: Metacognition, reflection, collaboration, self-regulated learning

paper_profiles.title: Promises and challenges of generative artificial intelligence for human learning
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (perspective paper; no empirical participant sample)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a perspective article that examines the promises, challenges, and research needs associated with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in human learning. Rather than reporting a primary empirical study, it synthesizes recent literature and conceptual arguments about how GenAI might affect learning support, resource creation, feedback, and assessment, while also highlighting risks such as hallucinations, privacy concerns, bias, and assessment disruption.

The paper discusses how tools like ChatGPT, Khanmigo, and other LLM-based systems could scale personalized tutoring, generate instructional materials, provide feedback, and enable adaptive assessment. It argues that these benefits are promising but not yet well established empirically, and calls for rigorous evidence, including longitudinal and randomized studies, to determine whether GenAI improves learning outcomes without undermining agency, critical thinking, or creativity.

The article does not study a specific student population or intervention in the United States middle school context. Instead, it reviews adjacent evidence from higher education, writing, feedback, and tutoring applications, using those examples to motivate future research on GenAI in education. Its main conclusion is that GenAI should be developed and evaluated through human-centered, evidence-based, and methodologically rigorous approaches rather than adopted on the basis of hype.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that GenAI may improve engagement, motivation, and perceived support in some contexts, but it also may reduce agency and create dependency or fluency bias. These claims are based on cited prior studies and conceptual synthesis rather than new data from this paper.
finding.measure: Learner engagement, motivation, agency, and perceived support (from cited prior studies)

finding.finding_summary: The article centrally discusses durable skills such as critical thinking, problem-solving, metacognition, creativity, and self-regulation, arguing that GenAI can support these skills but may also weaken them if learners over-rely on AI. No new empirical effect size is reported; the discussion relies on examples such as a cited randomized experiment where removing AI support lowered performance.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, metacognition, creativity, self-regulation

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that GenAI can scale personalized support, accelerate feedback generation, and reduce educator workload by automating parts of tutoring, resource creation, feedback, and assessment. These are presented as plausible benefits supported by illustrative prior studies, but the paper itself does not report original efficiency data.
finding.measure: Instructional support scalability, feedback generation efficiency, and educator workload

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes institutional implications such as privacy, transparency, equity, accountability, and assessment validity, arguing that GenAI could widen inequities or disrupt assessment systems if poorly governed. It recommends evidence-based policy, AI literacy, and ethical regulation, but provides no original institutional outcome data.
finding.measure: Transparency, privacy, equality, beneficence, and assessment validity in educational systems

paper_profiles.title: Proactive and Reactive Engagement of Artificial Intelligence Methods for Education: A Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a broad review of artificial intelligence methods in education, organizing the literature into two main phases: proactive engagement (e.g., admissions, curriculum and timetable design, content generation) and reactive engagement (e.g., tutoring systems, assessment, knowledge tracing, feedback, and outcome prediction). The authors sampled 194 peer-reviewed research articles published between 2003 and 2022 and used this corpus to describe major technical trends, common problem types, and how AI methods have evolved over time.

The review does not evaluate a single intervention on a defined student sample; instead, it synthesizes prior work across educational settings and learner groups, including pre-school, elementary, middle/high school, university, MOOCs, and professional education. It highlights the growing use of machine learning, deep learning, reinforcement learning, natural language processing, and related methods in intelligent tutoring, automated grading, content generation, and prediction systems.

The paper concludes that AI in education has expanded substantially, especially in reactive applications that directly support learning and assessment, while also noting persistent limitations such as fairness, transparency, privacy, data availability, and generalizability. It also emphasizes that COVID-19 accelerated interest in AI-enabled education. Because this is a conceptual/technical review rather than an outcome study, it provides no pooled effect sizes or causal estimates about student learning gains, including scientific reasoning.

finding.finding_summary: This review synthesizes how AI is being used across the education pipeline and argues that AI can improve institutional processes such as admissions review, scheduling, curriculum/content design, grading, and outcome prediction. At the same time, it emphasizes unresolved concerns around fairness, transparency, privacy, and bias, so the likely institutional effect is mixed rather than uniformly positive.
finding.measure: Breadth and nature of AI applications in education; discussion of institutional use cases and limitations

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly highlights AI systems as tools for reducing time and workload in educational operations, especially in admissions evaluation, automated grading, scheduling/timetabling, and question generation. These claims are based on the reviewed literature rather than a direct experiment, and no pooled effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Operational uses of AI such as admissions review time, grading automation, timetabling, and content generation

finding.finding_summary: The review discusses AI applications in writing and language-related tasks, including automated essay scoring, automated short-answer grading, automated writing evaluation, and mispronunciation/speech assessment. It argues these tools can speed feedback and support drafting or language practice, but it does not provide direct causal evidence for improved literacy outcomes in a specific student sample.
finding.measure: Essay scoring, short-answer grading, automated writing feedback, pronunciation/speech evaluation

finding.finding_summary: The paper covers AI work on mathematical word problem generation, automatic assessment of open-response math questions, mathematical derivations, and theorem proving. It portrays these as promising for practice generation and automated feedback, but the review itself does not estimate whether these tools improve math achievement or reasoning relative to standard instruction.
finding.measure: Math problem generation and automated scoring of mathematical responses/derivations/theorem proofs

finding.finding_summary: Scientific reasoning appears only indirectly through examples such as intelligent tutoring, automated question generation, and professional training applications in medicine and biology, rather than as a directly synthesized focal outcome. The review does not report direct evidence that AI tools improve scientific reasoning for middle school students or provide effect estimates comparing AI with non-AI instruction.
finding.measure: Discussion of AI tutoring, question generation, and science/medical training applications

paper_profiles.title: Beyond Voice Recognition: Integrating Alexa’s Emotional Intelligence and ChatGPT’s Language Processing for EFL Learners’ Development and Anxiety Reduction - A Comparative Analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This mixed-methods study examined whether an emotionally intelligent AI language-learning system built on Amazon Alexa improves English speaking outcomes and reduces anxiety compared with a ChatGPT-based speaking support condition. The paper is motivated by a perceived gap in research on real-time, emotionally adaptive feedback in language learning, especially for speaking practice where anxiety and confidence can strongly shape performance.

The study involved 40 Iranian high school students (ages 15–18) in Varamin, Iran, who were screened for intermediate English proficiency and then assigned to an experimental group using Amazon Alexa-Speak (n=20) or a control group using ChatGPT 3.5 (n=20). Over eight weekly sessions, both groups practiced speaking through AI-mediated activities, but the Alexa condition added emotional-state detection and emotionally calibrated feedback. Quantitative data came from pre/post speaking assessments and a perception questionnaire, while qualitative data came from semi-structured interviews and classroom observations.

Results indicated that the Alexa-based intervention outperformed the ChatGPT condition on speaking performance, with a significant group effect (F(1,38)=24.63, p<0.05) and a reported effect size of η²=0.42. The paper also reports 94% accuracy for Alexa’s emotional state detection and qualitative evidence suggesting improved confidence and reduced anxiety. The authors conclude that emotionally intelligent AI may be especially useful for supporting oral language learning by combining linguistic feedback with affective support, though the study is limited by its small sample, short duration, and focus on one high-school EFL context.

finding.finding_summary: The Alexa-Speak condition produced significantly better speaking performance than the ChatGPT condition after eight sessions. The paper reports a group effect of F(1,38)=24.63, p<0.05 with η²=0.42 on speaking performance measures that included pronunciation accuracy, fluency, and overall speaking quality.
finding.measure: TOEFL speaking test / researcher-developed speaking assessment focusing on pronunciation accuracy, fluency, grammar, vocabulary, and discourse coherence

finding.finding_summary: The intervention was designed to reduce speaking anxiety and improve emotional regulation, and the study reports qualitative and questionnaire evidence consistent with that goal. Alexa’s emotional-state recognition was reported at 94% accuracy, and participants described greater confidence, less anxiety, and better stress management during speaking tasks, although no separate quantitative anxiety effect size was provided.
finding.measure: Perception questionnaire, semi-structured interviews, and classroom observation checklists addressing anxiety, stress management, and confidence

paper_profiles.title: The impact of generative artificial intelligence on socioeconomic inequalities and policy making
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an interdisciplinary perspective/review on how generative AI may affect socioeconomic inequality across information, work, education, healthcare, and policy domains. Rather than testing a single intervention, it synthesizes prior research and uses those findings to identify likely benefits, risks, and future research directions, with a particular focus on whether generative AI will amplify or reduce existing inequalities.

In education, the paper argues that generative AI can support personalized learning, feedback, writing support, and concept understanding, but it may also widen gaps in access, reinforce bias, and increase teacher workload. The education discussion is largely conceptual and literature-based, with illustrative examples of AI tutors, personalized feedback in writing, and proposed future studies on science curricula and prompt/critical-thinking skills.

The paper does not present original empirical data on U.S. middle school science learning or scientific reasoning. Its most relevant adjacent evidence is a proposed future research direction suggesting that integrating generative AI into science curricula could improve students' understanding of complex concepts, while warning that over-reliance may hinder independent critical thinking. Overall, the paper concludes that generative AI has real promise for education but that outcomes will depend heavily on implementation, access, and safeguards.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not report original empirical evidence on scientific reasoning; instead, it cites prior work and proposes future research in which generative AI would be embedded in science classes to compare concept understanding against classes without AI tools. The authors argue that AI may enhance understanding through personalized learning, but over-reliance could undermine independent critical thinking; no effect size, sample size, or confidence interval is reported.
finding.measure: students' performance on concept understanding in science curricula

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses adjacent evidence that generative AI can improve writing support and proposes a future study on personalized AI feedback in essay writing. It summarizes prior work suggesting AI-assisted writing can improve writing proficiency and quality, but this article itself reports no original effect estimates; no sample size, effect size, or confidence interval is provided.
finding.measure: writing proficiency / essay writing quality

finding.finding_summary: A central argument is that generative AI may strengthen higher-order skills such as critical thinking, prompt engineering, and fact-checking if used intentionally, but it may also weaken independent thinking if students rely on it mechanically. The paper cites descriptive evidence that many students lack website-evaluation skills and frames AI use as a prompt to teach critical judgment; no original quantitative results are reported.
finding.measure: critical thinking, prompt engineering, fact-checking skills

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI can reduce teacher workload and lesson-planning time, and that AI-based feedback systems can provide more immediate support than standard teacher feedback. These claims are based on synthesis and proposed future research rather than new data in this paper; therefore, no sample size, effect size, or confidence interval is reported.
finding.measure: teacher preparation time / feedback delivery efficiency

paper_profiles.title: A scoping survey of ChatGPT in mathematics education
paper_profiles.population: Mixed (primary, secondary, tertiary; general education, with emphasis on mathematics education)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a scoping review and editorial on the emerging literature about ChatGPT in mathematics education. The authors ask what benefits and challenges arise when teachers and students interact with ChatGPT, with a particular focus on how the tool is being used across educational levels and mathematical content areas.

The paper synthesizes about 50 papers identified from Google Scholar, Web of Science, arXiv, HAL, conference proceedings, and books published between November 2022 and May 2024. Rather than evaluating one intervention, it maps themes across the literature, including content-area use, lesson planning, assessment, personalized learning, critical thinking, collaboration, and attitudes toward ChatGPT. Reported studies suggest that ChatGPT can support lesson planning, generate feedback and practice problems, and provide personalized explanations, but it often lacks deep mathematical understanding and may produce inaccurate or misleading responses.

Across the reviewed literature, the strongest recurring conclusion is that ChatGPT is best treated as a supplementary tool rather than a replacement for teachers or human tutors. The review highlights benefits such as faster lesson planning, immediate feedback, and possible support for self-regulated learning and collaborative work, but also emphasizes limitations including hallucinations, weak performance on harder tasks, and risks of over-reliance, bias, and reduced critical thinking. Because this is a scoping survey, it does not provide a single pooled effect estimate; instead, it offers a thematic map of early evidence and identifies the need for more rigorous studies, especially on actual classroom learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that ChatGPT can assist with some mathematical tasks, but performance is highly task-dependent. Across the cited studies, chatbots were accurate on straightforward arithmetic, algebraic expressions, and some knowledge-level questions, yet they struggled on more complex problems, with one study reporting performance dropping from 82% to 10% as difficulty increased and another noting GPT-4 was useful at undergraduate level but failed on graduate-level difficulty.
finding.measure: Accuracy/performance on mathematical problems, problem-solving tasks, geometry, algebra, calculus, statistics, and proof tasks

finding.finding_summary: The review reports potential gains in critical thinking, planning, and reflective reasoning, but also recurring concerns that heavy use of ChatGPT may weaken higher-order thinking if students accept outputs uncritically. Some studies described benefits for proof refinement, reflective lesson planning, and open-ended dialogue, while others warned about misinformation, confusing feedback, and reduced critical engagement.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, reflective thinking, reasoning, planning/reflection skills, and collaborative problem-solving

finding.finding_summary: Several reviewed studies suggest ChatGPT can support motivation, engagement, and self-regulated learning through immediate guidance, personalized explanations, and interactive dialogue. In the cited programming and mathematics-related studies, users reported higher motivation and more positive attitudes toward the learning experience, although the review also notes a risk of over-reliance.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, self-regulated learning, and attitudes toward learning with ChatGPT

finding.finding_summary: A major theme in the review is that ChatGPT can reduce teacher workload by helping with lesson planning, generating instructional materials, creating quizzes and practice problems, and supporting feedback and grading. The reviewed studies consistently frame this as a practical efficiency gain, though they also emphasize the need for human oversight because the generated materials may not always be pedagogically sound.
finding.measure: Lesson-plan generation, automated feedback, task generation, and assessment support

paper_profiles.title: DeBiasMe: De-biasing Human-AI Interactions with Metacognitive AIED (AI in Education) Interventions
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of Workshop: AI Augmented Reasoning (CHI ’25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper addresses a conceptual and design problem in AI-in-education: how to help learners use generative AI in ways that reduce cognitive biases rather than amplify them. The author argues that most current AI literacy tools emphasize technical or algorithmic bias, while giving too little attention to human biases such as anchoring, confirmation bias, and automation bias during AI use. The paper’s central question is how metacognitive supports can be built into AI interactions so that students become active, reflective collaborators rather than passive consumers of AI output.

The paper proposes DeBiasMe, a metacognitive AI literacy intervention for university students. The design includes two main components: a prompt refinement tool that provides friction and feedback before submission, and a bias visualization map that helps users interpret AI outputs after generation. These features are framed within a bi-directional human-AI interaction model that targets both the input and output stages of use, with adaptive scaffolding for different trust levels and engagement patterns.

Empirically, the paper does not report a controlled study of learning outcomes or a direct evaluation of scientific reasoning. Instead, it draws on initial mixed-methods user research with university students (surveys and interviews) to identify metacognitive support needs, and it references earlier prototype evaluation using usability heuristics, think-aloud studies, and expert reviews. The main conclusion is that bias-aware, friction-based AI literacy tools may support metacognition, critical thinking, and responsible AI use, but the paper remains a design/position contribution rather than outcome evidence.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the proposed DeBiasMe intervention can support metacognitive awareness and critical engagement with AI by making biases explicit at both prompt formulation and output interpretation stages. However, this is a conceptual/position paper: it reports no controlled effect estimate, and the only empirical basis mentioned is initial mixed-methods user research with university students plus earlier prototype usability reviews, not learning-outcome measurement.
finding.measure: Metacognitive support needs, bias awareness, critical thinking during AI interactions

paper_profiles.title: VLM@school – Evaluation of AI image understanding on German middle school knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents VLM@school, a benchmark for evaluating vision-language models on German middle-school–level questions that require combining image understanding with subject-matter knowledge. The dataset contains 486 images and 2,038 open-ended questions across nine school subjects (including biology, physics, geography, history, math, arts, music, religion, and sports), with many items designed to be answerable only if the model truly integrates visual cues and background knowledge rather than relying on text-only shortcuts.

The study does not test an AI instructional intervention in classrooms; instead, it evaluates thirteen open-weight VLMs on benchmark performance. Models were scored with a panel-of-LLMs judging approach, and the authors also examined adversarial questions that intentionally ask about objects or concepts not present in the image to test whether models can abstain or say “no.”

The main conclusion is that even strong current VLMs perform poorly on these middle-school tasks: the best overall score is under 45%, with particularly weak performance on music, math, and adversarial items. Performance varies by model family and size, with some medium-sized models (notably Qwen2.5 VL 32B and Mistral small 3.1) outperforming larger InternVL3 models on this benchmark. The paper argues that benchmark scores from popular multimodal datasets do not necessarily transfer to this more realistic, German-language, curriculum-grounded setting.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates VLMs on curriculum-grounded school-subject questions across nine domains and finds that the models often struggle on these tasks. Overall accuracy remained below 45% for the best model (n=2,038 questions on 486 images), with particularly weak performance in several non-science subjects such as music, history, arts, and religion.
finding.measure: Open-ended benchmark accuracy on German middle-school subject questions

finding.finding_summary: Math performance was notably weak relative to other domains. The best scores in math were around 34%, and the paper reports that models often failed on geometry, counting, and formula-selection tasks even when the arithmetic itself was simple and human-solvable.
finding.measure: Accuracy on math questions involving geometry, counting, and calculation from images

finding.finding_summary: The biology and physics items required visual interpretation plus background knowledge, but model performance was inconsistent and often poor. The best scores were about 46% in biology and 48% in physics, and the discussion notes frequent failures on explanation-oriented physics questions and on biology items requiring correct mapping of labels/colors to structures.
finding.measure: Accuracy on biology and physics questions requiring visual reasoning and subject knowledge
finding.study_size: n=169 biology questions; n=234 physics questions

finding.finding_summary: A major theme is whether models can reason robustly rather than exploit superficial cues. The authors conclude that current models often fail at this kind of integrated reasoning, especially on adversarial questions and on items requiring explanation, reverse lookup, or disambiguation from visual context alone.
finding.measure: Accuracy on adversarial and reasoning-heavy benchmark items

paper_profiles.title: The Denario project: Deep knowledge AI agents for scientific discovery
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces Denario, a modular AI multi-agent system intended to act as a scientific research assistant. The system can generate research ideas, check literature for novelty, develop methods, implement analyses, write papers, and review drafts, using multiple large language models and agent-orchestration frameworks.

The paper is primarily a system description and demonstration paper rather than an educational intervention study. The authors showcase Denario on example projects across several scientific domains, including astrophysics, biology, chemistry, medicine, neuroscience, and materials science, and report domain-expert feedback on AI-generated papers. They also discuss observed failure modes, implementation tradeoffs, limitations, and ethical/philosophical implications of AI-driven research.

For the purposes of this extraction, the paper does not provide direct empirical evidence about K-12 science learning or scientific reasoning outcomes for students. Its relevance is adjacent: it concerns AI tools for research production, not instruction or student learning, and the evidence presented is descriptive rather than comparative or outcome-based.

paper_profiles.title: Exclusive photoproduction of π0 up to large values of Mandelstam variables s, t and u with CLAS
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reports a high-statistics measurement of the exclusive photoproduction reaction γp → pπ0 using the CLAS detector at Jefferson Lab. The study was motivated by longstanding questions in hadronic physics about how π0 production behaves across the nucleon-resonance, Regge, and hard-scattering regimes, especially at large Mandelstam variables s, t, and u where theory predictions diverge.

The authors used a tagged photon beam from a 5.72 GeV electron beam and reconstructed π0 events through the Dalitz decay channel π0 → e+e−γ (or external conversion to the same final state). This approach allowed them to obtain a precise differential cross-section data set over Eγ = 1.275–5.425 GeV and a wide angular range, quadrupling the world database above 2 GeV and extending coverage into previously sparsely measured kinematics.

The main conclusions are that the measured cross sections at mid-to-large angles scale approximately as s^−6.89±0.26, consistent with the pQCD quark-counting expectation of s^−7, while Regge-based models describe the overall data better than the handbag/GPD-based model, which underestimates the cross sections by orders of magnitude at the highest energies. The paper does not study education or AI; it is included only because the retrieved set was broad and the paper is unrelated to the education sub-question.

paper_profiles.title: Promoting Real-Time Reflection in Synchronous Communication with Generative AI
paper_profiles.venue: ACM Workshop on Human-AI Interaction for Augmented Reasoning (AIREASONING-2025-01)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines how real-time reflection can be supported in synchronous communication using Generative AI. The authors review recent systems across meeting, lecture, presentation, and practice-talk settings and organize them by how they support reflection: increasing contextual awareness or evaluating performance and providing suggestions.

The paper does not test a new educational intervention with students. Instead, it synthesizes 11 recent systems and proposes design implications for human-AI interaction, including the use of proactive notifications, continuous displays, lightweight explanations, and context-sensitive role-play agents. In educational contexts, the discussion highlights tools such as EduLive, Glancee, and TutorUp as examples of supporting instructors or tutors in real time.

The main conclusion is that Generative AI can extend prior non-generative approaches by producing nuanced summaries, simulated audience feedback, and expert-like suggestions during live communication. However, the paper emphasizes limitations around interpretability, workflow disruption, and the quality of persona/context grounding for role-playing agents. Evidence about learning outcomes is indirect and descriptive rather than empirical, and the paper provides design guidance rather than effect estimates.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that Generative AI can reduce user workload in synchronous communication by proactively summarizing conversations, tracking agendas, and providing timely feedback or suggestions. However, it also notes risks of interruption, extra cognitive load, and workflow disruption when the interaction design is poorly matched to the task.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The review positions real-time reflection as supporting metacognition and communication strategy adjustment during ongoing interaction. It suggests that AI-generated summaries, audience-feedback simulations, and expert-like prompts can help users better monitor their performance and adapt behavior in the moment, but this is design-level evidence rather than a measured effect.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing Critical Thinking with AI: A Tailored Warning System for RAG Models
paper_profiles.venue: ACM Workshop on Human-AI Interaction for Augmented Reasoning (AIREASONING-2025-01)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how user-facing warnings affect reasoning in a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) educational question-answering task. The authors argue that while RAG systems can improve reliability by grounding answers in retrieved evidence, hallucinations and biased generation can still mislead users, especially in learning contexts. To address this, they propose a tailored warning system that generates context-specific alerts about potential hallucinations at both the retrieval and generation stages.

The study reports a pilot experiment using an AP U.S. history textbook database and an LLM-based quiz interface. Eighteen participants answered 18 multiple-choice questions that included correct answers, low-level hallucinations, and high-level hallucinations. Participants were split into no-warning, standard-warning, and tailored-warning conditions. The tailored warnings were designed to be specific to the detected problem in the model output, while the standard warning mirrored a generic ChatGPT-style disclaimer.

Results suggest tailored warnings improved answer accuracy and hallucination detection relative to both standard warnings and no warnings. Accuracy was highest in the tailored-warning group across all hallucination levels, and an ANOVA test indicated statistically significant differences across groups (p=0.006162). However, the authors also report a tradeoff: tailored warnings sometimes increased cognitive friction, confusion, and reduced ease of use, even as they improved trust calibration and awareness. The paper is best understood as a small pilot study with qualitative feedback and quantitative outcomes, intended to motivate future work on designing warnings that support reflective AI use rather than passive acceptance.

finding.finding_summary: Tailored warnings improved participants’ critical evaluation of AI-generated answers in a history quiz task. Across 18 participants (n=18), the tailored-warning group achieved higher accuracy than the standard-warning and no-warning groups, including 81% accuracy on high-level hallucination items versus 69% and 56%, respectively; the authors report a statistically significant overall group difference (ANOVA p=0.006162).
finding.measure: Multiple-choice accuracy on an AI-assisted question-answering quiz with correct, low-level hallucination, and high-level hallucination responses

finding.finding_summary: The intervention was tested in a textbook-based U.S. history Q&A setting rather than in a STEM domain. In the pilot with 18 participants, tailored warnings led to better performance on AP U.S. history quiz questions, especially when the system output contained biased or incorrect information, suggesting improved handling of subject-matter content in history learning contexts.
finding.measure: Accuracy on AP U.S. history multiple-choice questions answered with RAG-generated responses

finding.finding_summary: Warnings had a tradeoff effect on user experience and trust. Although tailored warnings increased trust relative to the other conditions by about 0.67 points on a 5-point Likert scale, participants also reported confusion and lower ease of use in the warning conditions, suggesting improved awareness but some cognitive friction.
finding.measure: Self-reported trust and ease-of-use ratings; qualitative interview feedback

paper_profiles.title: International Scientific Report on the Safety of Advanced AI: Interim Report
paper_profiles.venue: International Scientific Report on the Safety of Advanced AI (Interim Report)
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (policy/scientific synthesis; no study population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This interim report synthesizes the state of scientific understanding on advanced general-purpose AI, with a primary focus on safety, risks, and technical methods for assessing and mitigating those risks.
