The authors frame the problem as one of identifying high-performing researchers before their performance becomes widely visible, for uses such as recruitment, collaboration, networking, and funding decisions.

The study uses bibliometric data on AI-related publications from Scopus (2000–2019), combined with journal ranking data from SCImago, to construct features about publication productivity, citations, disciplinary diversity, gender and ethnicity, affiliation diversity, and co-authorship network structure. The analytical sample for prediction includes junior researchers whose first publication occurred between 2006 and 2010, with the task defined as predicting whether their h-index growth would classify them as rising stars over the first 10 years of their careers. Several classifiers were tested, and random forest performed best (AUC = 0.75).

The main conclusion is that early-career publication volume, citation count, disciplinary diversity, and network position are useful for distinguishing future rising stars from non-rising researchers. The authors also report that gender and ethnic diversity in collaboration are associated with collaboration structure and career development, although the paper is not an intervention study and does not examine student learning outcomes. Overall, it is a scientometrics / machine-learning paper about research careers in AI rather than an education intervention study.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that machine-learning-based prediction of rising AI scientists can support recruitment, collaboration, and funding decisions by identifying promising researchers earlier in their careers. The best model was random forest with AUC = 0.75, suggesting moderate predictive utility for institutional decision-making, but this is about researcher identification rather than educational outcomes.
finding.measure: Predictive classification performance for rising-star scientists (AUC; F1)
finding.study_size: n=9,391 authors for labeled junior-researcher analysis; train n=7,311, test n=2,313

paper_profiles.title: Generalizing Machine Learning Evaluation through the Integration of Shannon Entropy and Rough Set Theory
paper_profiles.venue: COLINS-2024: 8th International Conference on Computational Linguistics and Intelligent Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to evaluate machine learning models beyond standard predictive metrics such as accuracy. The authors propose combining Shannon entropy with rough set theory to create a broader evaluation framework that captures information uncertainty, data granularity, and model interpretability.

The approach is methodological rather than educational: it is presented as a general machine learning evaluation tool and tested on benchmark datasets including Titanic and Microsoft Malware Detection. The paper describes preprocessing, granulation, entropy calculations, and comparisons across several models (Decision Tree, Random Forest, Logistic Regression, and KNN), but it does not study students, teachers, schools, or any educational intervention.

The main conclusion is that integrating entropy with rough set theory can provide additional insight into how models behave as data complexity changes, and may help identify more robust hyperparameter configurations than traditional metrics alone. The reported findings suggest the framework can distinguish between configurations with similar accuracy by considering interpretability, generalization, and alignment with underlying data structure. However, the paper is primarily conceptual/technical and does not report a K-12 or education-focused application.

paper_profiles.title: Argumentation and Machine Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter surveys research that combines computational argumentation and machine learning (ML). It is organized around two main directions: using argumentation to improve or explain ML systems, and using ML to support argumentation. The review synthesizes a large body of work across supervised learning, reinforcement learning, and explainable AI, and classifies the ways the two paradigms interact as synergistic, segmented, or approximated.

On the argumentation-for-ML side, the paper reviews methods that inject expert knowledge, resolve classification conflicts, improve RL policies, and generate explanations for black-box models using abstract, structured, bipolar, value-based, and probabilistic argumentation frameworks. On the ML-for-argumentation side, it covers approaches that learn argumentation frameworks from data, compute acceptance statuses with graph neural networks, and use ML to approximate or explain argumentation-based reasoning. The chapter concludes that argumentation shows promise for both improving inference and enhancing explainability, but most evidence comes from small-scale, technical studies; broader real-world validation, user studies, and scalable implementations remain limited.

paper_profiles.title: Artificial Intelligence-based Decision Support Systems for Precision and Digital Health
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a methodological survey of reinforcement learning (RL) methods in precision health and digital health. It explains the RL framework, value functions, and common approaches for learning dynamic treatment regimes (DTRs), including indirect methods such as Q-learning and deep Q-learning, and direct methods such as inverse probability weighting, outcome weighted learning, and V-learning.

The paper is not an empirical evaluation of an AI intervention in schooling or education. Instead, it synthesizes existing healthcare applications and uses two illustrative case studies from smoking cessation and physical activity to show how RL has been applied in practice. The population and context are primarily adult patients in healthcare and mHealth settings, with no direct study of middle school science learners or scientific reasoning outcomes.

The main conclusion is that RL and related AI approaches are promising for personalized decision support in sequential healthcare problems, especially when interventions must adapt over time. The authors argue that these methods can improve decision quality in dynamic treatment regimes and just-in-time adaptive interventions, while noting methodological challenges such as confounding, finite versus indefinite horizons, and the need for robust estimation procedures.

paper_profiles.title: EARLI 2025 — Program
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This document is the conference program for EARLI 2025 rather than a research paper reporting a study. It lists sessions, symposia, posters, roundtables, and demos across the conference schedule, including several sessions related to generative AI, digital tools, teacher education, and learning sciences.

Because it is a program document, it does not present a research question, intervention, sample, measures, or results in the way an empirical study would. The text provides only the titles, authors, and session formats for presentations, so no substantive intervention evidence on student-facing AI tools or scientific reasoning outcomes can be extracted from this source.

paper_profiles.title: DeBiasMe: De-biasing Human-AI Interactions with Metacognitive AIED (AI in Education) Interventions
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of Workshop: AI Augmented Reasoning (CHI ’25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper addresses a gap in AI literacy and human-AI interaction research: most educational AI tools focus on technical or algorithmic bias, while giving less attention to human cognitive biases such as anchoring, confirmation bias, and automation bias. The author argues that these biases can interact with systemic and statistical biases in AI systems, creating feedback loops that undermine critical thinking and learning.

To respond to this problem, the paper proposes DeBiasMe, a metacognitive AI literacy intervention for university students. The conceptual design uses deliberate friction, bi-directional intervention across both prompt formulation and response interpretation, and adaptive scaffolding to help students notice, reflect on, and mitigate bias during AI use. The paper describes an illustrative prototype and ongoing development work, including a prompt refinement tool and a bias visualization map, but it does not report a controlled study or quantitative outcomes.

The paper’s evidence base is primarily conceptual and design-oriented, informed by prior work, mixed-methods user research with university students, usability heuristics, think-aloud studies, and expert reviews of an earlier prototype version. Its main conclusion is that AI literacy tools should move beyond operational prompting skills and include metacognitive support for critical evaluation of AI-generated content. The paper positions this as a promising direction for learner-centered AIED, but it remains an early-stage position paper rather than an empirical intervention study.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that DeBiasMe is intended to improve students’ metacognitive awareness, critical thinking, and self-regulation during AI use by introducing deliberate friction at both the prompt and response stages. However, no controlled outcome data are reported; the claim is based on design rationale and an earlier prototype evaluation that qualitatively suggested the intervention could make implicit biases explicit and actionable.
finding.measure: Metacognitive awareness, critical thinking, and self-regulation during human-AI interaction

paper_profiles.title: VLM@school – Evaluation of AI image understanding on German middle school knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces VLM@school, a benchmark dataset for evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) on middle school-level tasks in German. The authors argue that existing multimodal benchmarks are overly English-centric, often rely on multiple-choice formats, and may not reflect real-world visual reasoning demands. To address this, they assemble 2,038 open-ended questions tied to 486 images drawn from German school textbooks and other educational materials across nine domains: arts, biology, geography, history, math, music, physics, religion, and sports.

The study is not an intervention with students; instead, it evaluates thirteen open-weight VLMs on benchmark tasks that combine image interpretation with subject knowledge. The models are tested on free-response questions, and the authors use a panel-of-LLMs judging scheme to score answers against ground truth. They also include adversarial questions that are intentionally unanswerable from the image to test whether models can refrain from hallucinating. The benchmark is designed around German native-speaker questions and answers to avoid machine-translation artifacts.

Results show that the benchmark is challenging: the best overall model reaches only 43.26% accuracy, with notably weak performance on math, music, and adversarial questions. The paper concludes that middle school-level, image-grounded tasks can expose limitations in current VLMs even when the tasks are below university level, and that performance on popular public benchmarks (like MMMU) does not reliably predict performance on this German, open-ended benchmark. The authors also suggest that reasoning-oriented prompting or step-by-step methods may improve performance, and that German-language multimodal evaluation remains an underexplored area.

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark includes 308 math questions on 112 images, and the best model reaches only 34.09% accuracy on math (Qwen2.5VL 32B), with several models much lower (e.g., Ovis2 4B at 9.09%). The authors report that models were better at calculation than at counting or extracting geometric information from diagrams, but overall performance remained weak.
finding.measure: Open-ended middle school math question accuracy on image-grounded tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates biology and physics questions that require interpreting diagrams, labels, and explanations, which are closely related to scientific reasoning. Performance was modest at best: for example, the top reported physics score was 47.65% (Qwen2.5VL 32B), and the discussion notes repeated failures on explanation-based physics items such as why stars become red giants or how circuit components affect light emission.
finding.measure: Open-ended biology and physics question accuracy on visual reasoning tasks
finding.study_size: n=169 biology questions on 33 images; n=234 physics questions on 52 images

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark substantively studies arts, geography, history, music, religion, and sports as standalone school-subject domains. Performance varied by domain but remained limited overall; for example, the best scores were around 54% in history and religion, while music was especially difficult, with best performance around 31% overall in that domain.
finding.measure: Open-ended accuracy across non-STEM school subjects (arts, geography, history, music, religion, sports)
finding.study_size: Arts n=286; Geography n=251; History n=264; Music n=166; Religion n=206; Sports n=154 questions

paper_profiles.title: Supporting Data-Frame Dynamics in AI-assisted Decision Making
paper_profiles.venue: ACM Workshop on Human-AI Interaction for Augmented Reasoning (AIREASONING-2025-01)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a human-AI decision support problem: current AI systems often provide static recommendations and explanations, but they do not adequately support the dynamic process by which people iteratively refine evidence and hypotheses during complex decision making. The authors ground their work in Klein et al.’s data-frame theory of sensemaking and Miller’s evaluative AI framework, arguing that decision support should help users actively construct, revise, and compare hypotheses rather than merely accept or reject a model output.

The paper proposes a mixed-initiative interaction framework in which both humans and AI can contribute to three sensemaking functions: evidence extraction, hypothesis retrieval, and hypothesis scoring. To illustrate the framework, the authors describe a proof-of-concept AI-assisted skin cancer diagnosis prototype built with a concept bottleneck model trained on the derm7pt dataset. The prototype lets users inspect extracted evidence, refine or annotate evidence, add or exclude hypotheses, and adjust how evidence supports or contradicts diagnoses.

The paper is primarily conceptual and design-oriented rather than an evaluation of learning or decision outcomes. The demonstration context is clinical decision making with adult users in a medical setting, not K-12 education. The authors conclude that mixed-initiative, data-frame-aware AI could reduce cognitive burden, reduce overreliance, and better align AI support with human reasoning, but they explicitly note that future studies with dermatologists are needed to evaluate effectiveness and tradeoffs.

paper_profiles.title: Designing AI Systems that Augment Human Performed vs. Demonstrated Critical Thinking
paper_profiles.venue: ACM Workshop on Human-AI Interaction for Augmented Reasoning (AIREASONING-2025-01)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper addresses a conceptual problem in research on generative AI and human cognition: studies often claim to measure improvements in critical thinking, but may actually be measuring the quality of outputs produced with AI assistance rather than independent critical thinking ability. The authors argue that this distinction matters because AI can improve what users demonstrate in a task without improving what they can perform on their own.

The paper proposes a framework separating "performed" critical thinking, meaning independent cognitive work without AI support, from "demonstrated" critical thinking, meaning reasoning that occurs through collaboration with AI. It reviews prior evaluation approaches, including standardized tests, open-ended assessments, and classroom dialogue, and argues that many GenAI studies focus on final outputs rather than independent reasoning. The paper does not report a new empirical intervention; instead, it synthesizes prior work and offers design guidance for future AI systems that should scaffold users toward stronger independent thinking rather than simply producing better outputs.

Although the discussion is broadly relevant to education, the paper is not a direct student intervention study and does not focus on a specific grade band or subject area. Its main contribution is conceptual: it calls for future research designs that explicitly assess both performed and demonstrated critical thinking, especially in educational contexts where long-term skill development and autonomy matter.

finding.finding_summary: This is a conceptual position paper rather than an empirical study, so it does not report new effect sizes or sample-based results. It argues that generative AI may improve demonstrated critical thinking in task outputs while leaving performed critical thinking unchanged or potentially reduced through overreliance, but this claim is based on interpretation of prior literature rather than original data.
finding.measure: Critical thinking conceptualization and prior-study evaluation approaches

paper_profiles.title: AI Conversational Tutors in Foreign Language Learning: A Mixed-Methods Evaluation Study
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings 14th Panhellenic Conference iCT in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the design and quality of AI conversational tutors for foreign language learning. The author asks what design patterns characterize current tools, how specialized language tutors compare with general-purpose voice-capable AI models, and how to evaluate tutor quality in a systematic way.

The study uses a mixed-methods approach with three phases. First, the author manually interacted with four specialized AI language-learning apps (talkio, talkpal, univerbal, and langua) using a Spanish learner profile and evaluated the user experience, conversational flow, correction behavior, and handling of breakdowns. Second, the author compared that experience with two general-purpose conversational AI tools, ChatGPT and Gemini, used in voice mode for the same Spanish role-play task. Third, the paper proposes a 10-dimensional transcript-based evaluation framework and applies it with five LLM-based evaluators to score six tutors on dimensions such as learning value, supportive style, coherence, tutor initiative, vocabulary richness, and feedback quality.

The main conclusion is that specialized and general-purpose AI conversational tools can both support language practice, but they differ substantially in feedback, interaction style, and transcript handling. Some specialized tutors provided richer corrective scaffolding and annotated transcripts, while ChatGPT scored highly on several transcript-based quality dimensions despite lacking some specialized features. The paper argues that future AI language tutors should better preserve interaction flow, handle communication breakdowns, provide clearer contextual feedback, and address privacy concerns around voice data storage.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies conversational practice and speaking interaction quality in AI foreign-language tutors. Across the four specialized tutors and two general-purpose voice agents, the author reports generally fluid dialogue and supportive conversational practice, but also substantial differences in correction quality, turn-taking, latency, and handling of unfinished utterances. No standardized learning gain was measured; evidence is based on observed interaction behavior, transcript features, and comparative user experience.
finding.measure: Conversational interaction quality, speaking practice flow, corrective feedback, transcript completeness

finding.finding_summary: The paper explicitly evaluates qualities such as critical thinking, coherence, and learner scaffolding in tutor dialogue, and the discussion highlights the role of AI tutors in prompting further reasoning. T4 and ChatGPT are described as supporting more reflective or follow-up questioning, while the framework includes tutor initiative and coherence as central criteria. However, no direct measure of student durable-skill gains was reported.
finding.measure: Transcript-based rubric dimensions related to critical thinking, coherence, and learner initiative

finding.finding_summary: The paper assesses supportive style, friendliness, encouragement, and warmth as major aspects of tutor quality. The specialized tutors and ChatGPT are described as generally supportive, with empathetic or encouraging responses and constructive handling of communication breakdowns, especially in T2 and T4. These findings concern interaction quality rather than measured changes in student motivation or persistence.
finding.measure: Transcript-based supportive style, empathy, encouragement, and interaction quality ratings

finding.finding_summary: The paper identifies privacy and governance concerns as a substantive issue, noting that none of the examined apps clearly requested consent for storing private voice data and that voice-data warnings/disclaimers were absent. The study proposes an evaluation framework and an automated process intended to support future research and design practice, implying institutional relevance for assessment standards and data-handling norms. No policy intervention or institutional outcome was directly measured.
finding.measure: Presence/absence of consent, privacy warnings, and evaluation-framework applicability

paper_profiles.title: Promoting Real-Time Reflection in Synchronous Communication with Generative AI
paper_profiles.venue: ACM Workshop on Human-AI Interaction for Augmented Reasoning (AIREASONING-2025-01)
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable / no human study population
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper asks how generative AI can support real-time reflection during synchronous communication, especially in contexts such as meetings, lectures, presentations, and practice talks. Rather than reporting a new empirical intervention, the paper reviews prior systems that help users reflect during ongoing interaction and extracts design patterns for how information is presented and when it is delivered.

The authors focus on interaction designs that increase contextual awareness or provide actionable suggestions, including audience feedback augmentation, audience-status aggregation, real-time conversation summaries, and expert-suggestion systems. They argue that generative AI expands these systems by enabling natural-language summaries, richer cross-modal interpretation, and role-play agents that can simulate audience members or experts.

Because the paper is a review and design-implications piece, it does not study a specific student population or report original outcome data. Its main conclusions are conceptual: generative AI may improve real-time reflection, but designers must address interpretability, timing/proactiveness, and the limitations of role-play agents to avoid confusion, overload, or unconvincing feedback.

paper_profiles.title: Reasoning in Neurosymbolic AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter/paper surveys the problem of reasoning in modern AI, arguing that current large language models are powerful but unreliable, difficult to control, and prone to hallucination or regurgitation. The authors position neurosymbolic AI as an alternative that combines statistical learning with formal symbolic reasoning, aiming for better reliability, interpretability, and constraint satisfaction.

The core technical contribution is an energy-based neurosymbolic framework called Logical Boltzmann Machines (LBM), which maps propositional logic formulae into restricted Boltzmann machines (RBMs). The paper describes how logical clauses can be translated into hidden-unit energy terms, then used for reasoning via Gibbs sampling or free-energy minimization, and for learning from data plus knowledge. It also reviews related neurosymbolic and logic-based neural approaches and discusses how LBM can enforce logical constraints such as fairness or safety.

The empirical content is not an education study and does not involve students, teachers, or classrooms. Instead, it reports experiments on logical reasoning and benchmark learning tasks, including satisfiability-style problems and comparisons against symbolic, neural, and other neurosymbolic systems. The main conclusion is that LBM can represent propositional logic soundly and solve some benchmark learning tasks competitively, but the work is presented as a technical AI chapter rather than an intervention study in K-12 education.

paper_profiles.title: Demonstrative and non-demonstrative reasoning by analogy
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a philosophical analysis of analogical reasoning, focusing on how analogy functions in both demonstrative reasoning (e.g., proof and corroboration) and non-demonstrative reasoning (e.g., conjecture and hypothesis generation). The author reviews major traditions in the literature on analogy, including similarity-based, relevance-based, and typicality-based accounts, and argues that none fully solve the Logical Problem of Analogy because genuine analogy is both ampliative and non-monotonic.

The paper uses mathematical and scientific examples, especially Euler’s treatment of the Mengoli problem, proof transfer in theorem proving, and multiple analogies in archaeology, to show how analogy can support both discovery and justification. It ultimately defends a heuristic conception of analogy: rather than trying to make analogy fully well-founded, the point is to use it as a productive, context-sensitive method for generating and refining hypotheses.

This is not an intervention study in K-12 education and does not study students, schools, or AI tools. It is a conceptual/philosophical paper aimed at understanding analogy as a form of reasoning in mathematics and science.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that analogy can support scientific reasoning both as a demonstrative tool for justification and as a non-demonstrative heuristic for generating conjectures and hypotheses. However, it also concludes that analogical inference cannot be made fully sound in general, because ampliative analogies are inherently risky and only locally valid.
finding.measure: Conceptual analysis of analogical reasoning in theorem proving, hypothesis corroboration, and scientific problem solving

paper_profiles.title: The Interspeech 2026 Audio Reasoning Challenge: Evaluating Reasoning Process Quality for Audio Reasoning Models and Agents
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces and analyzes the Interspeech 2026 Audio Reasoning Challenge, a shared-task benchmark designed to evaluate the quality of intermediate reasoning chains in large audio language models and audio agents. The central problem is that prior audio reasoning benchmarks mostly judged only final-answer accuracy, which can hide whether a model arrived at the answer through sound logic or spurious shortcuts. To address this, the authors propose MMAR-Rubrics, an instance-level rubric-based evaluation method that scores reasoning paths on factuality, logic, and completeness.

The challenge includes two tracks: a Single Model Track for end-to-end audio reasoning models and an Agent Track for systems that orchestrate tools such as ASR, separation, diarization, and spectrogram analysis. The paper reports results from 156 registered teams across 18 countries, with 23 teams in the Single Model preliminary submissions and 24 in the Agent Track, and later final leaderboard results for 14 and 16 teams respectively. Across both tracks, agentic systems generally outperformed end-to-end models on reasoning quality, while top single models narrowed the gap through reinforcement learning, data pipeline improvements, and attention manipulation.

This is not an education intervention study and does not involve students, schools, or scientific reasoning instruction. Instead, it is a benchmark/challenge paper focused on evaluation methodology for audio AI systems. Its main conclusion is that instance-level rubrics are more reliable and better aligned with human judgments than system-level scoring, and that agent-based audio reasoning systems currently produce stronger, more transparent reasoning traces than single-model systems.

paper_profiles.title: ChaosBench-Logic: A Benchmark for Logical and Symbolic Reasoning on Chaotic Dynamical Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces CHAOSBENCH-LOGIC, a benchmark designed to evaluate large language models (LLMs) on logical and symbolic reasoning about chaotic dynamical systems. The core problem is that LLMs often confuse scientific concepts such as chaos, randomness, determinism, and nonlinearity, especially when reasoning requires multi-step inference or consistency across turns.

The benchmark contains 621 questions spanning 30 dynamical systems and seven task families, including atomic QA, multi-hop implication reasoning, analogies, counterfactuals, bias probes, dialogues, and compositional questions. It uses a shared first-order logic ontology with 11 predicates and a global axiom system to ensure questions are answerable from curated labels rather than numerical simulation.

The paper evaluates frontier and open-source LLMs, including GPT-4, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 2.5 Flash, and LLaMA-3 70B. Results show high single-item accuracy (about 91–94%) but much weaker dialogue-level coherence (about 53–76%), and all models score 0% on compositional items. The main conclusion is that current LLMs can often answer isolated scientific reasoning questions correctly but remain brittle when they must maintain globally consistent beliefs or avoid invalid converse inferences.

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark directly tests scientific reasoning in the domain of chaotic dynamical systems, especially logical consistency, implication directionality, and resistance to misconceptions such as chaos=randomness. Frontier and open-source LLMs achieved high per-item accuracy (91–94%; e.g., GPT-4 zeroshot 94.0%, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 91.6%, Gemini 2.5 Flash 91.9%, LLaMA-3 70B 91.6%) but failed completely on compositional items (0.0%) and showed substantially lower dialogue-level coherence (53.1% to 75.5%).
finding.measure: Logical accuracy, dialogue accuracy, compositional reasoning accuracy on CHAOSBENCH-LOGIC

paper_profiles.title: A Review on Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (narrative review of education research; no single study population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative review of artificial intelligence (AI) applications in education. It surveys broad categories of AI use, including adaptive learning, teaching evaluation, virtual classrooms, smart campuses, and intelligent tutoring robots, and discusses both benefits and challenges of AI-enabled education systems.

The article does not report a new empirical study or original intervention. Instead, it synthesizes prior literature and examples from K-12, higher education, language learning, assessment, and campus management, with examples drawn mainly from China, the United States, and other international contexts. The authors argue that AI can improve personalized instruction, assessment efficiency, classroom monitoring, and resource allocation, while also raising concerns about equity, ethics, teacher readiness, and student self-regulation.

For the sub-area of assessment and classroom monitoring, the review highlights tools such as ALEKS, E-rater, and face-recognition-based classroom/attendance systems. However, these are presented as examples from prior studies rather than as findings from this paper itself. The paper’s main conclusion is that AI has substantial promise for improving teaching and learning, but its educational value depends on careful implementation, teacher support, and attention to privacy, fairness, and infrastructure constraints.

finding.finding_summary: The review cites one U.S. middle school study of ALEKS showing a statistically significant positive impact on end-of-year mathematics scores. No effect size, confidence interval, or standard deviation is reported in the review, and the exact sample size of the original Yilmaz (2018) study is not given here.
finding.measure: End-of-year mathematics scores

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI-based assessment tools improve teacher efficiency by automating grading, scoring, and test-paper analysis. Examples include E-rater for essay scoring and AI-supported correction of assignments and exams, which are described as saving teachers time and reducing fatigue, but the review does not provide a single pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Teacher assessment workload / grading efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The review summarizes prior work on AI-supported English learning and spoken-language assessment, including speech recognition, oral practice, and automated speaking evaluation (e.g. SpeechRater). It reports that such tools can improve pronunciation practice and spoken English assessment, but provides no direct effect size and no single underlying sample size in the review text.
finding.measure: Oral English practice, pronunciation correction, spoken English assessment

paper_profiles.title: Anticipating and Preparing for Emerging Skills and Jobs: Key Issues, Concerns, and Prospects
paper_profiles.venue: Education in the Asia-Pacific Region: Issues, Concerns and Prospects
paper_profiles.population: K-12, TVET, Higher Education (primarily Asia-Pacific policy and practice context)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter is an introductory overview for an edited volume on how education and training systems should respond to emerging skills needs in the era of the Fourth Industrial Revolution. It argues that automation, globalization, and digital disruption are changing the nature of work, producing both new opportunities and serious skill mismatches, while many education systems continue to struggle with a learning crisis and weak alignment to labor market demands.

The chapter does not evaluate a single intervention; rather, it synthesizes themes and frames the book’s chapters around the need for foundational skills, vocational relevance, lifelong learning, and more future-oriented curricula. It highlights the potential of technology, including online learning and artificial intelligence, for continuous assessment, personalized learning, labor market intelligence, and better feedback, while stressing equity, teacher readiness, and cross-sector collaboration.

The context is broad Asia-Pacific education and workforce development, spanning kindergarten through grade 12, TVET, and higher education. The main conclusion is that education systems must be transformed to better support employability, adaptability, and lifelong learning in a rapidly changing economy, but the chapter itself provides conceptual and policy-oriented arguments rather than empirical tests of those claims.

finding.finding_summary: The chapter argues that education and training systems need substantial transformation to align with the Fourth Industrial Revolution, reduce skills mismatches, and improve employability. It frames AI, online learning, and partnerships as promising system-level tools, but provides no original empirical estimate, sample, or intervention effect.
finding.measure: Policy and system-level arguments about education and training reform; no quantitative measure reported

paper_profiles.title: The AIR and Apt-AIR Frameworks of Epistemic Performance and Growth: Reflections on Educational Theory Development
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a theory-development and reflection article, not an empirical intervention study. It revisits the authors’ AIR framework of epistemic thinking and the later Apt-AIR framework of epistemic performance, explaining how these models were developed to address educational problems such as students’ inquiry, argumentation, fact-checking, and model-based reasoning.

The paper emphasizes that epistemic education should help learners engage with valuable epistemic aims, use appropriate epistemic ideals, and apply reliable processes, while also developing the five aspects of fully apt epistemic performance: cognitive engagement, adaptive performance, metacognitive regulation/understanding, caring and enjoyment, and participation with others. The authors connect these frameworks to philosophy, metacognition, motivation, collaborative learning, and instructional design, and they illustrate how design work and empirical studies across contexts have informed refinement of the theories.

The article does not report a new study with participants, nor does it test an AI assessment, monitoring, or feedback tool in U.S. middle school science. Instead, it synthesizes prior work, especially studies involving elementary, secondary, university, and teacher populations, and argues that the frameworks provide a useful structure for designing and analyzing epistemic instruction. Its main contribution is conceptual: clarifying the theoretical foundations and design implications of epistemic performance for education research.

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central focus is epistemic thinking/performance, including metacognitive regulation, adaptive use of criteria and strategies, and collaborative epistemic activity. It argues that learners can improve these durable skills through instruction and design, but it does not report a single new quantitative effect size in this article; instead it synthesizes prior evidence that students and teachers can develop and use epistemic aims, ideals, and processes across contexts.
finding.measure: Epistemic thinking, metacognitive regulation, adaptive judgment, and collaborative epistemic performance

paper_profiles.title: “I’ll take care of you,” said the robot: Reflecting upon the legal and ethical aspects of the use and development of social robots for therapy
paper_profiles.population: Children and adolescents with autism spectrum disorder and traumatic brain injury; therapy practitioners and policymakers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the legal, ethical, and governance challenges created by the growing use of social robots and AI systems in therapeutic settings. The authors argue that as robots become more common in therapy, they raise unresolved issues related to safety, privacy, data protection, user awareness, trust, emotional manipulation, and the long-term consequences of human-robot interaction.

The paper is not an intervention study; instead, it is a conceptual and policy-oriented analysis grounded in literature review and examples from therapeutic robotics projects the authors have worked on or discussed. Those examples include robots used in therapy for children with traumatic brain injury and autism spectrum disorder, including LEGO-based robotics and cloud robotics systems that support social interaction, collaboration, and monitoring across therapy and home contexts.

The authors conclude that existing laws and technical standards are too general to govern therapeutic robots adequately, especially because these systems combine hardware, software, cloud services, and social interaction. They propose broader governance tools such as robot impact assessments, shared repositories for policymaking, new design principles (non-isolation, inclusive care, accessibility, compliance by design), and binding codes of conduct for robotics engineers. The paper’s main contribution is normative and conceptual rather than empirical, and it calls for multidisciplinary and longitudinal research to understand both immediate and long-term effects of therapeutic AI and robots.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that therapeutic robots require new governance mechanisms because existing medical-device, safety, and privacy frameworks are too general or fragmented to address robot-specific risks. It proposes robot impact assessments, shared data repositories for policymaking, and binding codes of conduct as institutional responses, but reports no empirical evaluation of these proposals.
finding.measure: Legal and policy analysis of regulatory frameworks and proposed governance tools

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes therapeutic robots as tools that can monitor children on and off therapy, support therapists, and collect data through cloud robotics systems, potentially extending therapist capacity. However, these claims are presented as conceptual benefits and illustrative examples rather than measured outcomes, so no empirical estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of therapist support, monitoring, and data collection functions

finding.finding_summary: The paper states that robot-based activities in ASD and TBI contexts are intended to elicit social behavior, foster social skills, and support collaboration and engagement, especially through LEGO robotics and socially assistive robots. These effects are described from prior projects and literature rather than as newly tested outcomes in this paper, so no quantitative effect size is provided.
finding.measure: Social skills, collaboration, joint attention, and social behavior in therapy contexts

paper_profiles.title: VLM@school – Evaluation of AI image understanding on German middle school knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces VLM@school, a benchmark for evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) on German middle-school curricular content. The authors argue that existing multimodal benchmarks overemphasize English, multiple-choice formats, and decontextualized tasks, making them less representative of real classroom-relevant reasoning. To address this, they build a dataset of 486 images and 2,038 open-ended questions spanning nine school subjects, including math, biology, physics, geography, history, arts, music, religion, and sports.

The study evaluates thirteen open-weight VLMs on the benchmark using automated LLM-as-a-judge scoring. The core finding is that even strong contemporary models struggle substantially: the best overall accuracy is under 45%, and adversarial questions that require the model to recognize when an answer is not supported by the image are answered especially poorly. Performance varies by domain, with relatively stronger results in history and religion and weaker results in math and music. The paper concludes that middle-school-level, German-language, open-ended visual reasoning tasks remain challenging for current VLMs and that benchmark performance on public datasets does not necessarily transfer to this more realistic setting.

This paper is not an intervention study in schools and does not examine student learning or teacher use directly. Its relevance to education research is as a benchmark/evaluation study for AI systems that could be used in educational settings, especially for subject-specific visual reasoning and feedback tasks.

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark shows that current VLMs struggle substantially with middle-school math tasks. The best model reached only 34.09% on math (Qwen2.5VL 32B), while several models were near or below 30%, indicating that even visually grounded, curriculum-aligned mathematical reasoning remains difficult for these systems.
finding.measure: Accuracy on open-ended middle-school math questions requiring visual reasoning and basic calculations

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes biology and physics as core curriculum domains and shows modest-to-poor performance on both. For example, biology accuracy ranged up to 48.53% and physics up to 47.65% on the best models, with many failures on explanation-based items and diagram interpretation, suggesting that scientific reasoning grounded in images is still weak.
finding.measure: Accuracy on open-ended biology and physics questions requiring diagram interpretation, background knowledge, and explanation
finding.study_size: biology n=169 questions; physics n=234 questions

finding.finding_summary: Across the nine-subject benchmark, the strongest models still achieved less than 45% overall accuracy, with domain scores varying widely. Performance was especially low in music (best 31.03%) and also limited in arts, geography, history, religion, and sports, indicating that broader curriculum-related multimodal understanding remains challenging.
finding.measure: Overall and domain-specific accuracy on open-ended German middle-school curriculum questions

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper is whether models can reason robustly rather than rely on shallow cues, especially on adversarial questions and open-ended prompts. Results show that models often fail to indicate uncertainty or reject unanswerable items, with adversarial accuracy far below overall accuracy (e.g., best overall adversarial score 32.83%), reflecting weak metacognitive-like behavior and limited contextual reasoning.
finding.measure: Accuracy on adversarial/unanswerable questions and open-ended reasoning performance
finding.study_size: adversarial subset size not_reported; overall dataset n=2038 questions

finding.finding_summary: Literacy is not a substantive focus of the paper, but the benchmark does include German-language question answering and model sensitivity to textual hints. The paper does not report dedicated reading or writing outcomes, so there is no direct evidence of impact on literacy outcomes beyond the language-mediated evaluation setting.
finding.measure: German-language question answering and reading of embedded text in images

paper_profiles.title: AI for Open Science: A Multi-Agent Perspective for Ethically Translating Data to Knowledge
paper_profiles.venue: NeurIPS 2023 AI for Science Workshop (arXiv preprint)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues that AI for Science systems, especially self-driving labs and other discovery-support tools, raise important ethical and organizational questions about openness in scientific knowledge production. The authors contend that while AI can accelerate discovery, closed systems may impede collaboration, limit dissemination, and amplify inequities by restricting who can access AI-derived knowledge.

To address this, the paper proposes a conceptual framework called AI for Open Science (AI4OS), modeled as a Multi-agent Discovery Support System (MaDiSS). The framework formalizes three roles in the knowledge-translation pipeline: experimenting, data mining, and labeling, and emphasizes that provenance, assumptions, and confidence information should be passed across roles to support accurate downstream interpretation.

The paper is theoretical rather than empirical. It develops a formal language grounded in Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (KDD), proposes a monotonic openness metric intended to maximize correct knowledge translation and minimize false knowledge, and offers an ethical argument for transparent, collaborative AI systems in science. Although the discussion briefly mentions broader societal implications, including education, the paper does not study schools, teachers, or students empirically and does not evaluate any educational intervention.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that openness in AI for Science should improve institutional knowledge translation by ensuring provenance, assumptions, and confidence scores are shared across collaborating agents. It presents a theoretical openness metric (Equation 4) and claims that more complete upstream information should monotonically increase knowledge aligned with ground truth and decrease false knowledge, but no empirical test or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Theoretical openness/knowledge-translation metric and conceptual provenance flow across multi-agent scientific systems

paper_profiles.title: A Review of Generative AI in Computer Science Education: Challenges and Opportunities in Accuracy, Authenticity, and Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews recent literature on generative AI in computer science education, focusing on three recurring issues: accuracy, authenticity, and assessment. The authors synthesize 52 papers published from 2019 to 2024 and organize the discussion around how tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, and GitHub Copilot affect learning, grading, feedback, authorship, and academic integrity.

The review argues that generative AI can improve efficiency, provide real-time feedback, and support creative work, but it also introduces substantial risks, including hallucinations, error propagation, bias, and blurred boundaries between AI-assisted and student-authored work. The paper concludes that effective use of GenAI in education depends on hybrid human-AI approaches, stronger bias-detection and assessment frameworks, and broader AI literacy for both students and educators. It emphasizes that human oversight remains essential, especially for complex or creative tasks that cannot be reliably evaluated by AI alone.

Although the paper is framed around computer science education rather than a specific school level or intervention study, it is primarily concerned with educational use cases in coding, assessment, and feedback. It does not present original experimental data; instead, it identifies gaps in the literature, especially the lack of longitudinal evidence on downstream effects of AI-generated inaccuracies and AI-driven assessments on student learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed literature, generative AI tools were consistently described as improving efficiency by automating routine grading and delivering timely, real-time feedback on programming tasks. The review notes that these tools can reduce educator workload in large classes, but no original effect estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Reported efficiency gains in grading and feedback; teacher workload

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that GenAI can support problem-solving and coding practice through iterative feedback, but it may also weaken critical thinking and independent problem-solving when students over-rely on AI-generated outputs. The paper does not provide original quantitative effects, but it repeatedly emphasizes the tension between AI assistance and deeper skill development.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, coding skill development

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on computer science education outcomes, especially coding accuracy, algorithm quality, and the evaluation of programming assignments. It concludes that GenAI can help students generate and troubleshoot code, but hallucinations, error propagation, and limited contextual understanding can reduce correctness and undermine learning in programming tasks.
finding.measure: Programming assignment correctness, code quality, algorithm generation, AI-generated feedback on coding tasks

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies substantial institutional implications, including the need for new assessment policies, hybrid human-AI evaluation models, AI-detection tools, and guidelines for ethical use. It argues that schools and universities must adapt governance and assessment practices to address academic integrity, bias, and transparency concerns, but it does not report quantitative institutional outcomes.
finding.measure: Assessment policy, academic integrity guidance, institutional AI-use frameworks

paper_profiles.title: LearnLens: An AI-Enhanced Dashboard to Support Teachers in Open-Ended Classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a common challenge in exploratory and open-ended science classrooms: teachers have difficulty quickly interpreting students’ open-ended responses and identifying misconceptions in time to adjust instruction. The authors present LearnLens, a generative AI-enhanced, teacher-facing dashboard intended to make student thinking more visible and actionable during middle school science instruction.

LearnLens ingests digital formative assessment data such as check-ins, exit tickets, and other open-ended responses, then presents teachers with multiple forms of support: tables of student responses, filters by class section, sample response viewers, word clouds, bar charts, and AI-generated summaries of collective understanding and misconceptions. The dashboard was prototyped within a 15-lesson, NGSS-aligned middle school Earth science curriculum focused on runoff, rainfall, and absorption.

The study used semi-structured interviews with two 6th-grade science teachers from an urban public school. Teachers viewed the dashboard in a guided walkthrough and commented on its usability, instructional relevance, and trustworthiness. The paper concludes that teachers valued the dashboard’s visualizations and especially the AI-generated insights for helping them notice gaps and misconceptions, but they were cautious about AI-generated prescriptive advice that went beyond the data. The authors frame LearnLens as a promising tool for supporting teacher decision-making in open-ended science learning environments, while emphasizing that further longitudinal and classroom-based evaluation is needed.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that LearnLens helped them interpret students’ open-ended science responses and identify misconceptions related to core Earth science concepts such as absorption, runoff, and rainfall. In a qualitative interview with two 6th-grade teachers, the AI-generated summaries and misconception detection were described as useful for making student thinking visible and for informing instructional adjustments, but no student learning gains or effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Teacher interview feedback on dashboard usefulness for interpreting open-ended science responses and identifying misconceptions

finding.finding_summary: The dashboard was intended to reduce the burden of manually sorting through open-ended formative assessment data by surfacing summaries, sample responses, and visualizations in one place. Teachers described current platforms as providing organization but no feedback, and they valued LearnLens for offering quicker sense-making support; however, the paper did not measure workload reduction quantitatively.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of dashboard support for reviewing and summarizing student responses

finding.finding_summary: The teachers indicated that the dashboard supported instructional sense-making, pattern recognition, and reflection on how to respond to student misconceptions, which are aspects of professional and pedagogical reasoning. These were qualitative impressions from a guided interview rather than a measured change in teacher skill or student durable skills, so no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher reflections on sense-making, pattern recognition, and instructional adaptation

paper_profiles.title: Designing AI Peers for Collaborative Mathematical Problem Solving with Middle School Students: A Participatory Design Study
paper_profiles.venue: CHI '26 Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how middle school students perceive an AI peer in collaborative mathematics problem solving and what features, behaviors, and controls they want from such a system. The authors argue that most prior GenAI in education has centered on AI tutors or teacher-facing tools, leaving little understanding of how students want AI to function as a teammate inside small-group work.

To address this gap, the researchers ran a five-day summer camp with 24 U.S. middle school students (grades 6-8). Students completed human-only collaborative math tasks, then worked with a web-based AI peer technology probe featuring two AI peers (Alice and Bob) during mathematics problem solving, and later co-designed their ideal AI peers through participatory design activities, posters, reflections, interviews, and preference surveys.

The study finds that students wanted AI peers to act less like instructors and more like deferential collaborators: they preferred hints, checks, and concept refreshers before direct answers; wanted explicit control over when the AI speaks and how much help it gives; and favored a friendly, expert but peer-like tone. Quantitatively, students reported lower temporal demand with AI peers than with human-only collaboration, but higher physical demand and lower group cohesion/task integration, suggesting a tradeoff between efficiency and interactional overhead. Overall, the paper concludes that AI peers for middle school math should prioritize scaffold-first support, co-agency, emotional attunement, and student controllability.

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on middle school mathematics collaborative problem solving rather than individual test performance. Students preferred AI peers that provided math hints, error detection, concept refreshers, and double-check prompts before direct answers, and the technology probe reduced perceived temporal demand during math tasks (M=5.67, SD=4.38 vs. M=9.62, SD=4.13; p=0.002, d=1.15) on n=22 paired comparisons.
finding.measure: Perceived workload during collaborative mathematics problem solving; math task interaction preferences and reflections
finding.study_size: n=24 enrolled; n=22 paired survey analyses
finding.std_deviation: SD=4.38 (AI condition temporal demand), SD=4.13 (human-only temporal demand)

finding.finding_summary: The study substantively examines collaboration, co-agency, turn-taking, and negotiation in small-group problem solving. Students reported lower Group Integration-Task scores with AI peers than with human-only collaboration (M=4.76, SD=1.58 vs. M=5.54, SD=1.52; p=0.047, d=0.81), and their qualitative feedback emphasized a desire for AI that works with them rather than doing the work for them.
finding.measure: Group Environment Questionnaire (Group Integration-Task and related cohesion measures); qualitative collaboration reflections
finding.study_size: n=22 paired survey analyses; interview sample n=18

finding.finding_summary: Students’ affective experience was worse with AI peers on some measures and in qualitative accounts. Attractions to Group-Social was lower in the AI-peer condition (M=5.21, SD=1.81) than in human-only collaboration (M=6.50, SD=2.05; p=0.029, d=0.94), and students described frustration, self-blame, and the need for encouragement when the AI failed to recognize emotional states.
finding.measure: Group Environment Questionnaire (ATGS) and interview/reflection themes about frustration, encouragement, and trust
finding.study_size: n=22 paired survey analyses; interview sample n=18

finding.finding_summary: The AI peer reduced perceived time pressure but increased interaction overhead. On NASA-TLX, temporal demand was significantly lower with AI peers (M=5.67, SD=4.38) than with human-only CPS (M=9.62, SD=4.13; p=0.002, d=1.15), but physical demand was higher in the AI condition (M=8.48, SD=4.65 vs. M=4.90, SD=2.41; p=0.014, d=1.14) because students had to type, navigate, and interpret text-based outputs.
finding.measure: NASA Task Load Index temporal demand and physical demand
finding.std_deviation: SD=4.38 vs. SD=4.13 (temporal demand); SD=4.65 vs. SD=2.41 (physical demand)

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes students’ prior attitudes toward math and notes the camp used grade-aligned mathematics standards, but it does not study a different academic subject beyond mathematics. No separate non-math academic outcome is substantively examined or reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Higher education assessment practice in the era of generative AI tools
paper_profiles.population: Undergraduate/Graduate (higher education, master's level case studies)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how generative AI tools such as ChatGPT and Google Bard (Gemini) perform on assessment tasks in higher education and what that implies for teaching, learning, and academic integrity. The authors are responding to concerns that GenAI can be used to complete student work in ways that undermine authentic assessment, while also potentially offering useful educational support.

The study uses three case-study assessments drawn from data science, data analytics, and construction management at the master's level. The authors prompted ChatGPT-4 and Bard to solve the assessment tasks, then evaluated the generated responses with criterion-referenced assessment and a standard grade scale, with moderation by academic tutors. The paper is not an intervention study with students; rather, it is an evaluative analysis of AI-generated answers in disciplinary assessment contexts.

The main conclusion is that GenAI tools can demonstrate subject knowledge, problem-solving, analytical, and sometimes critical-thinking skills, especially in data-intensive areas like data science and data analytics, but they struggle more with complex, contextualized project-based tasks. The authors argue that because these tools can produce plausible assessment solutions, they may limit learning when used unethically, and they recommend redesigning assessments, combining plagiarism and AI-detection tools, and using more contextualized and reflective tasks to preserve authentic learning.

finding.finding_summary: Across three master's-level case study assessments, ChatGPT and Bard demonstrated durable skills such as problem-solving, analytical reasoning, and some critical thinking, but performance varied by discipline and task structure. The paper reports that both tools handled data analytics/data science tasks relatively well, while struggling with more complex contextualized construction management work; no effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Performance on criterion-referenced assessment of AI-generated solutions, including comprehension, analysis, accuracy, discussion, and presentation criteria
finding.study_size: n=3 assessment case studies (ChatGPT and Bard applied to three tasks)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that GenAI is already affecting assessment design, academic integrity, and institutional policy in higher education, prompting recommendations for redesigned assessments, combined AI/plagiarism detection, and guidance for supervised use. These are qualitative recommendations based on the authors' evaluation of three assessment tasks rather than a measured institutional outcome.
finding.measure: Assessment design implications, academic integrity considerations, and policy/recommendation analysis

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that GenAI tools can assist in generating assessment solutions, evaluation metrics, and structured outputs quickly, implying potential productivity gains for teaching/learning workflows. However, the article does not directly measure teacher workload or efficiency, and its evidence is limited to qualitative observations from AI-produced responses.
finding.measure: Qualitative assessment of AI-generated outputs for solving and presenting assessment tasks

paper_profiles.title: Development of a test in German language to assess middle school students’ physics proficiency
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the lack of accessible, subject-specific German-language achievement tests for middle school physics. The authors argue that researchers in physics education often need a reliable way to measure students’ prior physics proficiency, but existing released TIMSS items are limited in German and open-ended items are costly to administer and score.

To address this gap, the authors developed a 20-item multiple-choice single-select test by translating and adapting released TIMSS science items for middle-school physics content. They administered a 40-item pilot version to 177 eighth-grade students in Hamburg, Germany, then used Rasch modeling to remove misfitting and differentially functioning items, yielding a final 20-item test. They also examined correlational validity by relating estimated proficiency scores to students’ science interest, science self-concept, physics grades, and cultural/economic capital.

The results suggest the resulting test has acceptable psychometric properties: adequate model fit, person-separation reliability of 0.78, item-separation reliability of 0.97, and correlations in expected directions with external variables. The authors conclude that the test is a valid, efficient, and objective tool for assessing middle-school students’ physics proficiency, while noting limitations in generalizability beyond eighth graders in Hamburg and some content underrepresentation (especially electrics).

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central contribution is the development and validation of a middle-school physics proficiency test that measures students’ content and procedural knowledge in physics, which is closely aligned with scientific reasoning in this context. In a sample of n=177 eighth-grade students, the final 20-item Rasch-scaled test showed acceptable fit, with person-separation reliability = 0.78 and item-separation reliability = 0.97, supporting its use as a valid measure of physics-related scientific knowledge and reasoning.
finding.measure: Middle-school physics proficiency test based on adapted TIMSS items; Rasch person parameters

paper_profiles.title: CAGI, the Critical Assessment of Genome Interpretation, establishes progress and prospects for computational genetic variant interpretation methods
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reports on the first decade of the Critical Assessment of Genome Interpretation (CAGI) community experiment, which benchmarks computational methods for interpreting the functional and clinical impact of human genetic variants. The central question is how well existing algorithms can predict variant effects from genomic data, and whether these predictions are accurate enough to support research and clinical use.

CAGI organized five rounds of challenges, spanning 50 tasks and 738 submissions, using blind prediction contests evaluated by independent assessors. The challenges covered missense variant effects on protein function and stability, splicing and expression effects, rare disease diagnosis, cancer-risk variant interpretation, and complex trait prediction. Across these settings, results show that computational methods are generally far better than random and often outperform older baselines, but accuracy varies by task and is still limited for individual variants.

The strongest and most clinically relevant performance was observed for missense-variant interpretation in rare disease and cancer contexts, where some methods achieved evidence levels that could contribute to ACMG/AMP classification frameworks. The paper also finds that methods can help identify diagnostic variants in difficult clinical cases and can provide auxiliary evidence for splicing/expression interpretation and polygenic risk estimation. However, the authors emphasize that performance is constrained by experimental noise, training-data contamination, and the complexity of mapping molecular effects to clinical outcomes, so broader clinical use requires careful calibration and integration with other evidence sources.

finding.finding_summary: The paper is a meta-evaluation of computational methods for inferring genetic variant effects, not an educational intervention. Across 50 CAGI challenges, top methods showed substantial but imperfect ability to predict biochemical and clinical variant outcomes, with Pearson correlations for missense functional challenges ranging from 0.24 to 0.84 (average r̄=0.55) and ROC AUCs for rare-disease variant classification ranging from 0.85 to 0.92 in the main ClinVar/HGMD analysis. This supports the conclusion that computational inference can meaningfully model scientific/biomedical phenomena, though accuracy remains limited for individual variants.
finding.measure: Accuracy of computational genetic variant interpretation methods; Pearson correlation, Kendall’s tau, ROC AUC, truncated ROC AUC

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates whether computational variant interpretation can support clinical decision-making and guideline use. It reports that some methods reached Supporting, and occasionally Moderate or Strong, evidence thresholds for clinical variant interpretation, and that CAGI results informed responsible data governance through an Ethics Forum and challenge procedures. These findings suggest meaningful institutional impact for clinical genomics practice and research infrastructure, though the study is not about education.
finding.measure: Clinical evidence calibration for variant interpretation; use within ACMG/AMP-style guidelines; challenge governance and ethics processes

paper_profiles.title: Opportunities in AI/ML for the Rubin LSST
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This white paper is a strategic, collaborative review of opportunities for artificial intelligence and machine learning within the Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) Dark Energy Science Collaboration (DESC). It addresses how AI/ML can be integrated into DESC’s cosmology workflows for photometric redshifts, weak and strong lensing, supernovae, simulations, deblending, and shape measurement, while preserving scientific rigor through uncertainty quantification, robustness testing, reproducibility, and governance.

The paper does not evaluate a single intervention or report a classroom-style experiment; instead, it synthesizes current uses of ML in DESC and proposes a roadmap for future AI/ML infrastructure, methods, and coordination. Key emphases include Bayesian inference at scale, physics-informed methods, foundation models, large language model/agentic AI governance, benchmarking, and software/compute infrastructure. The context is an international astrophysics collaboration preparing for LSST’s large, heterogeneous data streams, and the main conclusion is that AI/ML will be central to DESC science only if deployed with strong validation, human oversight, and collaboration-wide standards.

Because this is a qualitative white paper focused on scientific strategy rather than an empirical study of educational technology, it does not provide evidence about teacher-facing AI assessment, monitoring, or feedback tools in U.S. middle school science, nor downstream effects on scientific reasoning. Its relevance to the retrieval question is therefore indirect and domain-mismatched: it discusses AI/ML governance and workflows in astrophysics, not K-12 education.

paper_profiles.title: Artificial Intelligence–Based Student Activity Monitoring for Suicide Risk: Considerations for K–12 Schools, Caregivers, Government, and Technology Developers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This RAND research report examines the growing use of AI-based student activity monitoring tools in K–12 schools to detect suicide risk and self-harm. The report asks how these systems are implemented, what existing research suggests about their accuracy, and how stakeholders perceive their benefits and harms. It draws on a review of 132 research studies, gray literature from major EdTech vendors, and 22 semistructured interviews with school staff, technology company representatives, health care professionals, and advocacy group members.

The paper focuses on tools that monitor activity on school-issued devices and accounts and use proprietary machine-learning methods, including keyword, sentiment, and natural-language processing, to generate alerts for school staff. The report concludes that these systems may help identify at-risk students and reassure adults, but there is little evidence that they accurately detect actual suicide risk in school settings or improve student mental health outcomes. It also emphasizes major concerns about privacy, bias, and unequal impacts, especially for marginalized students, and notes that schools and communities may lack the resources needed to respond effectively even when alerts are generated. Overall, the report recommends cautious implementation, clearer notice and oversight, and stronger evidence on accuracy and downstream effects before broad reliance on these tools.

finding.finding_summary: The report finds that AI-based student activity monitoring for suicide risk may help schools identify some students at risk and can provide reassurance to staff and caregivers, but it also raises substantial concerns about privacy, equity, and implementation capacity. It concludes that there is a need for stronger evidence on accuracy and on whether these tools improve student mental health, and notes that schools and communities are often under-resourced to respond to alerts effectively.
finding.measure: Implementation analysis, stakeholder interviews, policy and privacy review

paper_profiles.title: Defning and Monitoring K-12 Civic Learning Opportunities in the United States
paper_profiles.venue: Promoting K-12 Civic Learning and Engagement Through Assessment
paper_profiles.population: K-12 students in the United States
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter addresses a policy and measurement problem: U.S. schools and education agencies lack a comprehensive, systematic way to define, document, and monitor students’ civic learning opportunities (CLO) over time. The authors argue that, because civic learning is distributed across classrooms, schools, and communities, existing data sources such as NAEP and sporadic surveys capture only a narrow slice of relevant opportunities and do not support ongoing equity monitoring or policy decision-making.

Rather than evaluating a specific intervention, the chapter proposes a conceptual framework for a CLO indicator system. It lays out proposed classroom-, teacher-, and school-level indicators (e.g., instructional activities, instructional quality, materials and assessments, teacher capacity, attitudes and beliefs, courses/curricula, student voice opportunities, service learning, school climate, and staffing supports) along with antecedent indicators that may enable or constrain these opportunities.

The chapter focuses on the K-12 U.S. context and is aimed primarily at policymakers, school and district leaders, researchers, and community partners who would design or use such an indicator system. The authors conclude that effective monitoring of civic learning requires multiple data sources, attention to measurement quality, longitudinal implementation, and linking opportunity data to civic readiness outcomes. They also note that emerging methods, including generative AI, may help with item generation, reporting, and analysis, but these are proposed possibilities rather than evaluated tools.

finding.finding_summary: This chapter does not evaluate an intervention or report outcome effects; it proposes a framework for building a U.S. K-12 civic learning opportunity indicator system. The main substantive contribution is conceptual and policy-oriented: the authors argue that current monitoring systems are incomplete and that a regular, multi-source, longitudinal indicator infrastructure is needed to support equity-focused decision-making.
finding.measure: Conceptual framework / policy analysis of civic learning opportunity indicators and monitoring systems

paper_profiles.title: LearnLens: An AI-Enhanced Dashboard to Support Teachers in Open-Ended Classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a common challenge in exploratory and open-ended science classrooms: teachers have difficulty quickly understanding students’ conceptual thinking from open-ended digital responses. The authors argue that current classroom tools often store responses but do not synthesize them into actionable feedback, leaving teachers without timely insight into misconceptions or class-wide patterns.

To address this, the paper presents LearnLens, a generative-AI-enhanced teacher dashboard that ingests students’ open-ended responses from formative assessments, exit tickets, and check-ins and then presents sample responses, word clouds, bar charts, and AI-generated summaries of understanding and misconceptions. The dashboard was designed through iterative co-design with teachers and implemented as a high-fidelity prototype in a 15-lesson middle school Earth science curriculum aligned to NGSS. The AI component used GPT-4o with prompt refinement and human validation to improve the quality of summaries and misconception identification.

The evaluation consisted of semi-structured interviews with two 6th-grade science teachers from an urban public school, during which they reviewed the dashboard in a guided walkthrough. Teachers valued the visualizations, the ability to see verbatim student responses, and especially the AI-generated summaries of gaps and misconceptions. They trusted descriptive summaries grounded in student data, but were more cautious about AI-generated instructional prescriptions that went beyond the data. The main conclusion is that GenAI dashboards like LearnLens may help teachers make sense of open-ended science work and support instructional adjustment, though the paper is limited to a small qualitative usability study and does not measure student learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the dashboard made it easier to review open-ended student responses and obtain timely summaries that existing tools (e.g., Google Forms, Schoology, EdPuzzle) did not provide. In a guided interview with two 6th-grade science teachers, they valued the table of responses, filtering, word clouds, bar charts, and AI-generated insights for reducing the effort needed to interpret student thinking and identify gaps or misconceptions.
finding.measure: Teacher interview feedback on dashboard usability, summary quality, and ease of interpreting student responses

finding.finding_summary: The dashboard was used in a middle school Earth science curriculum focused on understanding scientific concepts such as rainfall, runoff, absorption, and related misconceptions. Teachers indicated that the AI-generated insights helped them identify students’ gaps in conceptual understanding and could inform how they would reinforce vocabulary and address misconceptions, but the study did not measure student scientific reasoning directly.
finding.measure: Teacher interpretation of students’ open-ended Earth science responses and perceived value for diagnosing misconceptions
finding.study_size: n=2 teachers; student response data from one check-in and prior curriculum use

paper_profiles.title: A Pilot Study on Teacher-Facing Real-Time Classroom Game Dashboards
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how a teacher-facing, real-time dashboard can support educators while students play the educational game Lakeland. The authors argue that teachers often need to monitor gameplay and provide feedback without being able to easily inspect each student’s screen, and that a dashboard could make student progress, strategy, and signs of confusion or disengagement more visible during class.

The study used a participatory design approach followed by a small pilot implementation.
