In phase one, 12 teachers and teaching mentors participated in a workshop where they generated design ideas using prompt cards and mockups; these artifacts were used to build a dashboard prototype with 16 data models, including progress, strategy, indecision, frustration, give up, and game state indicators. In phase two, four teachers tested the prototype in classrooms serving grades 6-12, with one face-to-face class and the remainder online due to COVID-19 shutdowns. Teachers completed post-session surveys and interviews focused on co-design, feasibility, and usefulness.

Overall, teachers responded positively and reported that the dashboard reflected their input, was easy to use, and helped them notice when students were stuck, inactive, or making progress. The prototype appeared to improve their ability to facilitate gameplay and provide feedback, though some bugs, missing class-level overview features, and visualization issues limited effectiveness in some cases. Because the study is a small pilot with descriptive survey/interview data rather than a controlled comparison, it supports the feasibility and promise of the tool but does not establish causal effects on learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the real-time dashboard made it easier to monitor student gameplay, identify who needed help, and facilitate class sessions without checking each student's screen individually. Survey responses were generally favorable (e.g., 'If I were to play Lakeland again, I would use this tool' = 5/5; 'I will recommend my colleagues use this tool when they use Lakeland' = 5/5), but the study did not measure time savings or workload reduction with a controlled comparison.
finding.measure: Teacher survey ratings and post-session interviews about usability, feasibility, and facilitation
finding.study_size: n=4 teachers in classroom pilot; n=12 teachers/mentors in workshop

finding.finding_summary: The dashboard helped teachers detect signs of student disengagement, frustration, inactivity, and students 'stuck' in gameplay, which are indicators related to persistence and self-regulation during the game. Teachers described using alerts such as inactivity and tutorial completion to identify struggling students, but the paper did not directly measure student motivation or engagement outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of student engagement/disengagement indicators in dashboard visualizations

finding.finding_summary: Teachers valued dashboard models that represented strategy, indecision, and progress, suggesting the tool could support classroom facilitation of student problem-solving and decision-making in Lakeland. However, the paper did not directly assess gains in critical thinking, metacognition, or collaboration; evidence is limited to teacher judgments that the dashboard helped them understand gameplay strategies and student behavior.
finding.measure: Teacher feedback on strategy/indecision/progress dashboard models
finding.study_size: n=4 teachers in classroom pilot; 71 prompt cards from 12 workshop participants

paper_profiles.title: A Practical Guide for Supporting Formative Assessment and Feedback Using Generative AI
paper_profiles.population: Not explicitly studied; examples span K-12 and higher education contexts
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative review and practical guide on how generative AI, especially large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, can support formative assessment and feedback. The authors frame the discussion around a classic formative assessment model: helping students understand where they are going, where they currently are, and how to move forward. They argue that LLMs can assist with generating student-friendly learning objectives, co-constructing success criteria, creating sample work for critique, producing formative questions, and drafting feedback at task, process, and self-regulation levels.

The paper does not report a primary empirical study; instead, it synthesizes existing literature and illustrates use cases with prompt examples and AI-generated outputs from education contexts such as biology and undergraduate fMRI coursework. The examples are used to show both promise and limitations: LLMs can save time, scale feedback, and support assessment design, but outputs may vary, require educator review, and can be misaligned with pedagogical goals if used uncritically. The authors emphasize that educators should treat LLMs as augmenting, not replacing, expert pedagogy.

The review is broadly relevant to teachers and researchers interested in AI-supported formative assessment, including teacher-facing assessment and feedback tools. Its main conclusion is that LLMs are most useful when integrated thoughtfully into existing formative assessment frameworks, with careful prompting, human oversight, and attention to transferable skills, academic integrity, and contextual fit. The paper is conceptual rather than empirical and offers guidance rather than measured effects on student outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce teacher workload by automating or accelerating tasks such as rewriting learning objectives, generating sample work, creating formative questions, and drafting feedback. These claims are illustrated with prompt examples and qualitative discussion, but the paper does not report empirical effect sizes or a primary study sample.
finding.measure: Teacher time/workload and ease of generating formative assessment materials

finding.finding_summary: The authors suggest LLM-supported formative assessment may help build durable skills such as critical thinking, metacognition, and self-regulation when students critique AI-generated exemplars or receive process/self-regulation feedback. They also warn that over-reliance on LLMs may undermine these same skills if students passively accept AI-generated responses, so the likely effect is mixed rather than uniformly positive.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, metacognitive reflection, self-regulation, and skill transfer (conceptual discussion)

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents LLMs as useful for improving the clarity and quality of academic tasks across subjects, including generating student-friendly learning objectives, exemplars, and formative prompts. These are educational design applications rather than measured learning outcomes, so the finding is conceptual and not tied to a reported effect size or study sample.
finding.measure: Quality/clarity of learning objectives, exemplars, and formative assessment prompts

paper_profiles.title: Accessibility Gaps in U.S. Government Dashboards for Blind and Low-Vision Residents
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether six high-stakes U.S. government dashboard ecosystems are accessible to blind and low-vision residents who rely on screen readers and keyboard navigation. The author audits dashboards from CDC, HUD, California HCD, New York City, Houston, and Chicago using a rubric grounded in WCAG and prior accessibility research, focusing on discoverability, keyboard access, semantic labeling, plain-language narrative summaries, and machine-readable data access.

The central claim is that a recurring pattern, termed "urgency inversion," exists across these dashboards: the more time-sensitive and operational the information, the less accessible it tends to be for blind and low-vision users. In contrast, slower accountability dashboards are more likely to provide narrative explanations and downloadable structured data. The study argues that this creates a civic participation and equity gap, because sighted residents receive immediate situational awareness while blind and low-vision residents must rely on delayed channels or extra labor to obtain the same information.

The paper is situated in the context of public health, housing, permitting, and civic accountability dashboards, not educational settings. It concludes with design and policy recommendations for government dashboards, including plain-language status updates, machine-readable mirrors of visual content, and explicit accessibility commitments in public-facing descriptions.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds a structural accessibility failure across six U.S. government dashboard ecosystems: the most urgent, operational dashboards are typically the least accessible to blind and low-vision users. This "urgency inversion" creates an equity gap in civic leverage, because sighted users get immediate situational awareness while BLV residents are pushed toward slower channels or additional labor to access the same information. No effect size is reported; the finding is based on a qualitative accessibility audit of six dashboard ecosystems.
finding.measure: Accessibility audit of dashboard ecosystems using WCAG-informed rubric (discoverability, keyboard navigation, semantic labeling, narrative summaries, machine-readable data access)

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that operational dashboards, especially Houston's daily permitting dashboards, do not consistently provide accessible tables, CSVs, or narrative summaries, making it harder for users to quickly obtain time-sensitive status information. The study does not report a numeric effect size, but it concludes that BLV users must expend extra time and effort, or contact staff directly, to obtain the same operational information that sighted users can see at a glance.
finding.measure: Presence/absence of accessible affordances for time-sensitive dashboard information (e.g., downloadable tables, plain-language status updates)

paper_profiles.title: Exploring utilization of generative AI for research and education in data-driven materials science
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper explores how generative AI can support research and education in data-driven materials science. The authors organized the AIMHack2024 hackathon and used it as a case study to test three AI-enabled workflows: AI-assisted software trials, creation of an AI tutor for PHYSBO, and GUI development for a Bayesian optimization tool.

The first part shows that ChatGPT could generate step-by-step ImageJ instructions for object counting, including handling overlapping objects with watershed segmentation, enabling participants to learn unfamiliar software more quickly. The second part evaluates MyGPT as a tutorial generator for PHYSBO; it initially produced incorrect answers when given URLs alone, but became accurate when official documentation PDFs were uploaded, suggesting that structured source materials are important for reliable AI-generated tutorials.

The third part demonstrates that ChatGPT could help convert PHYSBO Python scripts into a Windows executable and add GUI features for file selection, parameter entry, output options, and user guidance. The paper concludes that generative AI can substantially reduce the effort needed to build software tutorials, small utilities, and educational materials, but human verification remains necessary because AI outputs can be plausible yet incorrect. The study is primarily an early-stage descriptive account of hackathon outputs rather than a controlled evaluation.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that generative AI substantially reduced the effort needed to learn unfamiliar software, generate tutorials, and build GUI tools. In the ImageJ example, ChatGPT provided step-by-step instructions that enabled object counting, and the authors state that several participants successfully used software they had not used before; no numerical effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Reported software-learning efficiency, tutorial generation usefulness, and workflow simplification during a hackathon

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes that participants were encouraged to critically evaluate AI-generated content by cross-checking it against literature, testing code, and using domain knowledge. This is presented as a central benefit of the hackathon experience, improving critical thinking about reliability and applicability of AI outputs; no quantitative measure is reported.
finding.measure: Critical evaluation of AI-generated content; verification behavior during software use

paper_profiles.title: LOFAR Transients and the Radio Sky Monitor
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes the scientific motivation and planned observing strategy for the LOFAR Transients Key Science Project, with a particular emphasis on the Radio Sky Monitor (RSM). The authors argue that LOFAR’s low-frequency, wide-field capabilities will enable detection and characterization of a broad range of transient and variable radio phenomena, including synchrotron outbursts, coherent bursts, pulsars, flare stars, exoplanetary emission, and possibly fast radio bursts before that term was in use.

The paper is not an empirical evaluation of a classroom or education intervention. Instead, it is a technical and conceptual overview of telescope capabilities, survey modes, data rates, and a proposed real-time analysis and alert pipeline. The RSM would regularly scan large fractions of the northern sky at 30 and 120 MHz, producing images every second and feeding detections into a classification/alert system for follow-up observations. The main conclusion is that LOFAR should be able to probe unexplored transient parameter space and serve as a powerful discovery engine for radio astronomy, with no educational intervention or student-related outcomes studied.

paper_profiles.title: Foundations of GenIR
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter provides a conceptual survey of generative information retrieval (GenIR), arguing that modern generative AI models create two major opportunities for information access: information generation and information synthesis. The paper explains how large language models and multimodal generative models differ from traditional AI and retrieval systems, and it organizes the discussion around model architecture, scaling, training, prompt optimization, multimodal applications, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), generative retrieval, and domain-specific modeling.

Rather than evaluating a specific intervention in a classroom or organizational setting, the chapter synthesizes existing technical research on how generative AI can improve information access systems. It discusses how LLMs can generate direct responses, rewrite prompts, support multimodal understanding and generation, and synthesize external information more reliably through RAG. It also examines limitations such as hallucination, retrieval planning, maintainability, inference cost, and the tradeoffs between large and small models.

The paper is not an empirical education study and does not examine teachers, students, schools, or science learning outcomes in U.S. middle school contexts. Its conclusions are primarily theoretical: generative AI is likely to reshape information access systems, but open problems remain around reliability, scaling, prompt design, retrieval optimization, and domain adaptation. The chapter suggests that future progress will depend on better integration between retrieval and generation and on more controllable, grounded, and efficient model designs.

paper_profiles.title: Learning Factors in AI-Augmented Education: A Comparative Study of Middle and High School Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how key learning-perception dimensions relate to one another in AI-mediated educational settings and whether those relationships differ between middle and high school students. The authors focus on four dimensions drawn from learning sciences research: experience, clarity, comfort, and motivation, arguing that prior work has mostly examined these factors outside AI-supported learning or in higher education settings.

The study was conducted in authentic extracurricular computer science classes. A total of 53 students participated: 25 middle school students (ages 10–13) and 28 high school students (ages 15–20). The groups used different AI tools in programming-related activities: middle school students used Teachable Machine in an introductory AI course, while high school students used Gemini and Claude in a vibe-coding/Python context. Data came from a 17-item questionnaire with Likert-scale and open-ended items, analyzed using correlation matrices, Mann-Whitney U tests, and text mining of reflections.

Results showed generally positive perceptions of the AI tools, but with a clear developmental difference in how students structured those perceptions. Middle school students showed strong positive intercorrelations across experience, clarity, comfort, and motivation, suggesting a holistic evaluation style in which positive impressions in one area generalized to others. High school students showed a more differentiated pattern, with weaker or near-zero relationships among some dimensions; they appeared to separate usability, clarity, and motivational value more independently. The authors conclude that AI integration in education should be developmentally sensitive, with younger learners benefiting from clarity and structured support, and older learners needing more sophisticated interactions and direct attention to usability and motivation.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported generally positive experiences with the AI tools across both age groups, including comfort and motivation. The only statistically significant between-group difference was for ease of use (Q3), where high school students rated the tool higher than middle school students (U=192.00, p=0.0013; means 3.68 vs 3.16), suggesting older students felt more comfortable using the tools.
finding.measure: Questionnaire items on overall experience, ease of use, comfort, and motivation (Q1, Q3, Q8, Q11, Q14)

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies how students perceive and evaluate AI-supported learning through the dimensions of clarity, experience, comfort, and motivation, which are interpreted as part of the learning process and associated with cognitive and evaluative development. Correlation patterns suggest middle school students evaluate AI more holistically, whereas high school students show more differentiated judgment, indicating a developmental shift in evaluative sophistication and reasoning about AI tools.
finding.measure: Spearman correlations among perceived learning dimensions and analysis of open-ended reflections about AI's influence on learning

paper_profiles.title: AI and Machine Learning for Next Generation Science Assessments
paper_profiles.venue: Machine learning, natural language processing and psychometrics
paper_profiles.population: K-12 (with examples from middle school, high school, and teacher assessment contexts)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter reviews how artificial intelligence and machine learning are being used to support next-generation science assessment, especially assessments aligned with the Framework for K-12 Science Education and the Next Generation Science Standards. The central problem is that traditional multiple-choice tests do not adequately measure knowledge-in-use, scientific practices, or three-dimensional learning, while performance-based tasks are difficult and time-consuming for teachers to score manually.

The chapter synthesizes the evolution of ML-based automatic scoring approaches for science assessment, including supervised, unsupervised, semi-supervised, pre-trained models such as BERT, zero-shot approaches, and fine-tuned ChatGPT/GPT-3.5. It also proposes a framework for understanding machine-human scoring agreement and the factors that influence scoring accuracy, such as assessment design, construct complexity, examinee characteristics, validation procedures, and algorithm choice.

The paper is not an empirical intervention study; rather, it is a research review and conceptual synthesis drawing on prior science assessment studies, including middle school science tasks, scientific argumentation, scientific explanations, modeling, and one teacher PCK assessment. The main conclusion is that ML can reduce teacher scoring burden and provide timely feedback, but careful attention is needed to validity, fairness, generalizability, and bias before these tools can be responsibly used in classrooms.

finding.finding_summary: Across reviewed studies, ML-based automated scoring was generally effective for assessing science reasoning tasks such as scientific argumentation, explanations, investigations, and student models. The chapter reports that supervised ML and newer pre-trained/fine-tuned models could achieve satisfactory to strong machine-human agreement for written and drawn science responses, including middle school tasks such as the red dye diffusion modeling item.
finding.measure: Machine-human agreement on scoring of science assessment responses; Cohen's kappa; scoring accuracy

finding.finding_summary: The chapter argues that ML-based automatic scoring can substantially reduce teacher workload by scoring open-ended science responses more quickly and consistently than human scoring. It gives a classroom example where scoring one middle school science task for 100 students could take about 100 minutes manually, illustrating the practical efficiency gains from automated scoring and immediate feedback.
finding.measure: Teacher scoring time / workload for performance-based assessments

paper_profiles.title: Large Synoptic Survey Telescope Dark Energy Science Collaboration
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This white paper describes the LSST Dark Energy Science Collaboration (DESC), a community-organizing effort created to prepare for dark energy analyses with the Large Synoptic Survey Telescope (LSST). The paper outlines why a coordinated collaboration is needed: LSST will produce enormous public datasets, but extracting dark-energy constraints will require substantial work on systematic uncertainties, analysis methods, simulations, computing infrastructure, and survey/technical coordination well before survey operations begin.

The paper presents the DESC’s scientific scope and organizational structure, including five dark-energy probes (weak lensing, large-scale structure, Type Ia supernovae, galaxy clusters, and strong lensing), plus cross-cutting work on photometric redshifts, simulations, software, and technical coordination. It describes a one-year minimal governance model, working groups, and a three-year work plan focused on preparing analysis pipelines and tools. Because the paper is a planning and coordination white paper rather than an empirical study, it does not report participant-level outcomes or experimental effects.

The intended context is the U.S.-led LSST collaboration and the broader astronomical community, not K-12 education. The main conclusion is that a large, structured preparatory effort is necessary to enable high-precision dark-energy science with LSST data and to manage the many systematics that could limit cosmological inference.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that establishing the LSST Dark Energy Science Collaboration (DESC) will improve the community’s ability to organize, coordinate, and prepare for LSST dark-energy analyses. It describes a governance model, working groups, and a three-year work plan intended to align scientific, technical, simulation, and computing efforts before data-taking begins.
finding.measure: Collaboration formation, governance structure, and work-plan development

paper_profiles.title: Pulsar science with the SKA Observatory
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This lead article introduces a special issue on pulsar science with the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKAO). Rather than evaluating an educational intervention, the paper surveys the planned capabilities of the SKA-Low and SKA-Mid telescopes and explains how those capabilities will affect multiple pulsar-science use cases, including pulsar discovery, timing, gravitational-wave searches, tests of gravity, and studies of neutron-star interiors and the interstellar medium.

The paper describes the telescope designs, data-processing subsystems, and expected survey strategies for the SKAO’s early AA* configuration and later AA4 configuration. It synthesizes projections from the accompanying topical papers, arguing that SKAO’s sensitivity, wide frequency coverage, and multi-beam processing will substantially expand known pulsar samples and improve timing precision. The article is a forward-looking overview of astronomy infrastructure and its scientific implications, not an empirical study of AI or education.

No U.S. middle school science population, teacher-facing AI assessment/monitoring/feedback tool, or scientific-reasoning intervention is studied. The paper contains only astrophysics content and makes no educational claims, so it does not provide evidence relevant to downstream effects on student scientific reasoning in classrooms.

paper_profiles.title: Determining middle school students' perceptions of the concept of artificial intelligence: A metaphor analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study investigates how middle school students perceive the concept of artificial intelligence (AI) using metaphor analysis. The authors argue that students’ perceptions of AI matter because AI is increasingly relevant in education and broader society, and these perceptions may shape future acceptance of AI-supported learning environments. The paper responds to a gap in the literature, noting that little research had examined secondary school students’ views of AI.

The study used a qualitative phenomenological approach with metaphor analysis. Data were collected from 339 seventh- and eighth-grade students in four secondary schools (public and private) in the central districts of Afyonkarahisar and Izmir, Turkey, during the 2019–2020 school year. Students completed the prompt, “Artificial intelligence is like ___, because ___,” and their responses were coded and analyzed through content analysis in NVivo, producing 80 valid metaphors grouped into 11 conceptual categories.

Findings show that students generally held positive views of AI, most often describing it as smart, brain-like, technological, human-like, and service-oriented. At the same time, some students expressed concern about AI as dangerous, threatening, or potentially harmful, reflecting a mix of optimism and anxiety. The authors conclude that educational computer systems and AI-assisted teaching could be designed to shape students’ perceptions and learning skills, and they suggest more research, including interviews and studies with high school and university students.

finding.finding_summary: Students’ metaphors suggest AI was viewed as supporting problem solving, information access, and assistance, but the study did not directly measure durable skills. The paper interprets positive metaphors such as smart assistant, source of information, and helper as indicating that students associated AI with reasoning-related and assistive capacities, while some metaphors also reflected uncertainty and concern.
finding.measure: Metaphor analysis of students' perceptions of AI
finding.study_size: n=339 (80 valid metaphors analyzed; 70 participants excluded from analysis)

finding.finding_summary: The central empirical result is that students largely held positive perceptions of AI, but a meaningful subset expressed negative emotions such as fear, concern, and distrust. Metaphors clustered around positive categories like smart, humanistic, and service, while security and dilemma-of-good-and-evil categories captured worries about danger, threat, and harmful uses.
finding.measure: Metaphor categories indicating attitudes/perceptions toward AI

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that students' perceptions of AI can inform educational design and policy, especially the design of AI-assisted teaching and educational computer systems. This is a conceptual implication rather than a measured institutional outcome, but it is a substantive focus of the discussion and conclusion.
finding.measure: Student perceptions used to inform educational system design implications

paper_profiles.title: Implementing artificial intelligence education for middle school technology education in Republic of Korea
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Technology and Design Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study addresses the lack of empirically tested AI-related instruction within middle school technology education, especially in South Korea’s free semester system. The authors argue that AI education should fit technology education’s emphasis on problem solving, social impacts of technology, and career exploration, rather than being limited to standalone computer science or programming instruction.

The researchers developed a 16-hour artificial intelligence theme-selection program for first-year middle school students in Seoul and implemented it as a free-semester elective. The program was designed in three stages—preparation, development, and improvement—and included AI basics, AI social impacts, AI ethics, physical computing with Micro:bit, communication technology, and group-based problem-solving projects using AI-related tools and activities.

The study used a single-group pretest-posttest design with 23 students and measured outcomes using two attitude toward technology constructs from PATT and three AI competency constructs. Results showed significant increases in interest in technology, career aspirations in technology, social impact of AI, and AI performance; interaction with AI did not change significantly. The authors conclude that an AI-centered, technology-problem-solving approach can support both technology attitudes and AI-related competencies in middle school free-semester settings.

finding.finding_summary: Students showed significant gains in attitudes toward technology after the 16-hour AI program. Mean interest in technology increased from 3.96 to 4.17 and career aspirations in technology increased from 3.83 to 4.12 in a single-group pretest-posttest study with n=23; both changes were statistically significant on Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.
finding.measure: Pupils’ Attitude toward Technology (PATT): interest in technology; career aspirations in technology

finding.finding_summary: The program improved AI performance, which the authors operationalized as problem-solving ability in AI-based technological tasks. Mean AI performance rose from 2.96 to 4.04 (n=23), with a significant Wilcoxon signed-rank result (Z = -4.023, p < 0.001), suggesting stronger problem decomposition, troubleshooting, and iterative problem solving.
finding.measure: AI performance competency scale (modified from computational thinking performance for technological problem solving)

finding.finding_summary: The paper is centrally about implementing an AI elective within the middle school free-semester system and argues that the developed program is valid and useful for technology education policy and practice. The intervention was designed for immediate use by in-service teachers in Seoul, and the authors conclude it demonstrates the feasibility of bringing AI into technology education within this institutional structure.
finding.measure: Program development and implementation within the free-semester technology education context

finding.finding_summary: The intervention targeted middle school technology education content rather than a core academic test domain. The developed 16-hour program integrated AI basics, AI ethics, physical computing, communication technology, and project-based problem solving, and the authors concluded it was effective for technology education and career exploration in the free semester.
finding.measure: Technology education program implementation and AI-related curriculum content

paper_profiles.title: Examining the Effect of Assessment Construct Characteristics on Machine Learning Scoring of Scientific Argumentation
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether internal characteristics of assessment tasks are associated with the accuracy of machine-learning (ML) scoring models for students’ written scientific argumentation. The authors build on prior work showing that AI can score short constructed responses in science, and they focus on three construct characteristics: Complexity, Diversity, and Structure.

The study uses 17 scientific argumentation assessment items originally developed for middle school students in grades 5–8 and aligned to a validated learning progression of scientific argumentation. Using 361 student responses per item for ML training and validation, the authors built one supervised text-scoring model per item and compared predicted scores with human consensus scores using Cohen’s kappa, accuracy, Spearman correlations, precision, recall, and F1.

Across items, ML scoring performance was generally substantial, but it varied by item characteristics. Higher Complexity, greater Diversity of science-learning dimensions, and more advanced Structure levels were all associated with lower machine-human agreement. The paper concludes that AI scoring is more feasible for simpler, single-dimension argumentation tasks, while more complex and multidimensional scientific argumentation items remain challenging and may require improved modeling approaches or larger training sets.

finding.finding_summary: This study found that as scientific argumentation assessment items became more complex, more multidimensional, or more structurally advanced, machine-human scoring agreement decreased. Across 17 items scored from 361 responses each, Cohen’s kappa averaged 0.60 overall, but item-level performance was significantly lower for higher construct levels; for example, Complexity was negatively correlated with kappa (rs=-0.752, p<.001, n=17), Diversity with kappa (rs=-0.718, p<.01, n=17), and Structure with kappa (rs=-0.764, p<.001, n=17).
finding.measure: Machine-learning scoring accuracy for middle school scientific argumentation responses, measured by Cohen’s kappa, accuracy, and Spearman correlations against human consensus scores
finding.study_size: n=17 items; 361 responses per item used for model training/validation
finding.std_deviation: SD=0.15 for Cohen’s kappa across models

finding.finding_summary: The paper supports the operational value of automated scoring for science argumentation by showing that ML models can achieve substantial agreement with human scores for many items, with mean Cohen’s kappa of 0.60 and mean accuracy of 0.79 across 17 models. The authors argue this suggests automated scoring can reduce the time and labor burden of evaluating large numbers of open-response science assessments, although performance drops for more complex items.
finding.measure: Human-machine agreement and classification accuracy for automated scoring of open-response scientific argumentation tasks
finding.study_size: n=17 items; n=361 responses per item in model development
finding.std_deviation: SD=0.15 for Cohen’s kappa across models

paper_profiles.title: Metaphorical Perceptions of Middle School Students Regarding the Concept of Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Education & Literacy Studies
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study investigates how middle school students conceptualize artificial intelligence through metaphors. The paper responds to the broader question of how students perceive AI as AI and coding become increasingly relevant in education and curricula, especially in middle school settings. Rather than evaluating an instructional intervention, the study examines students’ existing perceptions and the meanings they attach to AI.

The author used a phenomenological qualitative design with 86 students in grades 5-8 from a private school in Turkey affiliated with the Ministry of National Education. Students completed the prompt, “Artificial intelligence is like... because...,” and their responses were analyzed with content analysis. The study identified 51 metaphors clustered into four categories: technical/object, human/subject, nature-related, and interesting/other.

The main conclusion is that students mostly understand artificial intelligence through human-centered meanings, often framing it as a helper, assistant, brain, or human-like agent. Students also saw AI as a technical concept and, in some cases, used abstract or imaginative metaphors. The paper concludes that middle school students hold broad and creative perceptions of AI and that AI/coding literacy will likely be important for future education, but it does not test any educational effect on learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not evaluate an intervention or policy outcome, but it does substantively discuss the institutional importance of integrating AI and coding literacy into curricula. It concludes that AI and related literacies are likely to become important in future school systems, based on students' metaphorical understandings rather than measured institutional change.
finding.measure: Students' metaphorical perceptions of artificial intelligence and discussion of curriculum relevance

paper_profiles.title: Automated Analysis of Middle School Students’ Written Reflections During Game-Based Learning
paper_profiles.venue: AIED 2020 / Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence (LNAI)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of automatically assessing middle school students’ written reflections in a game-based learning environment. The authors argue that reflection is an important part of inquiry-based learning and self-regulated learning, but manual coding is time-consuming and difficult to scale. They investigate whether modern natural language representations can better predict the depth of student reflection than simpler bag-of-words baselines.

The study uses data from 153 middle school students who interacted with Crystal Island, a game-based learning environment for middle school microbiology, across two classroom studies. Students responded to periodic in-game reflection prompts and post-game prompts, producing 728 short written reflections. Two coders rated reflection depth on a five-point scale, and the authors trained several regression models using binary unigrams, tf-idf, GloVe, and ELMo representations. The best-performing model was an SVM with ELMo embeddings, which achieved the highest predictive accuracy (R2 = 0.64, MSE = 0.26, MAE = 0.40). The paper also reports that average reflection depth was positively correlated with post-test microbiology scores (r(601) = .29, p < .001), suggesting that deeper reflection is associated with better learning outcomes. The main conclusion is that automated reflection assessment, especially using contextual embeddings like ELMo, shows promise for supporting real-time adaptive feedback in middle school inquiry learning environments.

finding.finding_summary: Average reflection depth ratings were positively correlated with students’ post-test microbiology scores, suggesting that deeper reflective thinking is associated with stronger learning in the science context. The correlation was modest but statistically significant, r(601) = .29, p < .001, based on 728 reflection responses from 153 middle school students.
finding.measure: Microbiology post-test scores; reflection depth ratings

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally measures students’ reflection depth as a proxy for metacognition and self-regulated learning during inquiry-based problem solving. Two coders rated 728 written reflections on a five-point rubric, and the resulting continuous reflection scores (M = 2.41, SD = 0.86) were used as the target for machine learning models; higher scores represented clearer hypotheses, planning, reasoning, and awareness of knowledge gaps.
finding.measure: Reflection depth rubric scores (metacognition/self-regulated learning proxy)

finding.finding_summary: The paper uses student written reflections in a middle school microbiology game and shows that language-model-based features can predict the quality of those reflections. This is an assessment study rather than an instructional efficacy study, but it directly concerns students’ written science-related responses in the learning environment.
finding.measure: Written reflection response quality

paper_profiles.title: Designing AI Peers for Collaborative Mathematical Problem Solving with Middle School Students: A Participatory Design Study
paper_profiles.venue: CHI '26 (Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how middle school students perceive and want an AI peer to function during collaborative mathematical problem solving. The authors argue that most prior AI-in-education work treats AI as a tutor or coach, whereas middle-school mathematics often relies on peer collaboration, shared reasoning, and student control. To explore this gap, they used a child-centered participatory design study in a five-day summer camp where students first experienced human-only collaborative math work and then worked with two AI peers inside a technology-probe system.

The intervention was not an instructional curriculum in the usual sense, but an exploratory prototype of AI peers embedded in group math tasks. Twenty-four rising grades 6-8 students in the U.S. engaged with grade-aligned mathematics problems and then co-designed their ideal AI peer through posters, dialogue scripting, surveys, reflections, and interviews. The AI peers were framed as classmates with different proficiency levels and conversational styles, and the study compared human-only collaboration to AI-assisted collaboration using NASA-TLX and GEQ measures plus qualitative analysis.

The main conclusion is that students preferred AI peers that supported collaboration without taking over: they wanted hints, checks, and explanations before full answers; explicit student control over when and how the AI spoke; and a peer-like but knowledgeable tone. Quantitatively, AI peers reduced perceived temporal demand but increased physical demand and lowered some group-cohesion and coordination ratings. Qualitatively, students reported tensions around didactic control, social norms, and emotional support, indicating that an effective AI peer for middle school math should be scaffold-first, socially attuned, and designed to preserve co-agency rather than replace student reasoning.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined middle school students’ collaborative mathematics problem solving with and without AI peers. Quantitatively, AI peers reduced temporal demand during CPS (M=5.67, SD=4.38) compared with pure human CPS (M=9.62, SD=4.13), d=1.15, p=0.002, but students also reported higher physical demand (M=8.48 vs. 4.90), d=1.14, p=0.014, and lower group integration-task scores (M=4.76 vs. 5.54), d=0.81, p=0.047; these findings suggest mixed effects on mathematics collaboration processes rather than direct achievement gains.
finding.measure: NASA-TLX workload during mathematics CPS; GEQ group integration-task and related collaboration ratings during grade-aligned math problem solving
finding.study_size: n=22 for paired quantitative comparisons; n=24 enrolled

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that AI peers reduced time pressure but felt colder and less emotionally attuned than human peers. On the GEQ, attractions to group-social were lower with AI peers (M=5.21, SD=1.81) than in pure human CPS (M=6.50, SD=2.05), d=0.94, p=0.029, indicating reduced social engagement, while interviews showed that students wanted encouragement, empathy, and recognition of frustration during problem solving.
finding.measure: GEQ attractions to group-social; interview/reflection accounts of frustration, encouragement, and emotional support during CPS
finding.study_size: n=22 for paired quantitative comparisons; interview sample n=18

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively focuses on collaborative problem solving, co-agency, turn-taking, reasoning negotiation, and student control as durable skills. Students preferred AI peers that asked questions, offered examples, and supported shared reasoning rather than giving direct answers; however, when AI peers presented divergent approaches without adequate scaffolding, students found them distracting and felt the collaboration was fragmented.
finding.measure: Qualitative themes from interviews, whole-class reflections, and participatory-design artifacts about collaboration, co-agency, and reasoning support
finding.study_size: n=24 enrolled; interviews n=18; whole-class discussions across 5 sessions

finding.finding_summary: AI peers improved perceived task efficiency by lowering temporal demand, but they also increased operational burden because students had to type, navigate the interface, and interpret AI outputs. This indicates that the system made collaborative math work faster in some respects while making the interaction more cumbersome in others.
finding.measure: NASA-TLX temporal demand and physical demand during human-only CPS versus CPS with AI peers

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not directly study a non-math academic domain or report achievement outcomes outside mathematics, but it does present students’ preferences for AI-generated hints, examples, and concept refreshers as design features for learning support. Because these results are specific to mathematics rather than another academic subject, this category is only weakly relevant and yields no separate non-math academic effect.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: VLM@school – Evaluation of AI image understanding on German middle school knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents VLM@school, a new benchmark for evaluating vision-language models on German middle-school-level knowledge tasks. The authors argue that existing multimodal benchmarks are often English-only, overly multiple-choice oriented, and sometimes solvable without truly integrating image and text understanding. To address this, they compiled 2,038 open-ended questions grounded in 486 images spanning nine school subjects, including biology, physics, geography, history, math, arts, music, religion, and sports.

The benchmark is not an instructional intervention but an evaluation study of 13 open-weight VLMs on real curriculum-aligned tasks. Models were tested on open-ended answers, scored with a panel-of-LLMs judge approach, and also on adversarial questions designed to be unanswerable from the image alone. The strongest models reached under 45% overall accuracy, with especially weak performance in math, music, and adversarial items. The authors conclude that middle-school tasks are sufficiently challenging to reveal important weaknesses in current VLMs, and that benchmark performance on public datasets does not reliably transfer to this German, open-ended, curriculum-grounded setting.

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark includes biology and physics items that require visual reasoning plus background science knowledge, and current VLMs performed poorly on these tasks. The paper reports that even the best models struggled to explain scientific diagrams and causal relations, with domain accuracies in physics around 32%-48% depending on the model family, indicating limited scientific reasoning in multimodal middle-school contexts.
finding.measure: Open-ended accuracy on physics and biology benchmark questions
finding.study_size: n=486 images; n=403 questions across biology and physics combined (biology n=169, physics n=234)

finding.finding_summary: Models showed weak performance on middle-school math questions that required visual interpretation, counting, geometry, and simple calculations. The best reported math accuracy was about 34.09% (Qwen2.5VL 32B), while some smaller models were far lower (e.g. Ovis2 4B at 9.09%), suggesting substantial difficulty with visually grounded numeracy and geometry.
finding.measure: Open-ended accuracy on math benchmark questions

finding.finding_summary: Across non-science academic domains such as arts, history, religion, music, and sports, model performance varied widely. The strongest models reached roughly 54% in some domains (history/religion), but music was especially difficult, with best scores around 31%, and adversarial questions in these domains were answered correctly only infrequently.
finding.measure: Open-ended accuracy across arts, history, music, religion, and sports benchmark questions
finding.study_size: n=487 questions across arts (286), history (264), music (166), religion (206), sports (154); domains overlap in some analyses

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively examines reasoning-related abilities needed to combine image cues with background knowledge, including handling misleading or unanswerable questions. Models often hallucinated or guessed instead of indicating uncertainty, especially on adversarial items, suggesting weak metacognitive/critical-reasoning behavior in this benchmark context.
finding.measure: Accuracy on adversarial open-ended questions and error analysis of model responses
finding.study_size: n=486 images; adversarial questions drawn from the full benchmark

paper_profiles.title: The Illusion of Understanding: How Middle-Schoolers Fail to Regulate Inquiry with ChatGPT in a Science Task
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how middle-school students use ChatGPT during science investigation tasks, with a focus on whether they can initiate, evaluate, and regulate question-asking cycles in ways that support learning. The authors frame the study around meaningful question-asking (QA) and metacognitive regulation, arguing that effective use of GenAI in education requires more than technical familiarity with the tool; it requires the ability to pose precise prompts, judge answer quality, and decide when to follow up.

The study recruited 63 French middle school students aged 14–15 from four schools. Students completed six science tasks using ChatGPT 3.5, while researchers manipulated suggested prompts into efficient versus inefficient versions and asked students to judge prompt quality, evaluate every AI answer, and decide whether to continue or stop the QA cycle. The design also measured prior knowledge, attitudes toward AI, and metacognitive skills, then related these to interaction quality and task outcomes.

Findings show a strong pattern of over-reliance and weak epistemic vigilance. Students were near chance at distinguishing efficient from inefficient prompts (mean d′=0.19, SD=0.8; t=1.77, p=0.08) and at evaluating answer quality (mean d′=0.07, SD=1.2; t=-0.45, p=0.65). Only 14 students asked any follow-up questions, and final task success was modest (M=0.51, SD=0.25). Higher positive AI attitudes and higher prior confidence predicted worse prompt/answer discrimination, while metacognitive regulation and more critical perceptions of AI were associated with better interaction quality and more follow-up questioning. The authors conclude that middle-schoolers often experience an "illusion of understanding" with ChatGPT in science tasks and argue for AI literacy interventions that explicitly teach metacognitive regulation and critical evaluation.

finding.finding_summary: Middle school students showed only modest success in science investigation tasks with ChatGPT, with an average final correct-solution rate of M=0.51 (SD=0.25) across six problems. The authors interpret this as evidence that students' ability to generate and verify explanations for scientific concepts was undermined by weak prompt quality, poor answer evaluation, and premature termination of inquiry cycles.
finding.measure: Accuracy of final written scientific explanations across six science investigation tasks

finding.finding_summary: Students displayed low persistence and limited self-regulation in LLM-mediated inquiry. Only 14 of 63 students asked any follow-up questions, and even when they judged answers as unsatisfactory they initiated follow-up only 31.8% of the time, indicating frequent premature termination of the QA cycle.
finding.measure: Follow-up question frequency / continuation of QA cycle after AI responses

finding.finding_summary: Students were near chance at judging prompt quality (mean d′=0.19, SD=0.8; t=1.77, p=0.08) and at evaluating AI answer quality (mean d′=0.07, SD=1.2; t=-0.45, p=0.65). Higher metacognitive regulation predicted better prompt discrimination (r=0.30, p=0.022), while positive AI attitudes and higher prior confidence predicted worse discrimination and weaker epistemic vigilance.
finding.measure: Signal detection sensitivity (d′) for prompt discrimination and answer evaluation; metacognitive regulation scores
finding.effect_size: d′=0.19; d′=0.07; r=0.30; β values reported in text

finding.finding_summary: For the non-science-specific process of prompt generation, efficient prompt suggestions produced high-level AI answers in 84.4% of cases, compared with 38.9% for self-generated prompts and 31.1% for inefficient suggestions. This suggests that prompt quality materially shaped the informational quality of AI outputs, though the paper uses this primarily as a proxy for students' prompting skill rather than as a standalone academic content outcome.
finding.measure: Quality of AI responses elicited by efficient vs. inefficient vs. self-generated prompts

paper_profiles.title: Pedagogy-driven Evaluation of Generative AI-powered Intelligent Tutoring Systems
paper_profiles.population: Not reported (paper is a review/proposal focused on ITS evaluation rather than a studied learner population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines a central challenge in AI in education: how to evaluate generative AI-powered intelligent tutoring systems (ITSs) in ways that reflect pedagogy rather than only surface-level response quality. The authors argue that existing approaches often rely on self-report, generic natural language generation metrics, or narrow human judgments, all of which miss important educational properties such as pedagogical guidance, metacognition, and active learning.

The paper is not an intervention study; it is a conceptual review and position paper synthesizing prior ITS evaluation literature. It reviews traditional, NLG-based, and pedagogy-oriented evaluation methods, then identifies two major obstacles: diverse evaluation pragmatics and lack of unification across learning science principles, metrics, and benchmarks. It proposes three research directions: unified evaluation frameworks, quantitative measurement of pedagogical guidance, and graph-based measurement of active learning.

The context is generative AI tutoring systems and educational dialogue systems, with examples drawn from math, science, and language tutoring benchmarks and prior work such as AutoTutor, MathDial, and BEA shared tasks. The authors conclude that progress in GenAI tutors depends on reliable, scalable evaluation methods that capture both correctness and pedagogical quality, and they call for the AIED community to develop standardized taxonomies, benchmarks, and automated evaluators grounded in learning science.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that existing ITS evaluation methods inadequately capture durable skills such as metacognition, critical thinking, and reflective learning. It does not report new learner outcomes, but synthesizes prior evidence and proposes that better evaluation should measure whether tutoring systems support these skills through guidance, questioning, and dialogue structure.
finding.measure: Metacognitive support, active learning, pedagogical guidance in tutoring interactions

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s main practical claim is that unified and automated evaluation frameworks would improve the scalability, reliability, and efficiency of ITS assessment. No empirical effect is reported, but the authors repeatedly argue that current human evaluation is costly and non-scalable, while proposed automated approaches would reduce evaluation burden and enable larger-scale benchmarking.
finding.measure: Evaluation scalability, reliability, and cost of assessing ITS responses

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly focuses on field-level implications for AIED evaluation standards, benchmarks, and research infrastructure. It argues that a unified evaluation taxonomy and standardized benchmarks would improve comparability across systems and support more responsible development of GenAI tutors, but it does not present empirical policy or institutional outcome data.
finding.measure: Evaluation unification, benchmark standardization, research framework development

paper_profiles.title: Perspectives on astronomy: probing Norwegian pre-service teachers and middle school students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reports the adaptation and translation of the Introductory Astronomy Questionnaire (IAQ) into Norwegian (the NIAQ) and uses it to probe astronomy-related knowledge, beliefs, and response styles among Norwegian pre-service teachers and middle school students. The authors are interested in whether a questionnaire originally developed in another context can reveal students’ understanding of astronomy content, their views about science and astronomy, and how those views change after instruction.

The study administered the NIAQ to 41 pre-service teachers enrolled in Physics II at the largest teacher education institution in Norway, and to 535 year 8 and 387 year 10 middle school students in eight schools around Oslo. The pre-service teachers completed pre- and post-instruction versions; the middle school students were used as pre- and post-samples around the astronomy module. The instrument included free-response, ranking, explaining, and multiple-choice items focused on astronomy concepts such as object sizes, distance scales, the Big Bang, astronomy vs. astrology, and the motion of Earth around the Sun.

Because this is an early report of ongoing analysis, the paper presents preliminary findings rather than a full inferential evaluation. The main results suggest that pre-service teachers improved in explaining astronomical concepts and became more able to provide detailed scientific explanations after instruction, but their responses to hypothetical students became less pedagogical and more authoritative. In contrast, middle school students showed little to no improvement on several astronomy knowledge tasks from year 8 to year 10, and substantial misconceptions about sizes and distances in the universe persisted, with notable gender differences. The authors conclude that the adapted instrument is useful for revealing both content knowledge and response patterns, and that further study of astronomy instruction and teacher preparation is warranted.

finding.finding_summary: The paper primarily examines students’ astronomy content understanding and their ability to give scientific explanations. Pre-service teachers showed significant gains in explaining astronomical objects and the Earth’s orbit after instruction, but middle school students showed little to no improvement from year 8 to year 10 on object-size and distance tasks. Sample sizes were n=40 pre/post pre-service teachers, n=535 year 8 students, and n=387 year 10 students.
finding.measure: NIAQ astronomy explanation, ranking, and content-response tasks (e.g. explaining stars/planets, ranking sizes and distances, Earth orbit explanations)

finding.finding_summary: The study also assesses astronomy-specific conceptual knowledge that does not fit neatly into literacy, numeracy, or general scientific reasoning categories. Pre-service teachers improved on explanatory items about astronomical objects and concepts, while middle school students’ scores on these same content questions were statistically identical or slightly lower post-instruction. The paper reports these patterns descriptively without effect sizes.
finding.measure: Astronomy content knowledge on the NIAQ (object explanations and related concept questions)

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly analyzes whether pre-service teachers’ written explanations were pedagogical versus authoritative, which reflects communication, perspective-taking, and metacognitive judgment. Pre-instruction, more than one-third of responses were pedagogical, but post-instruction fewer than 10% were pedagogical, indicating a marked shift toward authoritative responses. No effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Categorization of free-response explanations as pedagogical vs. authoritative

finding.finding_summary: The paper asks about interest in astronomy and physics, perceived importance to society, and how much remains to be discovered. Although pre-service teachers’ ratings increased slightly, the changes were not statistically significant, and middle school students’ high baseline ratings also did not change significantly pre- to post-instruction. The study reports averages on a 5-point scale but no effect size.
finding.measure: Ratings of interest, importance to society, and perceived openness of physics/astronomy on 5-point scales
finding.study_size: n=40 pre/post pre-service teachers; n=535 year 8; n=387 year 10

paper_profiles.title: Changing Data Sources in the Age of Machine Learning for Official Statistics
paper_profiles.venue: UNECE Machine Learning for Official Statistics Workshop 2023
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the risks that arise when official statistical agencies rely on external data sources for machine learning–based statistical production. The authors focus on how changing data sources can create technical, legal, ethical, and operational problems that affect the reliability, consistency, and continuity of statistics.

The paper is a conceptual workshop paper rather than an intervention study. It outlines types and causes of data-source change, including schema changes, API changes, concept drift, interruptions, ownership changes, legal changes, and shifts in ethics or public perception. For each type of change, it describes likely consequences for machine learning pipelines and statistical outputs, such as broken pipelines, prediction shift, model staleness, reduced validity, and discontinuation of statistics.

The context is official statistics production in national statistical offices and related public-sector agencies, with examples such as Twitter API changes and the use of external data for timelier and more flexible reporting. The paper concludes that agencies should use risk analysis, monitoring, diversification of data sources, technical robustness, and legal agreements to reduce vulnerability, but it emphasizes that no mitigation fully removes the underlying trade-offs and loss of control associated with external data dependency.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that changing external data sources can materially affect institutional statistical production, including timeliness, validity, accuracy, completeness, neutrality, and even the continued availability of statistics. It does not report an empirical study or effect size; instead, it provides a conceptual risk analysis of how data-source changes can disrupt agency workflows, governance, and public trust.
finding.measure: Official statistical production quality, continuity, and reliability under changing external data sources

paper_profiles.title: Blue Sky Ideas in Artificial Intelligence Education from the EAAI 2017 New and Future AI Educator Program
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a collection of short perspective essays written by participants in the EAAI New and Future AI Educator Program. The central purpose is not to evaluate a specific instructional intervention, but to propose ideas for improving AI education, especially for secondary school and early undergraduate settings and for interdisciplinary teaching.

Across the essays, the contributors discuss how AI might be taught earlier, how ethics should be embedded throughout AI curricula, how project-based and peer-learning formats could better connect AI with other disciplines, and how AI concepts might be made more accessible through games, hands-on activities, and student-centered discovery. Several essays specifically argue that introductory AI experiences can build technical imagination, reasoning, collaboration, and appreciation for ethics, while others emphasize that AI education should be designed to support broader societal and interdisciplinary goals.

Because the paper is primarily a set of conceptual recommendations and future-looking teaching proposals, it does not report experimental evidence or student outcome data. Its main value is as a theoretical and practice-oriented overview of plausible directions for AI education, including ideas that may be relevant to K-12 and undergraduate instructional design.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that interdisciplinary seminars, project-based collaboration, and student-centered discovery could strengthen collaboration, communication, independent thinking, reasoning, and metacognitive skills. These claims are conceptual rather than empirical; no sample sizes, effect sizes, or measured outcomes are reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Several essays suggest that early, hands-on, game-like, and student-driven AI experiences may increase curiosity, willingness, passion, engagement, and ownership of learning. The paper does not provide outcome data, so these are author expectations rather than measured effects.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The closest science-adjacent relevance is the argument that early exposure to AI concepts, reasoning, and modeling can support deeper understanding of how scientific and computational systems work, including logic, search, planning, and machine learning. However, the paper does not study scientific reasoning directly and reports no empirical measures.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Multiple essays argue for curriculum redesign, interdisciplinary program structures, ethics codes, IRB-like risk review for AI research, and institutional support for peer learning and project-based courses. These are policy and program proposals with no evaluated implementation results.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Machine Learning in Python: Main developments and technology trends in data science, machine learning, and artificial intelligence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a broad survey of the Python machine learning ecosystem, focusing on the main developments and technology trends across scientific computing, classical machine learning, automated machine learning (AutoML), GPU-accelerated data science, deep learning, model interpretability, and adversarial learning. Rather than testing a specific educational intervention, it synthesizes tools, libraries, and technical paradigms such as NumPy, Pandas, Scikit-learn, Dask, XGBoost, LightGBM, Auto-sklearn, TPOT, RAPIDS, and related systems.

The paper is written for practitioners and researchers who want an overview of how Python-based machine learning workflows are built, optimized, and scaled. It explains the roles of feature engineering, hyperparameter optimization, neural architecture search, distributed computing, and GPU acceleration, and it compares popular libraries and their design tradeoffs. The authors emphasize the accessibility and productivity benefits of Python for data science and the growing role of unified APIs and interoperable ecosystems.

Because the article is a technical review rather than an empirical study, it does not evaluate student learning, teacher practice, or educational outcomes directly. Its relevance to K-12 education research is indirect: it can inform background understanding of AI tools and the broader machine learning landscape, but it does not provide evidence about effects on scientific reasoning or other student outcomes in schools.

paper_profiles.title: 3DG: A Framework for Using Generative AI for Handling Sparse Learner Performance Data From Intelligent Tutoring Systems
paper_profiles.venue: LAK 2024 Workshop on Generative AI for Learning Analytics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of sparse learner-performance data in intelligent tutoring systems (ITSs), which can undermine learner modeling and knowledge tracing. The authors propose 3DG (3-Dimensional tensor for Densification and Generation), a framework that first imputes missing performance values with tensor factorization and then augments the data with generative models.

The study is implemented on an AutoTutor dataset from the Center for the Study of Adult Literacy (CSAL), specifically a reading-comprehension lesson with 118 adult learners. The framework clusters learners by estimated learning patterns, then compares GAN-based simulation with GPT-4-based simulation for generating additional learner-performance samples. The paper reports that tensor completion can effectively densify sparse data and that GAN produces more reliable simulations than GPT-4, with GAN yielding narrower and more consistent parameter distributions for the modeled learning-curve parameters.

Overall, the paper concludes that generative AI can help address sparsity in ITS data, potentially improving downstream learner modeling and personalized instruction. However, it is primarily a methodological paper about simulation and data engineering rather than a study of direct student learning outcomes. The empirical evidence is limited to comparing synthetic-data generation quality and the plausibility of reconstructed learning-pattern parameters, not educational achievement or behavioral outcomes in students.

finding.finding_summary: The paper uses an AutoTutor lesson in reading comprehension as the source domain for sparse learner-performance data, but it does not test whether the framework improves reading outcomes. The study focuses on imputing and simulating performance data from 118 adult learners rather than measuring gains on literacy assessments, so no educational effect on literacy can be inferred.
finding.measure: reading comprehension learner-performance data; synthetic-data generation quality rather than literacy achievement

finding.finding_summary: The 3DG framework is designed to improve the efficiency and completeness of sparse ITS datasets through tensor completion and generative augmentation. The paper reports that the approach effectively generated scalable, personalized simulations and could support more comprehensive analysis and modeling in ITSs, but it does not provide a quantified productivity effect size for operational outcomes.
finding.measure: data imputation/augmentation success; scalability of simulated learner-performance data

paper_profiles.title: Linking Artificial Intelligence Principles
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Workshop on Artificial Intelligence Safety (AAAI-Safe AI 2019)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the landscape of published artificial intelligence (AI) principles and governance statements, asking how different proposals overlap, differ, and can be semantically linked. The authors compiled 27 AI-principle documents from academia, non-profits, governments, and industry, then built the LAIP platform to extract key terms, expand them with word2vec-based semantic similarity, and map shared topics using RDF/OWL.

The main approach is a text-analytic comparison rather than an intervention study. The paper defines 10 high-level topics for AI principles (e.g., humanity, fairness, transparency, privacy, safety, accountability) and analyzes topic coverage and keyword coverage across the collected documents. It also compares topic frequencies by publisher type and argues that different organizations emphasize different considerations, which can complement one another in a more comprehensive AI governance framework.

The paper is not about students or schools, and it does not study learning outcomes, scientific reasoning, or educational implementation. Its substantive contribution is a conceptual and computational framework for organizing AI ethics principles and identifying gaps, especially around safety and long-term AGI/ASI considerations. The conclusions are policy- and governance-oriented: the authors recommend linking diverse AI principles into a unified framework and using semantic search to explore complementary perspectives.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that AI principles differ substantially across publishers and that no single proposal covers all major governance topics completely. Using semantic keyword expansion, the authors show that topic coverage can increase substantially, and they argue for linking multiple principles into a comprehensive governance framework rather than adopting any single one wholesale. No effect size is reported because this is a comparative text-analysis study of 27 documents, not an intervention study.
finding.measure: Topic coverage and keyword coverage across 27 AI principle documents; comparative frequency of topics by publisher type

paper_profiles.title: Natural Language Query Engine for Relational Databases using Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of making relational databases accessible to non-technical users who do not know SQL. The author proposes a natural-language interface that uses generative AI to translate user questions into SQL, validate the queries syntactically and semantically, incorporate business rules, and then generate natural-language answers from the retrieved data.

The system is prototyped using IBM watsonx.data, watsonx.ai, and Milvus as a vector database for schema and business-rule retrieval. The evaluation is conducted on the BIRD-SQL benchmark, which includes real-world text-to-SQL tasks of varying difficulty. The paper reports that over 50% of queries were translated correctly on the first attempt (over 58% for simple queries), and that iterative refinement improved success rates further. A small informal test with a dozen nontechnical users suggested the generated natural-language responses were coherent and easy to understand, but this was not a controlled study.

Overall, the paper concludes that generative AI plus vector-based retrieval can improve the usability and correctness of database querying for enterprise users, especially by reducing reliance on SQL expertise and by embedding domain/business rules into the query process. The contribution is primarily a systems/prototype paper rather than an education study, and its evidence comes from benchmark evaluation and informal user feedback rather than a K-12 or instructional intervention.

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI and Its Impact on Personalized Intelligent Tutoring Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper discusses how generative AI, especially large language models such as GPT-4, may change personalized intelligent tutoring systems (ITS). It focuses on the promise of AI for generating customized questions, delivering real-time feedback, and supporting interactive dialogue that adapts to individual learners' needs. The central question is not whether a specific intervention works in a measured experiment, but rather how generative AI can be integrated into ITS and what capabilities and constraints such systems present.

The paper is a conceptual report/literature synthesis rather than an empirical study. It reviews prior work on automated question generation, personalized feedback, and conversational tutoring, and then discusses challenges including pedagogical accuracy, model bias, learner engagement, multimodal integration, affective computing, and ethical/policy concerns. The context is broad educational technology, not a specific grade level, subject, or geographic setting.

Its main conclusion is that generative AI could substantially increase the personalization and interactivity of ITS, but realizing that potential requires strong validation, human oversight, and bias mitigation. The paper does not present original outcome data or causal evidence; instead, it argues that future systems should combine generative flexibility with pedagogical controls to improve educational effectiveness and equity.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not report empirical results on academic achievement or subject-specific learning outcomes; it is a conceptual report about how generative AI might be used in intelligent tutoring systems. It discusses applications such as automated question generation and contextual science examples, but provides no measured effects on academic performance.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The report argues that generative AI-enhanced ITS may improve learner engagement, motivation, and support by offering personalized feedback and interactive dialogue. However, these claims are not backed by original empirical data in the paper; they are presented as anticipated benefits from the literature.
finding.measure: learner engagement, motivation, and perceived support

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that AI-generated explanations, hints, and step-by-step guidance can support deeper understanding and adaptive problem solving, which may relate to critical thinking and metacognition. No direct assessment of durable skills is reported, so this is a theoretical implication rather than an observed effect.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The report claims generative AI can improve the efficiency of ITS by automating question generation and producing real-time personalized feedback, reducing the need for static question banks and repetitive authoring. These benefits are described conceptually, without measured productivity or workload outcomes.
finding.measure: authoring efficiency / automated question generation / feedback generation

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (position paper; discusses elementary through professional education contexts, with examples for middle and high school students)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities and challenges of large language models, especially ChatGPT and GPT-3, for education. Rather than testing a specific intervention, the authors synthesize early research and provide a conceptual overview of how LLMs may support learning, teaching, assessment, and educational innovation across school levels and professional contexts.

The paper argues that LLMs could help generate educational content, support personalized feedback, improve engagement, and assist with lesson planning, writing, and assessment. It also highlights risks such as bias, plagiarism, privacy concerns, overreliance, difficulty distinguishing machine-generated from human-generated text, and access inequities. The authors conclude that LLMs may be beneficial if used responsibly, with strong human oversight, critical thinking, fact checking, and institutional guidance.

The paper is not an empirical study of students in one setting; instead, it discusses prior studies and plausible applications of LLMs in elementary, middle, high school, university, and teacher education contexts.
