It recommends that educators and policymakers adopt careful implementation strategies and further research on best practices, especially for responsible and fair use in classrooms.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that large language models may support critical thinking, problem-solving, and question asking by generating prompts, explanations, and step-by-step solutions, but also warns that overreliance could weaken learners’ independent reasoning. No original effect size is reported because this is a position paper synthesizing prior work rather than an intervention study.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, and question-asking support/risks discussed conceptually

finding.finding_summary: The paper consistently frames LLMs as tools that can reduce teacher workload and improve efficiency through automated quiz generation, feedback, assessment, lesson planning, and content drafting. These claims are illustrative and synthesis-based rather than empirically estimated in this paper, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher time/effort, grading burden, and content-generation efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes institutional issues including bias mitigation, privacy and security, copyright, governance, sustainability, and fair access to LLMs in education. It concludes that successful adoption requires policies, human oversight, and infrastructure support, but it does not provide quantitative institutional outcome data.
finding.measure: Policy, governance, privacy, fairness, and access considerations

finding.finding_summary: The paper states that LLMs can support reading comprehension, writing style, grammar, summaries, outlines, and feedback on written work, especially for elementary and secondary learners. These are proposed and supported by cited examples, not new experimental results in this paper.
finding.measure: Reading and writing support, including comprehension, grammar, summaries, and feedback

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that LLMs can assist language learning through conversation practice, pronunciation practice, translations, grammar explanations, and vocabulary support. No direct empirical estimate is reported here; the claim is based on prior studies and conceptual argumentation.
finding.measure: Language learning support, including speaking/pronunciation and vocabulary practice

finding.finding_summary: The paper indicates that LLMs can be used to generate explanations, step-by-step solutions, and related questions in science-related subjects such as physics, and cites prior work in chemistry and scientific argument feedback as evidence of potential. It does not present direct science-intervention outcomes, so no quantitative effect size is available.
finding.measure: Science-related problem solving and scientific argumentation support (conceptual and cited examples)

paper_profiles.title: AI literacy in K-12: a systematic literature review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This systematic literature review examines how artificial intelligence (AI) literacy is being introduced into K-12 education worldwide. The authors searched Scopus and screened 750 records, ultimately reviewing 179 documents to characterize the field and identify recurring approaches, gaps, and implementation trends.

The review distinguishes two broad types of work: learning experiences and theoretical perspectives. Learning experiences focus on helping students recognize AI, understand how AI works, use AI tools, and think critically about AI’s role in society; theoretical work includes curriculum design, standards, teacher training, resources, and national or regional implementation schemes. The paper emphasizes that most experiences are short, technical, and applied, and that few studies rigorously assess student learning outcomes. It also highlights that the U.S. and China are leading broader implementation efforts, but that K-12 AI education remains fragmented and underdeveloped.

The paper’s main conclusion is that AI literacy should be integrated into existing disciplinary subjects rather than added as a standalone subject, and that it should be competency-based, interdisciplinary, contextualized, and co-designed with teachers. The review also argues that ethical, social, and security dimensions of AI need stronger attention, and that teacher preparation is central to successful integration. Because this is a synthesis paper rather than an intervention study, it does not estimate causal effects on student outcomes, but it provides important guidance for future science-adjacent AI education research.

finding.finding_summary: The review suggests that AI literacy can be leveraged to enhance learning in disciplinary subjects, including science, by integrating AI into the teaching process. However, the paper does not report direct experimental evidence that K-12 AI literacy interventions improve scientific reasoning; instead, it synthesizes mostly descriptive and theoretical work and notes that rigorous learning-outcome assessment is largely absent in the literature.
finding.measure: not_reported
finding.study_size: 179 documents reviewed; no direct scientific-reasoning outcome study reported

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed literature, AI literacy is framed as supporting critical thinking, critical consumption of AI, and ethical reflection about technology. The review highlights student-facing work on attitudes, intentions, and the development of critical capacity, but it does not aggregate quantitative effect sizes or provide a causal estimate.
finding.measure: Student attitudes, intentions, and critical/ethical understanding of AI

finding.finding_summary: The reviewed studies include student-focused work on interest and intention to learn AI, as well as engagement-oriented and motivating design features such as real-world and socially relevant contexts. The review concludes that such approaches may support motivation and involvement, especially when AI is contextualized around meaningful problems, but it does not provide pooled empirical effects.
finding.measure: Interest, intention, motivation, and engagement with AI learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper strongly emphasizes curriculum development, national implementation schemes, teacher training, and policy guidance for AI literacy in K-12. It identifies the U.S. and China as leading broader-scale implementation efforts and argues that competency frameworks and co-designed curricula are needed for institutional adoption.
finding.measure: Curriculum proposals, policy schemes, teacher-training frameworks, and implementation models

paper_profiles.title: Promises and challenges of generative artificial intelligence for human learning
paper_profiles.population: Not specific to a single empirical sample; broad human learning / K-12 through higher education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a Perspective article examining how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), especially large language models and diffusion models, may reshape human learning. It does not test a single intervention; instead, it synthesizes prior research to outline where GenAI may support learning through personalized tutoring, resource generation, faster feedback, and new forms of assessment, while also warning about hallucinations, bias, privacy, inequality, and the risk of over-reliance.

The authors organize the discussion around four promise areas—learning support, learning resources, learning feedback, and learning assessment—and then contrast them with major challenges and research needs. They argue that GenAI could improve access to guidance and feedback at scale, help educators produce richer materials, and enable more authentic assessments, but emphasize that current evidence is still limited and often mixed. They conclude that future work should prioritize AI literacy, evidence-based decision-making, and rigorous research designs to understand GenAI’s true effects on cognition, metacognition, creativity, and learner agency across educational contexts.

Because the article is a theory-and-evidence synthesis rather than an empirical study, it does not report a new sample, effect size, or direct outcome estimates. Its main contribution is a conceptual roadmap for researchers, educators, and policymakers on how GenAI should be evaluated and integrated responsibly into education.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that GenAI may support inquiry-based and conceptually guided learning by prompting students to think through problems, unpack concepts, and engage in step-by-step reasoning, which could support scientific reasoning in science-adjacent contexts. However, it also stresses that empirical evidence on whether these tools actually improve deeper reasoning is limited and that overreliance may weaken critical thinking and problem-solving.
finding.measure: Conceptual synthesis of prior studies on inquiry-based learning, problem-solving, and reasoning support

finding.finding_summary: The article reviews evidence that GenAI can generate instructional materials, quiz questions, videos, and other learning resources across subjects, including programming, biology, poetry, and STEAM. It cites examples where GenAI-produced materials increased engagement, satisfaction, and learning performance, but also notes that higher-order tasks and pedagogical accuracy remain weak points requiring expert human oversight.
finding.measure: Quality and usefulness of AI-generated learning resources and instructional materials

finding.finding_summary: The paper synthesizes evidence that GenAI feedback and tutoring may increase learner motivation, engagement, and positive emotions, and that students often respond positively to personalized support. At the same time, it warns that AI assistance can create a performance illusion, reduce agency, and foster dependency, so any benefits for motivation and engagement may be unstable or context-dependent.
finding.measure: Learner engagement, motivation, positive emotions, and agency in GenAI-supported learning contexts

finding.finding_summary: A central theme of the paper is GenAI’s likely influence on durable skills such as critical thinking, metacognition, problem-solving, creativity, and self-regulation. The authors argue GenAI can scaffold these skills through dialogic prompting and guided inquiry, but they also emphasize evidence of reduced performance when AI support is removed, suggesting that some apparent gains may reflect augmentation rather than genuine skill development.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, metacognition, problem-solving, creativity, and self-regulated learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that GenAI can improve efficiency by scaling personalized tutoring, automating feedback, generating learning materials, and reducing educator workload associated with routine instructional tasks. It presents this as one of GenAI’s clearest promised benefits, though it notes costs, computational demands, and the need for human validation.
finding.measure: Instructional productivity, feedback efficiency, and educator workload reduction

finding.finding_summary: The paper devotes substantial attention to institutional implications, including AI literacy, privacy, transparency, equity, beneficence, and assessment policy. It argues that GenAI could reshape educational systems and assessment practices, but also warns that unequal access, opaque model behavior, and weak governance could exacerbate inequities and undermine trust.
finding.measure: Policy, governance, equity, transparency, and assessment implications of GenAI adoption in education

paper_profiles.title: Speculative Futures on ChatGPT and Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI): A Collective Reflection from the Educational Landscape
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper responds to the rapid rise of ChatGPT and generative AI in education by asking what future educational landscapes might look like if these tools become widely adopted. Rather than testing an intervention, the authors use a speculative methodology and collective writing to create fictional narratives that explore both optimistic and pessimistic futures for AI in education.

The paper is grounded in the broader K-12 and higher education AI-in-education literature, but its own contribution is conceptual and reflective. Across multiple fictional scenarios written by an international group of educators and researchers, the authors imagine AI as supporting personalized learning, accessibility, multilingual communication, feedback, assessment, and productivity, while also raising concerns about bias, privacy, academic integrity, dependence on technology, inequity, and the erosion of human agency.

The population is not a single empirical sample; the work is authored by adult education researchers and framed around educational practice in general, including K-12, higher education, and lifelong learning. The main conclusion is that AI in education is context-dependent and should be adopted critically, ethically, and with human educators retaining the central role. The paper argues for new AI literacies, new assessment approaches, and careful attention to access, governance, and the human purposes of education.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI can support writing and language development by providing instant feedback, suggestions, and assisted composition. In the positive narratives, ChatGPT-like tools are described as helping students improve writing, summarize concepts, and generate text more easily, but no empirical study or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Writing assistance, feedback, and language-related composition tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes AI as useful for removing language barriers, improving language skills, and supporting oral/written communication through conversational practice and translation. These claims are illustrated in speculative narratives about language learning and multilingual communication, but they are not backed by empirical measurement in this paper.
finding.measure: Oral and written communication, pronunciation, translation, and conversational practice

finding.finding_summary: The narratives suggest that AI may increase engagement, motivation, confidence, and emotional support through personalized prompting and encouragement, but they also warn about dependency and dehumanization. Because the paper is speculative, these are proposed effects rather than measured outcomes.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, confidence, and affective support

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly centers critical thinking, collaboration, creativity, and learner agency as key issues. It suggests AI may support brainstorming, collaboration, and tailored scaffolding, but also may weaken creativity and critical thinking if over-relied upon; no empirical data are reported.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, creativity, collaboration, learner agency, and problem-solving

finding.finding_summary: A major theme is that ChatGPT-like tools can save time and reduce educator workload through automated grading, lesson planning, email writing, summarization, and question generation. The paper treats operational efficiency as one of the central promised benefits of generative AI, but does not provide empirical estimates.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, grading, lesson preparation, and task automation

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI could reshape educational systems by changing assessment practices, access, equity, policies, and the role of human educators. It also warns about privacy, ethics, bias, surveillance, and widening digital divides; these are conceptual implications derived from speculative narratives rather than measured institutional outcomes.
finding.measure: Assessment policy, access/equity, privacy, governance, and institutional roles

paper_profiles.title: Teacher’s Perceptions of Using an Artificial Intelligence-Based Educational Tool for Scientific Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 STEM teachers perceive an artificial intelligence-enhanced scaffolding system (AISS) designed to support scientific writing and argumentation. The authors focus on whether hands-on experience with the tool changes teachers’ views of AI in instruction and what concerns teachers raise about using AI in the classroom.

The study was conducted with nine in-service teachers enrolled in a doctoral program at a U.S. university in the southeast region. Participants, who taught elementary, middle, or high school subjects such as science, math, physics, and English, first reviewed readings and examples of AI in education, then used the AISS to complete an authentic writing task about air quality. The system used GPT-2 to generate individualized sentence and paragraph completions intended to serve as conceptual and strategic scaffolding for scientific writing.

Using interviews, log files, and thematic analysis, the authors found that teachers generally viewed the AI tool positively because it provided immediate, individualized, expert-like scaffolding, supported reasoning and evidence-based writing, and could be useful for middle and high school students. Teachers also identified important concerns, especially possible reductions in the teacher’s role and the need for transparency, explainability, accuracy, and validity in AI-generated support. The study concludes that teacher experience with AI tools can improve receptiveness to AI integration, but successful adoption will require professional development and careful attention to classroom roles and trust in the system.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the AI-enhanced scaffolding system helped with scientific writing by generating well-written sentences and paragraphs, modeling stronger structure, and supporting revision. The intervention was used with n=9 teachers completing an essay task, and the system was perceived as improving sentence structure, paragraph sequencing, and evidence-based writing, though no quantitative writing-score effect was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of scientific writing support; writing task outputs and interview reflections

finding.finding_summary: Participants said the system strengthened claim-evidence reasoning, argumentation, and justification of claims in the context of an ill-structured air-quality writing task. Teachers described the AI as an expert model that prompted them to reflect on their argument process and connect claims with supporting evidence, but the study provides qualitative perceptions rather than measured gains in reasoning performance.
finding.measure: Perceived support for argumentation, reasoning, and evidence-based scientific writing

finding.finding_summary: Teachers believed the AI tool promoted higher-order thinking, problem-solving, and self-directed reflection because users had to compare AI suggestions with their own ideas and revise accordingly. The evidence is qualitative and based on interview themes about reasoning, metacognition, and learner-centered problem solving, with no standardized durable-skill outcome measure reported.
finding.measure: Interview themes on higher-order thinking, reasoning, self-directed learning, and problem-solving

finding.finding_summary: Teachers perceived the AI system as providing immediate individualized feedback and reducing some burdens associated with creating expert-like scaffolds for students. However, this was framed as a potential benefit rather than a measured reduction in workload, and some teachers also worried that AI might complicate their role by inserting an intermediary system between teachers and students.
finding.measure: Perceptions of feedback speed, personalization, and teacher-role implications

paper_profiles.title: A Review on Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.population: K-12 and higher education (mixed; broad education context)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews the application of artificial intelligence in education, focusing on how AI technologies are being used across teaching, learning, assessment, classroom management, virtual learning environments, smart campuses, and tutoring robots. The authors synthesize prior literature rather than reporting a single empirical study, and frame AI as a set of tools that can support personalized learning, automate routine instructional tasks, and improve management and access in educational settings.

The review discusses several AI applications, including adaptive learning systems, automated scoring and feedback, virtual classrooms and laboratories, smart campus infrastructure, and intelligent tutoring robots. Across these examples, the paper argues that AI can improve teaching efficiency, support student learning quality, and enable more individualized instruction, while also warning about challenges such as equity, ethics, privacy, teacher readiness, and student self-regulation.

The paper is broad in scope and not limited to one country, subject area, or age group, although it draws on K-12, higher education, and online learning examples. It includes some empirical studies cited within the review, such as ALEKS math use with middle school students, but the paper itself does not present new primary data. Its main conclusion is that AI has meaningful potential in education, but implementation must be handled carefully to avoid widening inequalities and to ensure responsible use.

finding.finding_summary: The review cites Yilmaz (2018), who investigated ALEKS use with middle school students and found a statistically significant positive impact on end-of-year mathematics scores. Fang et al. (2019) are also summarized as finding that ALEKS performs about as well as traditional classroom teaching, but not better overall unless used for shorter periods.
finding.measure: Middle school mathematics achievement / end-of-year mathematics scores

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that AI-supported adaptive learning can increase students’ autonomy, self-regulation, and engagement, especially through personalized learning paths and customized practice. However, these claims are drawn from cited studies rather than a new empirical test in this paper.
finding.measure: Autonomous learning ability, self-regulation, engagement, motivation

finding.finding_summary: The paper summarizes prior work showing positive effects of AI-supported language learning and speech technologies, including improved autonomous learning and English ability in a college English platform study and benefits from pronunciation correction and oral practice tools. These findings are presented as review evidence rather than original results from this article.
finding.measure: English ability, oral practice, pronunciation correction, autonomous language learning

finding.finding_summary: A central conclusion of the review is that AI improves efficiency in assessment, classroom management, and teacher workload by automating grading, scoring, paper analysis, attendance, and other repetitive tasks. The paper does not report a single pooled effect size, but repeatedly describes reduced teacher burden and more accurate/faster evaluation as key benefits.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, grading/scoring efficiency, classroom management efficiency, attendance processing

finding.finding_summary: The review discusses virtual laboratories and virtual reality for science learning, noting that they can help students understand science concepts and complete experiments safely in simulated settings. At the same time, it cites Makransky et al. (2019) to note that VR can increase presence but also cognitive overload and distract learners, leading to poorer learning outcomes in science-related tasks.
finding.measure: Science concept understanding, virtual lab learning outcomes, VR science learning

paper_profiles.title: AutoTutor and Family: A Review of 17 Years of Natural Language Tutoring
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review paper synthesizes 17 years of research on AutoTutor and related natural-language tutoring systems. It asks what tutoring strategies, interface features, and supporting technologies make conversational tutoring effective, and it organizes the evidence around human-inspired tutoring strategies, pedagogical agents, and natural-language tutoring technologies.

The paper is not a single intervention study; instead, it reviews many empirical evaluations of AutoTutor-family systems across domains such as computer literacy, physics, biology, critical thinking, reading comprehension, and self-regulated learning. The central intervention pattern is a dialogue-based tutor that uses deep reasoning questions, pumps, hints, prompts, assertions, and adaptive discourse to scaffold student explanations. The review also summarizes later extensions that add affect detection, gaze sensitivity, collaborative lecturing, learning progressions, and metacognitive supports.

Across the reviewed studies, the authors conclude that AutoTutor-style systems generally produce learning gains relative to static materials and can approach the performance of human tutors in some contexts. Reported effects vary by domain and outcome type, with stronger gains often appearing for deep reasoning and cloze-type assessments than for shallow factual questions. The review also highlights that affect-sensitive support can help low-knowledge learners, collaborative lecturing can be effective, and macro-adaptive learning-progressions-based systems may improve outcomes, though many findings are drawn from heterogeneous studies with different designs and populations.

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that AutoTutor and related systems improved learning in physics and science-reasoning contexts, with a representative study showing gains of 0.61σ over a control group and 1.22σ over a read-textbook condition on physics learning tests (n=not_reported in the review excerpt). Another review summary reports DeepTutor with macro-adaptivity producing 0.79σ pretest-posttest gains in a small-scale evaluation (n=30) after 1 hour of training. These findings support positive effects on conceptual scientific reasoning and explanation-based understanding, especially when tutoring targets deep reasoning questions.
finding.measure: Physics/science concept learning tests; pretest-posttest assessments; multiple-choice and essay measures adapted from the Force Concept Inventory

finding.finding_summary: The paper summarizes evidence that AutoTutor-family systems improved computer literacy and biology learning. For example, AutoTutor for computer literacy produced learning gains of about 0.5σ over textbook controls, and Guru for biology produced approximately 0.72σ gains over classroom instruction only. These results indicate positive effects in non-science academic domains as well, though the paper is primarily a synthesis rather than a new experimental report.
finding.measure: Computer literacy tests; biology posttests

finding.finding_summary: The review notes that AutoTutor-family work extended to reading comprehension systems such as iSTART, which improved reading comprehension for both skilled and less-skilled readers, including middle-schoolers. The reported pattern was differential by skill level: less-skilled readers improved on single-sentence content questions, while more skilled readers improved on bridging questions that connect multiple sentences. Exact effect sizes are not provided in the excerpted review text.
finding.measure: Reading comprehension questions (single-sentence content and bridging questions)

finding.finding_summary: A substantial portion of the review concerns critical thinking, metacognition, scientific inquiry, and self-regulated learning. The paper reports positive gains for Operation ARA on scientific research skills (1.4σ versus no-instruction controls) and describes SEEK and MetaTutor as targeting deep questioning, information evaluation, and self-regulated learning, although SEEK itself did not significantly improve relevant information-finding skills. Overall, the synthesis indicates that AutoTutor-family systems can support durable skills, especially when instruction is structured, extended, and aligned with the targeted metacognitive process.
finding.measure: Scientific research skills; critical thinking; metacognitive and self-regulated learning tasks
finding.study_size: not_reported; ARA intervention described as 8-12 h

finding.finding_summary: The review summarizes affect-sensitive tutoring studies showing that adapting to student emotion can help some learners but not others. Supportive AutoTutor produced higher posttest gains for low-knowledge students (0.71σ) when compared with standard AutoTutor, but benefits appeared mainly on a second session and were not observed for high-knowledge students, who sometimes learned less with emotional support. GazeTutor also increased attention to the tutor and produced small overall gains (0.26σ, not statistically significant) with moderate gains on deep learning (0.45σ).
finding.measure: Posttest scores; attention to tutor; deep-learning performance

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that AutoTutor-family systems can scale tutoring-like support and reduce reliance on static instruction, but it does not report a direct operational-efficiency evaluation such as time savings or teacher workload reduction. The closest evidence is that AutoTutor produced learning gains about 0.8σ above static materials for the same amount of study time, suggesting more efficient learning per unit time than textbook study. This is an indirect efficiency signal rather than a direct operational measure.
finding.measure: Learning gains per equivalent study time versus static instructional materials

paper_profiles.title: Transdisciplinary AI Education: The Confluence of Curricular and Community Needs in the Instruction of Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.venue: AIET 2023 / Lecture Notes in Design and Digital Technologies
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of how to teach artificial intelligence in K-12 settings in ways that are not siloed as standalone computer science content. The authors argue that existing AI curricula often focus on discrete technical concepts and do not sufficiently connect AI to broader curricular, community, ethical, and societal contexts.

The paper presents the design of a transdisciplinary AI curriculum developed for Neom Community School in Saudi Arabia, spanning kindergarten through eighth grade. The approach combines project-based learning, problem-based learning, inquiry-based lessons, and an International Baccalaureate Units of Inquiry framework. Students engage with AI through topics such as computer vision, facial recognition, emotional recognition, invasive species, and hybrid cars, using tools such as Cozmo and Calypso, Teachable Machine, and block-based programming.

The paper is primarily a program design and implementation description rather than an empirical evaluation with outcome data. It argues that transdisciplinary AI instruction can make AI more meaningful, accessible, and connected to students’ lives and communities, while also fostering awareness of ethical, social, and practical implications. The authors conclude that AI should be integrated across the curriculum rather than taught in isolation, especially for middle-school-aged learners who are beginning to form views about AI and related careers.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the curriculum is designed to foster critical thinking, collaboration, communication, and problem solving through challenge assignments, mini-projects, inquiry activities, and project-based tasks. However, the paper does not report empirical effect sizes or student outcome data; the claimed benefits are descriptive and design-based rather than measured.
finding.measure: Not reported; described through curriculum activities emphasizing collaboration, critical thinking, and problem solving

finding.finding_summary: The curriculum is intended to increase student engagement, willingness, and motivation to learn AI by embedding hands-on, relevant, and community-connected activities. The paper repeatedly claims that project-based and inquiry-based lessons make AI less stressful and more appealing, but it does not provide quantitative engagement outcomes or sample-based estimates.
finding.measure: Not reported; described in terms of engagement, willingness, and interest in AI learning

finding.finding_summary: A central claim of the paper is that AI should be integrated transdisciplinarily across the school curriculum and supported by collaboration among homeroom teachers, AI teachers, and community stakeholders. The paper frames the Neom Community School implementation as an institutional model for curriculum design, but it reports no empirical evidence on policy, governance, or schoolwide outcomes.
finding.measure: Not reported; institutional curriculum design and cross-disciplinary implementation model

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that learning AI through inquiry into tools such as facial recognition, computer vision, and invasive-species classifiers can help students understand how AI works and how it is applied in scientific contexts. This is presented as a curricular rationale, not as measured evidence of gains in scientific reasoning, and no direct science outcome data are reported.
finding.measure: Not reported; science-adjacent inquiry into AI applications such as invasive species classification and computer vision

paper_profiles.title: AISCliteracy: Assessing Artificial Intelligence and Cybersecurity Literacy Levels and Learning Needs of Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the current level of artificial intelligence (AI) and cybersecurity literacy among secondary students in Chitwan District, Nepal, where AI and cybersecurity are not yet fully integrated into the school curriculum. The authors frame the problem as a gap between rapid technological change and the limited preparation students receive to understand AI concepts, applications, risks, and ethical implications.

Using a mixed-methods approach, the study surveyed 303 students in grades 9–12 from multiple schools in Chitwan District and complemented the survey with qualitative interviews. The questionnaire measured students’ self-reported understanding of AI, awareness of AI benefits and risks, familiarity with AI technologies, cybersecurity practices, and school support for AI/cybersecurity learning, with responses analyzed using Relative Importance Index (RII).

Findings suggest students report moderate to high AI literacy and fairly strong cybersecurity awareness, but weaker exposure to formal instruction and training. Students were generally optimistic about AI and interested in learning more about it, yet they also indicated that schools provide limited AI resources and limited cybersecurity education or workshops. The paper concludes that Nepalese schools need more structured AI and cybersecurity curriculum support, especially in advanced AI topics and hands-on cybersecurity learning, to better prepare students for the digital age.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported moderate to high self-assessed AI literacy, including understanding what AI is (RII=0.78020), recognizing everyday AI uses (RII=0.78548), and feeling comfortable discussing AI topics with peers or teachers (RII=0.80528). They were also interested in learning more about AI (RII=0.83696), suggesting positive engagement with a topic relevant to critical thinking and future-oriented problem solving.
finding.measure: Self-reported AI literacy, awareness, and interest survey items (Relative Importance Index scores)

finding.finding_summary: The study found that schools in the sample were not providing sufficient formal AI or cybersecurity education, with relatively low ratings for school-provided AI resources/courses (RII=0.65215) and adequate online safety education (RII=0.75050). It also found very limited participation in cybersecurity training or workshops (RII=0.45149), indicating an institutional gap despite students' generally positive attitudes and awareness.
finding.measure: Perceptions of school-provided AI/cybersecurity resources and education; self-reported training exposure

paper_profiles.title: AI as a Teaching Partner: Early Lessons from Classroom Codesign with Secondary Teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report examines how secondary teachers used a generative AI classroom platform, Colleague AI Classroom, during a seven-week co-design pilot. The core question is not whether the tool raises student achievement in a controlled sense, but how teachers design and implement AI-supported classroom activities, how teacher judgment and AI fluency shape those activities, and what supports are needed for effective integration.

The pilot involved 21 in-service teachers across five Washington State districts and one independent school, with more than 600 students in grades 6-12. Teachers integrated four features: a Teaching Aide for structured student-AI conversations, AI-assisted assessment and grading, an AI Tutor, and Student Growth Insights (SGI) for teacher-facing analytics. Data came from surveys, planning/reflection forms, interviews, group meetings, exit tickets, and platform logs, making this an exploratory mixed-methods implementation study rather than an experimental efficacy trial.

Findings suggest that AI was most useful when tightly scaffolded by teachers and aligned to clear instructional goals. Teachers generally reported that the Teaching Aide supported inquiry, engagement, and learning when prompts were explicit and the teacher stayed present; AI-generated assessment feedback was valued mainly as formative narrative feedback, while numeric scores were viewed as inconsistent and less trustworthy. SGI reduced teacher workload by surfacing common misconceptions and student growth patterns, and teachers reported that these features could improve feedback loops and instructional adjustment. However, outcomes varied by subject, grade band, and teacher AI experience, with middle school students needing shorter, more structured interactions and STEM/math applications facing more accuracy and reasoning challenges.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that AI-supported student conversations often increased engagement, confidence, and willingness to participate, especially when the activity was scaffolded and framed as a thought partner. Across Teaching Aide implementations, 28% of teachers reported most students engaged thoughtfully, 66% reported mixed engagement, and only 6% reported limited engagement overall (n=18 teachers reporting on implementation experiences).
finding.measure: Teacher-reported student engagement with Teaching Aide conversations
finding.study_size: n=18 teachers (across 21 classrooms; up to 600 students)

finding.finding_summary: The pilot suggests AI conversations and feedback could support reasoning, revision, and inquiry when aligned to instructional goals. Teachers described students using AI to deepen seminar preparation, revise work, and engage in evidence-based reasoning, although the report does not provide a formal effect size or controlled comparison.
finding.measure: Teacher reports of reasoning, revision, inquiry, and conversational depth

finding.finding_summary: The strongest and most consistently documented benefit was reduced teacher workload through faster feedback, streamlined grading, and automated aggregation of student growth patterns. Platform logs showed 92.2% median AI grading coverage on submitted work and 54.8% mean submission rate across 58 assessments, while teachers reported that SGI saved hours of scanning and AI feedback served as a usable first draft that reduced commenting burden.
finding.measure: AI grading coverage, submission rates, and teacher-reported workload/efficiency
finding.study_size: 58 assessment records across 33 classrooms; 19 teachers in assessment phase

finding.finding_summary: The study found that AI-supported activities could improve subject-specific learning tasks outside literacy and mathematics, especially in science, Spanish, and interdisciplinary STEM contexts. Teachers reported that science conversations supported inquiry and culturally relevant content, while AI feedback in Spanish aided real-time proficiency feedback; however, these findings were descriptive and varied by subject, with math and earth science showing more mixed results.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported subject-specific learning outcomes and implementation experiences
finding.study_size: n=21 teachers; science feature use reported across 7 science classes

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that AI-assisted writing and prewriting activities improved essay quality and supported brainstorming/prewriting in ELA. In the assessment feature, teachers valued narrative feedback for revising student written responses, although the report does not provide a controlled measure of writing gains.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported effects on writing, brainstorming, prewriting, and revision

finding.finding_summary: Science-related implementations were described as supporting inquiry and expanded opportunities for reasoning, but the evidence is exploratory and based on teacher report rather than direct science achievement measures. The report also notes that science and earth science sometimes produced mixed results because AI struggled with diagrams and technical reasoning, indicating both promise and limitations for scientific reasoning support.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported inquiry support and reasoning quality in science/earth science implementations

paper_profiles.title: Rise of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Science
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether generative AI (GenAI) is diffusing into scientific research, how it is distributed across disciplines and countries, and whether it is associated with different collaboration patterns than other forms of AI. The authors position the study as an exploratory bibliometric analysis intended to clarify the scope of GenAI use in science and to inform debates about its possible benefits, risks, and organizational consequences.

Using OpenAlex metadata for publications from 2017–2023, the authors identify GenAI-related papers through title/abstract keyword searches and compare them with a broader corpus of other-AI papers. They examine disciplinary diffusion across OpenAlex root concepts, geographic distribution by country, and collaboration intensity using Poisson regression models on a cleaned dataset of 958,343 publications with complete institutional information. The analysis shows rapid growth in GenAI publications, especially after 2022, and broad diffusion beyond computer science into fields such as medicine, chemistry, geography, psychology, and sociology.

The study finds that U.S. researchers account for the largest share of GenAI publications, that GenAI research is slightly more internationally collaborative than other AI research, and that GenAI papers have slightly smaller author teams on average than other-AI papers. The authors interpret these patterns cautiously, noting that the effects are small but may reflect easier access to GenAI tools and evolving research practices. Because the paper is about publication patterns in science rather than student learning or classroom use, it is only indirectly relevant to education research.

finding.finding_summary: The paper documents rapid diffusion of GenAI in scientific publishing across disciplines and countries, indicating a broad institutional shift in how research is being conducted. GenAI publications grew especially quickly after 2022, and the U.S. accounted for 39% of global GenAI output, but the study is descriptive and does not estimate causal policy effects.
finding.measure: Bibliometric publication trends, disciplinary diffusion, and country-level publication shares in OpenAlex
finding.study_size: n=14,417 GenAI publications; n=1,422,683 Other-AI publications; n=958,343 for regression analysis

finding.finding_summary: In the regression analysis, GenAI papers were associated with slightly smaller collaboration teams than other-AI papers (4.18 vs. 4.28 authors, p<.001). At the same time, GenAI papers showed slightly higher international collaboration intensity (1.35 vs. 1.30 countries, p<.001), suggesting modest changes in research organization rather than a clear uniform efficiency gain.
finding.measure: Collaboration intensity (number of authors) and international collaboration intensity (number of countries represented by author affiliations)
finding.effect_size: -0.100 for collaboration intensity; 0.0490 for international collaboration intensity

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not directly measure student durable skills, but it substantively discusses collaboration as a core research-organizational outcome associated with GenAI. GenAI is linked to slightly smaller teams yet more international collaboration, which the authors interpret as a shift in collaborative structure rather than a large change in performance.
finding.measure: Author team size and countries represented on publications
finding.effect_size: -0.100 for team size; 0.0490 for international collaboration intensity

paper_profiles.title: Do intelligent tutoring systems benefit K-12 students? A meta-analysis and evaluation of heterogeneity of treatment effects in the U.S.
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether intelligent tutoring systems (ITS), an AI-enabled instructional technology, improve learning outcomes for U.S. K-12 students and under what conditions their effects are strongest. The authors focus on heterogeneity in treatment effects, using the MUTOS framework to examine how study methods, student characteristics, intervention features, outcome measures, and settings relate to effect sizes.

The meta-analysis includes 18 experimental studies from U.S. elementary, middle, and high school settings, yielding 77 effect sizes across 11 ITS. The overall impact of ITS on learning was positive and statistically significant (g=0.271, SE=0.011, p=0.001). Effects were similar for elementary and middle school students, and across many subgroups, but were smaller in rural settings and declined as intervention duration increased. MetaForest results indicated that worked-out examples, intervention duration, intervention condition, and immediate measurement were among the most important moderators.

The paper also evaluates internal validity using What Works Clearinghouse standards and finds that only a subset of studies reported enough attrition information to assess differential attrition. Studies with high, low, and unreported attrition had broadly similar effect sizes, so the authors do not find strong support for the hypothesis that stronger WWC-compliant studies would show larger effects. Overall, the paper concludes that ITS can produce modest positive learning gains in U.S. K-12 education, including for middle school students, but that effects depend on implementation features and measurement choices.

finding.finding_summary: Across 18 experimental U.S. K-12 studies (77 effect sizes from 11 ITS), intelligent tutoring systems produced a statistically significant positive effect on student learning outcomes overall (g=0.271, SE=0.011, p=0.001). This meta-analytic estimate indicates a modest positive impact on academic achievement across the included interventions and settings.
finding.measure: Student learning outcomes / academic achievement

finding.finding_summary: For mathematics outcomes, the meta-analysis reported a positive and statistically significant effect of ITS (g=0.253, SE=0.007, 95% CI 0.224 to 0.281, p<0.001). The authors also found that math ITS were one of the key moderators in the MetaForest model, though reading/writing ITS showed somewhat larger effects.
finding.measure: Mathematics achievement

paper_profiles.title: Survival and grade of the glioma prediction using transfer learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of predicting glioma tumor grade and patient survival from multimodal medical imaging data. The authors argue that accurate early prognosis is important for treatment planning and demonstrate a transfer-learning approach that can work well even when labeled data are limited.

The study uses the BraTS 2020 dataset, which includes MRI-derived images and clinical variables from 369 patients. The authors preprocess the images by reorienting, normalizing, and segmenting them into 2D slices, then compare several pre-trained convolutional neural networks including ResNet, EfficientNet, VGG16, InceptionV3, InceptionResNetV2, and DenseNet variants. They combine image features with clinical metadata such as age and tumor resection status, and separately train models for two tasks: glioma grade classification and survival prediction.

The best-performing model is DenseNet121 with task-specific hyperparameters. On the test set, the optimized grade model achieves 97% accuracy/F1-macro for classifying LGG vs HGG, while the optimized survival model achieves 65% accuracy and 0.60 macro F1 for three survival categories. The authors conclude that transfer learning substantially improves performance over prior state of the art on this dataset, especially for tumor grade classification, and suggest the approach may be useful for clinical decision support. The work is medical AI research, not an education study, so it does not directly inform K-12 learning outcomes beyond very indirect methodological parallels.

finding.finding_summary: not_reported
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Improving ensemble extreme precipitation forecasts using generative artificial intelligence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of accurately forecasting extreme precipitation events over the conterminous United States, especially when operational ensemble weather models have too few members to characterize rare, high-impact events well. The authors ask whether generative AI can be used to post-process ensemble precipitation forecasts to create a larger, more skillful set of spatiotemporally consistent forecast trajectories.

The proposed method, ViT-LDM, combines a 3-D Vision Transformer for bias correction with a latent diffusion model to generate additional ensemble members in a compressed VQ-VAE latent space. It is trained on GEFSv12 reforecasts from 2002-2019 and evaluated on 2021 operational GEFS forecasts against CCPA precipitation analyses. The study also includes explainability analyses to show how the latent space separates forecast and analysis fields, how the ViT shifts forecasts toward the analysis distribution, and how the diffusion model increases ensemble spread.

Results indicate that ViT-LDM improves probabilistic forecast skill over the raw GEFS ensemble and an Analog Ensemble + Ensemble Copula Coupling baseline, with stronger gains for extreme precipitation thresholds than for mild events. The generated ensembles were reported to be reliable, better calibrated at high thresholds such as 40 mm per 6 hours, and spatiotemporally consistent for 6-day accumulated precipitation. The authors conclude that generative AI is promising for extreme-weather post-processing, while noting weaker performance for mild and moderate precipitation events.

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not study student scientific reasoning or any educational outcome. It focuses on AI methods for weather-forecast post-processing, so there is no empirical evidence about effects on scientific reasoning in learners.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Disparate Impact of Artificial Intelligence Bias in Ridehailing Economy’s Price Discrimination Algorithms
paper_profiles.venue: AIES ’21 (ACM Conference on Artificial Intelligence, Ethics, and Society)
paper_profiles.population: Adult (Chicago ridehailing users/neighborhoods; census-tract level analysis)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI-driven dynamic pricing in ridehailing platforms produces disparate impact across neighborhoods in Chicago. The authors ask whether fare prices, trip frequency, and trip duration are systematically associated with neighborhood demographics such as race/ethnicity, poverty, age, education, citizenship, and home value, and whether these patterns differ from taxi pricing over the same period.

The study analyzes a large administrative dataset of 100,717,117 Chicago ridehail trips from November 2018 to September 2019 (about 68 million after filtering) and compares it with Chicago taxi trip data. Neighborhood-level demographic data from the American Community Survey are merged at the census-tract level, and the authors estimate demographic associations using Cohen’s d combined through a random-effects model, with significance assessed via permutation testing.

Results indicate that ridehailing fare prices are higher in neighborhoods with larger non-white populations, higher poverty, younger residents, and higher education levels, with reported combined effect sizes of d=-0.32, -0.28, 0.69, and 0.24, respectively. Trip frequency is positively associated with fare pricing and with demographic composition, while taxi pricing shows weaker or nonsignificant associations for many of the same variables. The authors conclude that dynamic pricing and possible supply-routing mechanisms may contribute to algorithmic disparate impact, and that greater transparency about demand, supply allocation, and pricing logic is needed to mitigate bias.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that ridehailing pricing algorithms create disparate impact across Chicago neighborhoods, with higher fares in majority non-white, higher-poverty, younger, and more highly educated areas. Using combined effect sizes from a random-effects model, the authors report d=-0.32 for % non-white, d=-0.28 for % below poverty line, d=0.69 for % older than 40, and d=0.24 for % high school education or less, indicating systematic differences in pricing outcomes tied to neighborhood demographics.
finding.measure: Ridehailing fare price per mile by census-tract demographic attributes; comparison with taxi fare pricing
finding.study_size: n=100,717,117 ridehailing trips initially; ~68 million ridehailing trips after filtering

finding.finding_summary: The paper links fare pricing to neighborhood ride demand proxies and trip duration, suggesting the pricing algorithm responds to operational factors such as pickup/dropoff density and trip seconds per mile. Ridehailing trip frequency is strongly positively associated with fare price per mile (e.g., pickup frequency/m2 d=-1.57 and dropoff frequency/m2 d=-1.57), while trip seconds per mile is negatively associated with some neighborhood groups, indicating that the platform’s pricing reflects operational patterns in ways that may also encode bias.
finding.measure: Trip frequency per square meter and trip seconds per mile at pickup/dropoff census-tract level
finding.study_size: n=100,717,117 ridehailing trips initially; ~68 million ridehailing trips after filtering
finding.effect_size: d=-1.57, -1.59 for pickup/dropoff frequency vs fare price per mile; trip seconds/mile effects include d=-0.31, -0.25 for % non-white and % below poverty line

paper_profiles.title: NeuroChat: A Neuroadaptive AI Chatbot for Customizing Learning Experiences
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 7th ACM Conference on Conversational User Interfaces (CUI '25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether a neuroadaptive AI tutor that uses real-time EEG-based engagement estimates can improve learner engagement and learning relative to a non-adaptive chatbot. The authors argue that large language model tutors can personalize content, but they lack awareness of the learner’s cognitive state; NeuroChat is introduced as a closed-loop system intended to dynamically adjust response depth, specificity, and style based on engagement inferred from a consumer-grade EEG headband.

The system combines a Muse 2 EEG headband, a browser-based web app, and GPT-4-turbo. Participants complete a short calibration task, then interact with the chatbot while EEG engagement is computed every second and embedded into prompts. In a within-subject study with 30 recruited adults (24 analyzed after exclusions), participants studied two topics (T. rex and the Taiping Rebellion) under NeuroChat and a control GPT chatbot, then completed quizzes, essays, surveys, and interviews.

Quantitatively, NeuroChat increased normalized EEG-measured engagement relative to control after accounting for order effects, but it did not improve short-term quiz or essay learning outcomes. Qualitatively, many participants found NeuroChat more human-like, enjoyable, and exploratory, though some preferred the control chatbot’s more structured, information-dense style for efficient fact retrieval. The authors conclude that real-time neuroadaptive LLM tutoring is feasible and can increase engagement, but stronger learning gains may require better pedagogical tuning, longer-term adaptation, and richer assessment.

finding.finding_summary: In a within-subject study (initially n=30 recruited; n=24 analyzed after excluding 6 participants with missing/poor EEG and 1 non-compliant participant), NeuroChat significantly increased normalized EEG-measured engagement relative to the control chatbot when task order was included in the model (β=0.216, p=0.029; 95% CI [0.022, 0.410]). The authors also report that participants self-reported higher engagement and satisfaction with NeuroChat, with 14 of 24 interviewees describing it as more lifelike, enjoyable, or engaging.
finding.measure: EEG-derived normalized engagement score; self-reported engagement/satisfaction from post-study survey and interviews

finding.finding_summary: NeuroChat did not produce significant short-term learning gains on the study’s non-science content topics. Quiz performance was essentially identical across conditions (mean proportional scores: NeuroChat 61.02% vs control 60.66%), and essay performance was also similar (18.27 points vs 17.69 points).
finding.measure: Quiz scores (fill-in-the-blank and multiple choice) and 15-minute essay scores

finding.finding_summary: The qualitative results suggest NeuroChat sometimes supported deeper thinking and exploration, but not uniformly. Several participants said it encouraged curiosity and deeper exploration, while others found its Socratic, conversational style distracting or less effective for direct fact retrieval; the paper does not report a quantitative effect size for critical thinking or metacognitive outcomes.
finding.measure: Interview and open-ended survey themes about exploration, curiosity, and depth of thinking

paper_profiles.title: An AI-Driven Thermal-Fluid Testbed for Advanced Small Modular Reactors: Integration of Digital Twin and Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents an AI-enabled thermal-fluid research platform for advanced small modular reactor (SMR) development. The authors describe a physical three-loop thermal-fluid facility, a high-fidelity digital twin built in SAM (System Analysis Module), a GRU-based machine learning model for faster-than-real-time prediction and control, and an LLM interface for operator assistance.

The study’s central question is whether these physical and digital components can be integrated into a single cyber-physical testbed that supports validation, predictive control, and human-machine interaction for nuclear thermal-fluid systems. The paper reports validation of the digital twin against experimental transients, GRU forecasting of future temperatures and control actions, and an LLM workflow that interprets sensor data and digital-twin outputs to provide natural-language operational guidance.

The context is nuclear engineering research at Texas A&M University, not K-12 education. The main conclusions are that the SAM digital twin can reproduce facility behavior with high fidelity, the GRU model can forecast system states with about 1.4 K temperature prediction error and accelerate simulation by roughly 600×, and the LLM can summarize complex operational states and recommend cautious control actions. The paper is primarily a technical systems and methods contribution for reactor research and operator support.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies AI-supported prediction, simulation, and operational reasoning in a thermal-fluid/nuclear engineering context. The SAM digital twin was validated against experiments with mean temperature prediction errors of 1.2°C and the GRU model achieved temperature prediction MAE of 1.16 K and RMSE of 1.42 K across 16 temperature channels, indicating strong predictive modeling performance for complex scientific systems.
finding.measure: Temperature prediction accuracy in a thermal-fluid digital twin and GRU forecasting model

paper_profiles.title: Making AI Inevitable: Historical Perspective and the Problems of Predicting Long-Term Technological Change
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual and historical analysis of debates about the future of AI, especially arguments over whether artificial general intelligence (AGI) will be transformative for society and whether that transformation would be beneficial or harmful. The authors argue that these debates are driven less by objective technical disagreement than by deeper philosophical assumptions about history, technology, prediction, and expertise.

The paper does not study an intervention, program, or empirical sample. Instead, it traces intellectual lineages of two broad camps—"transformationalists" and "skeptics"—and distinguishes strong versus weak versions of each. The discussion draws on historical examples, philosophical arguments, and selected literature from AI, big history, and economics to show how people justify very different forecasts about AI’s trajectory.

The main conclusion is that forecasting long-term technological change is highly uncertain and fundamentally shaped by non-technical beliefs. The authors argue that strong claims about AI inevitability carry a heavy argumentative burden and can create self-reinforcing competitive pressures, while more cautious skepticism better captures the limits of prediction. They conclude that public and policy debates about AI should broaden beyond technical experts to include philosophers, historians, epistemologists, and political theorists.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that beliefs about AGI and AI inevitability can shape institutional and policy behavior, including competitive pressures for first-mover advantage and the tendency of governments and corporations to treat AI as strategically urgent. It is a conceptual claim rather than an empirical effect estimate, so no sample size or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Policy and institutional discourse about AI governance, expertise, and competitive dynamics

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes the role of heuristics, metaphors, and folk theories in how both experts and non-experts reason about AI and long-term technological change, implicitly highlighting epistemic judgment and critical evaluation rather than measuring them directly. No quantitative measure of critical thinking or metacognition is reported.
finding.measure: Reasoning about technological change, predictive frameworks, and epistemological assumptions

paper_profiles.title: Intelligent Computer Numerical Control Unit for Machine Tools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper proposes an intelligent CNC control unit that can automatically generate NC part programs for machining centers using a neural network. The motivation is to reduce or eliminate the need for manual intervention by skilled NC programmers during part-program creation and post-processing, especially when working from 2D, 2.5D, or 3D CAD models of prismatic parts.

The system described combines a CNC control unit, a neural-network-based learning module, and a CAD/CAM workflow. In the learning phase, teaching programs are created from conventional CAD/CAM systems and used to train the neural network on machining operations such as milling, drilling, reaming, sinking, and threading. In operational mode, the trained neural network identifies geometric and technological features in a CAD model and outputs NC programs including tool paths and process parameters automatically.

The paper is primarily a technical concept and system-description paper, not an empirical evaluation with human participants. Its conclusions are that the proposed approach could improve automation, save time, and reduce dependence on expert operators in CNC programming, while potentially helping programmers make better decisions. No direct evidence is reported on educational or student outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that an NN-based CNC control unit could automate NC program generation from CAD models and reduce manual intervention, post-processing, and programming time. However, these claims are conceptual; no empirical study, sample size, or quantified performance results are reported.
finding.measure: NC program generation automation, operator intervention, and time-saving in CNC programming

finding.finding_summary: The author suggests the system can serve as an orientation tool or aid for NC programmers in making decisions about machining strategies and parameters. This is a proposed cognitive support function rather than an empirically tested effect, and no measures or participant outcomes are reported.
finding.measure: Decision support for NC programming / machining strategy selection

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article is a conceptual discussion of how artificial intelligence can be integrated into education, with emphasis on AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. It argues that the rapid spread of tools such as ChatGPT creates both opportunities and risks, including hallucinations, overreliance on AI, and unclear academic integrity boundaries.

The paper uses informal discussions at a Swiss university of applied sciences and a narrative literature review to develop a set of practical guidelines and recommendations. The main institutional case is Kalaidos University of Applied Sciences in Zurich, where the author describes internal AI guidelines for student use of generative AI in academic writing and suggests that students should treat AI as a sparring partner rather than a ghostwriter.

The article also surveys classroom uses of AI at the university level, such as student AI experiments, AI-generated case studies, curriculum support, gamification, and immersive/virtual reality applications. Its main conclusion is that institutions should build an AI culture through explicit guidelines, workshops, transparency requirements, and instruction in AI literacy and prompt engineering so that students and teachers can use AI responsibly and critically.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that prompt engineering, AI literacy, and critical thinking are central skills that can help students use AI more effectively and avoid overreliance on machine-generated outputs. No quantitative effect size is reported, as this is a conceptual and narrative discussion rather than an intervention study.
finding.measure: Conceptual emphasis on AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking

finding.finding_summary: The article suggests that AI tools can improve efficiency for educators by supporting curriculum creation, generating case studies, and helping to construct interactive classroom activities. These claims are illustrative and qualitative only; the paper reports no measured workload outcomes or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Instructor workflow and curriculum/task support

finding.finding_summary: A central focus of the paper is institutional policy and governance around AI use, especially the development of formal AI guidelines at Kalaidos University of Applied Sciences. The paper describes requirements for transparency, documentation of AI use, and restrictions on direct copy-pasting, but provides no quantitative institutional outcome data.
finding.measure: Institutional AI guidelines, governance, and policy implementation

paper_profiles.title: A Review on Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative review of artificial intelligence (AI) applications in education. It surveys major AI-enabled education functions, including adaptive learning, teaching evaluation, virtual classrooms, smart campus systems, and intelligent tutoring robots, and discusses both their reported benefits and implementation challenges.

The review is not an empirical study of a single intervention, but a broad synthesis of prior literature across educational levels and contexts. The authors argue that AI can improve personalization, classroom management, assessment efficiency, and learning support, while also warning about equity, ethics, data privacy, teacher readiness, and student self-regulation concerns.

For the specific area of adaptive learning, the paper cites examples such as ALEKS, DreamBox Learning, BYJU’S, Knewton, Cognitive Tutor, IBM Watson Education, and Duolingo, but it does not report new original data from U.S. middle school science classrooms. The paper’s main conclusion is that AI has substantial potential to support teaching and learning, but implementation must be handled carefully to avoid widening inequities and to ensure appropriate teacher and student support.

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that Yilmaz (2018) found ALEKS instruction had a statistically significant positive impact on middle school students’ end-of-year mathematics scores. The paper does not provide the effect size, confidence interval, or standard deviation for that study in the review text.
finding.measure: End-of-year mathematics scores

finding.finding_summary: The review summarizes studies of AI-supported English learning tools such as Duolingo, noting improved autonomous learning and higher English ability among users of AI-based college English platforms. The paper does not provide a pooled effect size or detailed sample sizes for these language outcomes.
finding.measure: English ability / autonomous learning outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that AI-based assessment tools and intelligent tutoring systems reduce teacher workload by automating grading, scoring, and routine instructional tasks. Examples include automatic essay scoring (e-rater), speech scoring (SpeechRater), and homework/test paper correction, but no original effect size is reported in this paper.
finding.measure: Teacher assessment and grading workload; automated scoring/correction efficiency

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed literature, AI adaptive learning and tutoring systems are described as improving student autonomy, motivation, and engagement. For example, the review notes that Duolingo increased learners’ autonomous learning ability, but the paper provides no new primary estimates or standardized effect sizes.
finding.measure: Autonomous learning, motivation, engagement

finding.finding_summary: The review concludes that AI can support smart-campus development, education equity, and teaching reform, but also warns of algorithmic divide, privacy, and ethical risks. These institutional impacts are discussed conceptually rather than measured empirically in this paper.
finding.measure: Smart campus development, equity, governance, and data/privacy concerns

paper_profiles.title: Role of AI in Education
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (narrative review; no empirical study population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative review of artificial intelligence (AI) in education. It discusses how AI technologies such as machine learning, natural language processing, intelligent tutoring systems, chatbots, automated grading, and adaptive learning platforms can be used to personalize instruction, increase engagement, automate routine tasks, and support data-driven decision-making in schools.

The article does not report a primary empirical study, intervention trial, or defined participant sample. Instead, it summarizes perceived benefits, challenges, and ethical concerns associated with AI in education, drawing on cited examples from prior literature and commercial products. Its main conclusion is that AI has strong promise for making education more personalized and efficient, but implementation requires attention to privacy, bias, transparency, accessibility, cost, and teacher training.

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that AI can save teachers time by automating grading, assessment, scheduling, and other routine administrative tasks. It cites examples such as chatbots and automated grading systems, but provides no original empirical estimate, sample size, or effect size from the paper itself.
finding.measure: Teacher workload / task automation / administrative efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper broadly claims that AI-based personalized learning can improve academic performance by tailoring pace, difficulty, and feedback to individual students. It references examples like Carnegie Learning and Duolingo, but does not present a study-specific sample, effect size, or statistical estimate in the paper.
finding.measure: General academic performance in AI-supported personalized learning contexts

finding.finding_summary: The review states that AI-supported personalized and interactive learning can increase student engagement and motivation. This is described qualitatively rather than through original outcome data, and no sample size or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Student engagement and motivation

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims AI can support individualized feedback and data-driven decisions that may improve learning behaviors and problem-solving, but it does not directly measure durable skills such as metacognition or critical thinking. No empirical effect estimate is provided.
finding.measure: General learning support associated with individualized feedback and data analysis

paper_profiles.title: VLM@school – Evaluation of AI image understanding on German middle school knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces VLM@school, a benchmark for evaluating vision-language models on German middle-school-level knowledge questions. The authors are motivated by shortcomings in existing AI benchmarks: many are English-only, multiple-choice, text-answerable without the image, or do not reflect authentic school-curriculum tasks. Their dataset includes 486 images and 2,038 open-ended questions across nine school subjects, with some questions embedded in the image and some adversarial questions intentionally unanswerable from the image alone.

The study evaluates 13 open-weight vision-language models, including InternVL3, Ovis2, Qwen2.5 VL, Gemma 3, Llama 4 Scout, and Mistral Small 3.1, using an LLM-as-a-judge / panel-of-LLMs evaluation setup. The main finding is that these models struggle substantially on real curriculum-grounded German questions: the best overall accuracy is under 45%, with especially weak performance on music, math, and adversarial items. Performance is much lower on adversarial questions than on the full set, indicating that current VLMs often cannot reliably abstain or recognize when an image-based question is unsupported by the visual evidence.

The paper’s conclusions are primarily about benchmark design and model capability rather than an educational intervention. It argues that middle-school-level multimodal tasks are a meaningful stress test for current VLMs, that German language and open-ended formats expose weaknesses not seen in some public benchmarks, and that model rankings on popular benchmarks do not necessarily transfer to this more realistic setting.

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark found that all tested models struggled on middle-school math questions, with the best model reaching only 34.09% accuracy on math and the weakest model 9.09%. The paper reports that models were often better at calculation than at counting or geometric interpretation, but overall performance remained low across 308 math questions.
finding.measure: Accuracy on open-ended math benchmark questions involving geometry, area, circumference, counting, and simple calculations

finding.finding_summary: The biology and physics sections show substantial difficulty in scientific reasoning tasks that required interpreting diagrams, maps, circuits, and labeled illustrations. Best-model accuracy was 48.53% for biology and 47.65% for physics, with many failures on explanation-based questions and diagram interpretation; the dataset includes 169 biology and 234 physics questions.
finding.measure: Accuracy on biology and physics questions requiring diagram reading, technical term identification, and explanation of scientific phenomena

finding.finding_summary: Across non-STEM school subjects, model performance varied widely but remained limited, especially for history, arts, music, religion, geography, and sports. The best overall scores by domain were 54.36% in history and 52.92% in religion, while music was particularly difficult at 31.03% best accuracy; the paper also reports frequent failures on maps, art-style identification, and sport-situation interpretation.
finding.measure: Accuracy on curriculum-based questions in arts, geography, history, music, religion, and sports
finding.study_size: n=1,127 questions across 306 images (arts 286, geography 251, history 264, music 166, religion 206, sports 154)

finding.finding_summary: The paper implicitly assesses multimodal reasoning and the ability to integrate visual clues with background knowledge, especially on open-ended and adversarial items that require abstention when the image does not support an answer. Performance was substantially lower on adversarial questions than on the full set, indicating weak metacognitive/critical-reasoning behavior rather than a dedicated instructional gain.
finding.measure: Accuracy on adversarial questions requiring recognition that the answer is not supported by the image
finding.study_size: subset of the full dataset; adversarial item count not consistently reported in aggregate

paper_profiles.title: Artificial Intelligence for Sustainable Wine Industry: AI-Driven Management in Viticulture, Wine Production and Enotourism
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how artificial intelligence could support sustainability and efficiency in the wine industry, with a focus on viticulture, wine production, and enotourism in Poland.
