The study combines a questionnaire survey of Polish winemakers with a conceptual review of AI methods that might be applied to environmental, economic, and social aspects of the wine sector. It is not an intervention study; rather, it documents current practices and proposes AI use cases aligned to sustainability goals.

The empirical portion surveyed 75 vineyards/winemakers in Poland and found broadly positive attitudes toward sustainability across environmental, economic, and social dimensions. Respondents commonly reported actions such as reducing crop protection products, using renewable energy, supporting local economies, and offering enotourism services. The paper then maps these themes to potential AI tools and methods, including drone monitoring, predictive irrigation, process-control systems, chatbots, recommendation systems, route optimization, sentiment analysis, and virtual tasting simulations.

The authors conclude that AI could help Polish winemaking become more sustainable by improving resource management, optimizing production, and enhancing tourism and marketing functions. However, they also note that most surveyed winemakers are not currently using advanced AI tools, and they emphasize the need for locally tailored implementation, further longitudinal research, and broader stakeholder perspectives. The paper’s contribution is primarily descriptive and conceptual, offering a framework of possible AI applications rather than testing specific educational or agricultural outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Can Autism be Catered with Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Intervention Technology? A Comprehensive Survey
paper_profiles.population: Not specified; mixed ASD populations across childhood, adolescence, and adulthood
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a broad literature survey on technology-based interventions for Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), with emphasis on computer-aided systems (CAS), computer-vision-assisted technologies (CVAT), virtual reality (VR), and AI-assisted approaches. The paper asks whether these technologies can support the perception and production of facial expressions, emotion recognition, and related social-communication skills in individuals with ASD.

The review synthesizes prior studies spanning children, adolescents, and adults with ASD or related diagnoses such as HFA, AS, and LFA. It discusses systems such as TeachTown, Emotion Trainer, FEFA, MindReading, FaceSay, SmileMaze, JobTIPS, and VR social-scenario environments, many of which are designed to be used directly by learners while some support teacher/therapist-mediated instruction. The paper argues that technology-based interventions often show promising behavioral gains and may offer advantages over traditional instruction because they can provide repetition, consistency, and access at scale.

At the same time, the authors emphasize major limitations in the evidence base: many studies have small samples, limited generalizability, and weak experimental rigor, and several reported outcomes are not clinically conclusive. Their main conclusion is that AI-assisted intervention for ASD remains promising but underdeveloped, and that more standardized, empirical, and clinically meaningful research is needed before firm conclusions can be drawn.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed ASD intervention studies, many CAS/CVAT/VR tools improved emotion recognition, social interaction, and related social behavior, but results were uneven and often limited by small samples or narrow tasks. Examples in the review include TeachTown improving receptive language and social skills in 47 children with ASD after 8 weeks, FaceSay improving social interaction and emotional recognition in 49 youths with HFA/LFA, and several emotion-training systems showing gains on specific recognition tasks without broad generalization.
finding.measure: Emotion recognition tasks, social skills ratings, social interaction observations, receptive language/social skill assessments

finding.finding_summary: Some reviewed interventions reported improvements in receptive language and related communication outcomes, especially in younger children with ASD. The clearest example cited is TeachTown: Basics, which reportedly improved receptive language after 8 weeks in 47 children aged 3-6 years, though the paper also notes implementation limitations and incomplete logging.
finding.measure: Receptive language, communication-related classroom tasks

paper_profiles.title: Games for Artificial Intelligence Research: A Review and Perspectives
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a broad survey of publicly available games and game-based platforms used for artificial intelligence research. It asks how different games can serve as testbeds for AI methods, and how to match particular AI techniques with appropriate games for playing, planning, learning, and game design.

The review organizes prior work by game type (tabletop, video games, social/text), by agent setting (single-agent, multi-agent, cooperative, competitive, mixed), by observability, and by programming language and competition use. It also separately surveys games and platforms used for AI-driven game design, including level generation, narrative generation, rhythm-chart generation, and game tuning. The paper’s contribution is classificatory and methodological rather than empirical: it synthesizes the landscape of platforms such as Gym, PettingZoo, GVGAI, Procgen, StarCraft II, ViZDoom, Science Birds, Mario AI, and others, and offers guidance on selecting environments for different AI research goals.

Because the paper is a review, it does not report a new intervention, participant sample, or outcome evaluation in an education study. Its main conclusion is that games remain valuable, controllable benchmarks for AI research, with grid-based platforms often best for scalability and rapid experimentation, while pixel-based and 3D environments better capture complexity and realism. For education-relevant use, it notes that games and game-based platforms can support AI research and education, but it does not present a study of K-12 learners or classroom implementation.

paper_profiles.title: OAK4XAI: Model towards Out-Of-Box eXplainable Artificial Intelligence for Digital Agriculture
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper proposes OAK4XAI, an ontology-based knowledge map framework for explainable AI in digital agriculture. The central problem addressed is that machine learning models often behave as black boxes, making their predictions and underlying concepts difficult for domain users to understand and trust. To address this, the authors separate stored knowledge from its explanation: mined knowledge items are represented in a knowledge map (KMap), while explanations are provided through a domain ontology, AgriComO.

The approach is not an educational intervention or a study of students; it is a system design and implementation paper for agricultural data mining and explainability. The framework supports representation and explanation of classification, clustering, regression, and association-rule outputs, and it is demonstrated with examples involving soil pH prediction and transformation definitions. The paper also describes a web-based Knowledge Browser that can retrieve knowledge items, generate SPARQL queries, and present explanations at different levels of detail for managers, data scientists, developers, agronomists, and experts.

The paper’s main conclusion is that an ontology-backed knowledge map can improve transparency, usability, trust, and interpretability of mined knowledge in agriculture. It reports implementation details and counts of ontology resources (e.g., 176 algorithms, 110 pre-trained models, 51 evaluation metrics), but it does not evaluate student learning or any K-12 science outcome. As a result, it is relevant to AI explainability infrastructure rather than AI interventions in U.S. middle school science.

paper_profiles.title: Conceptual Modeling and Artificial Intelligence: Mutual Benefits from Complementary Worlds
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an editorial preface to the 3rd International Workshop on Conceptual Modeling Meets Artificial Intelligence (CMAI’2021). It does not report an empirical education study; instead, it frames the relationship between conceptual modeling and artificial intelligence, arguing that each field can contribute to the other.

The paper presents a research framework that positions CMAI work into four categories: exaptation, CM-driven, AI-driven, and CM- & AI-driven research. It briefly summarizes the invited papers in the workshop program and explains how each fits into the framework, including examples involving machine learning, conceptual models, and hybrid AI/modeling techniques.

Because this is a workshop preface and overview, there is no study population, intervention in an educational setting, or measured outcome. The paper’s main contribution is conceptual and programmatic rather than empirical.

paper_profiles.title: Certifiable Artificial Intelligence Through Data Fusion
paper_profiles.venue: AAAI FSS-21: Artificial Intelligence in Government and Public Sector
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual review and position paper about how to certify artificial intelligence and machine learning systems, especially in safety- and mission-critical settings. Rather than evaluating a specific educational intervention, it surveys certification concepts such as verification and validation, model cards, explainability, uncertainty, and robustness bounds, then proposes the Multisource AI Scorecard Table (MAST) as a checklist for assessing AI systems.

The paper organizes certification into phases of concept, design, implementation testing, and managed deployment, emphasizing that intended use, data sources, operating conditions, and user context all matter. It discusses example application areas such as image fusion, autonomous systems, UAVs, and security/aviation domains, and illustrates how quantitative metrics and qualitative review can be combined to judge whether an AI system is ready for deployment.

No K-12 instructional intervention, school-based population, or scientific-reasoning outcome is studied empirically. The paper does not report a human-subject experiment; instead it offers a framework and examples from AI systems engineering. As a result, it is not directly about education research, and there are no extractable student-facing or teacher-facing educational tools from the text.

paper_profiles.title: Intelligent behavior depends on the ecological niche
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an interview-format perspective piece about the future of AI, especially human-like intelligence in socio-cultural environments. The authors argue that intelligence should be understood relative to an ecological niche rather than as a single general scale, and that human cognition is shaped by embodiment, social interaction, language, and cultural evolution.

The paper does not test an intervention or report a new empirical study. Instead, it synthesizes developmental AI and developmental robotics ideas, highlighting prior work on curiosity-driven learning, intrinsic motivation, language grounding, and developmental trajectories in robots and learning systems. The discussion emphasizes that current AI benchmarks underrepresent social and cultural problems, and calls for training and evaluation ecosystems that better reflect human-like learning and development.

Because this is a conceptual interview rather than a study with participants, it has no U.S. middle school science population and no concrete classroom intervention. It is relevant only at the level of general AI research directions, not empirical educational outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Bias Amplification in Artificial Intelligence Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an opinion/position piece about a broad societal problem: how artificial intelligence systems can amplify bias present in training data and thereby produce harmful outcomes for marginalized groups. Rather than evaluating a specific intervention, it argues that bias in datasets, model design, and deployment can lead to representative and allocative harms across domains such as hiring, advertising, criminal justice, healthcare, and public policy.

The author uses illustrative examples from prior reports and news articles to explain several categories of machine-learning bias, including dataset bias, association bias, automation bias, interaction bias, and confirmation bias. The paper’s central recommendation is that government and public-sector actors should set data standards, improve transparency, regulate AI deployment, and promote more diverse and representative datasets. It emphasizes that preventing bias amplification is a governance and accountability problem, not merely a technical one.

The paper does not study an educational intervention, school-based AI tool, or student outcomes, and it contains no empirical analysis of K-12 learning. It is best understood as a conceptual policy essay about responsible AI and equity.

paper_profiles.title: Ontology-Based Context Modelling for Designing a Context-Aware Calculator
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (method/design paper; no student sample reported)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to model didactic context in order to design a context-aware calculator called MazCalc, intended to measure differences between two learning contexts and predict context effects. The authors argue that ontological engineering is necessary to formally represent context parameters, their relationships, and the semantics needed to compare contexts in educational settings.

The paper presents a design-based, qualitative account of the development of MazCalc across multiple iterations (MazCalc 1, 2, and 3). It describes the creation of an ontology for didactic context, a class diagram and database schema for the calculator, and the roles of multiple stakeholders including a cognitionist, expert designer, specialist of the object of study, and instructional designer.

The educational use cases discussed are conceptual and focus on context-based teaching scenarios such as geothermal energy, language, socio-history, and environmental/sustainable development. The paper does not report a student outcome study or any empirical evaluation of learning gains; instead, it concludes that the calculator and ontology are still under development and that the articulation between theory-modeling and artifact design remains a key challenge. It also positions MazCalc as a future component of a context-aware intelligent tutoring system (CAITS) and as a support tool for instructional design and data analysis.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not report an empirical study of scientific reasoning outcomes; rather, it proposes and iteratively designs a context-aware calculator and ontology for future use in science learning research. It references prior design experiments in geothermal energy and science learning, but provides no student outcome data, effect sizes, or measured gains in reasoning.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: The Illusion of Understanding: How Middle-Schoolers Fail to Regulate Inquiry with ChatGPT in a Science Task
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how middle-school students regulate inquiry when using a generative AI tool, ChatGPT, during science investigation tasks. The central question is whether students can formulate good prompts, judge the quality of AI answers, and decide when to continue or stop an inquiry cycle in ways that support conceptual understanding.

The study was conducted with 63 students aged 14–15 from four schools in France. Students completed six validated science tasks with ChatGPT 3.5 on laptops, using paper-based task descriptions and prompt suggestions, while evaluating every AI response on a 3-point usefulness scale. The researchers compared students’ judgments and behaviors against expert coding of prompt and answer quality, and they also measured prior domain knowledge, AI attitudes, and metacognitive skills.

Results showed generally weak performance across the inquiry cycle: students were near chance at distinguishing efficient from inefficient prompts (mean d′=0.19, SD=0.8) and at judging answer quality (mean d′=0.07, SD=1.2), and only 14 students asked any follow-up questions. Students often accepted low-quality prompts and answers, frequently terminated inquiry prematurely, and achieved only moderate task success (mean success rate=0.51, SD=0.25). Positive AI attitudes and higher prior confidence were associated with worse evaluation quality, whereas metacognitive regulation and critical perceptions of AI were associated with better prompt discrimination and more follow-up questioning. The authors conclude that middle-schoolers need explicit AI literacy and metacognitive scaffolding for meaningful, science-oriented use of GenAI.

finding.finding_summary: Students used ChatGPT in six science investigation tasks and showed only moderate conceptual task success despite unrestricted access. Their average final success rate across tasks was 0.51 (SD=0.25), while performance on prompt discrimination and answer evaluation was near chance (prompt d′=0.19, answer d′=0.07), indicating weak science-inquiry reasoning with the tool.
finding.measure: Science task conceptual understanding / final written explanations; prompt discrimination and answer evaluation during science inquiry
finding.effect_size: success rate M=0.51; prompt d′=0.19; answer d′=0.07
finding.std_deviation: SD=0.25 for success rate; SD=0.8 for prompt d′; SD=1.2 for answer d′

finding.finding_summary: Students frequently ended inquiry prematurely and rarely engaged in follow-up questioning, suggesting weak persistence and self-regulation during AI-supported science work. Only 14 students asked follow-up questions (22 total across six tasks), and follow-up occurred in just 31.8% of cases even after low-level answers were identified.
finding.measure: Follow-up questioning / termination of QA cycles

finding.finding_summary: The study directly measured metacognitive regulation, prompt discrimination, and answer evaluation as core inquiry skills. Prompt discrimination was near chance overall (mean d′=0.19, SD=0.8), answer-evaluation sensitivity was also near chance (mean d′=0.07, SD=1.2), but higher metacognitive regulation predicted better prompt-quality sensitivity (β=.30, p=.022) and more follow-up inquiry was associated with critical perceptions of AI.
finding.measure: Metacognitive regulation; prompt quality sensitivity; answer evaluation sensitivity; follow-up questioning
finding.effect_size: β=.30 for metacognitive regulation predicting prompt sensitivity; β=-.39 for positive AI attitudes predicting prompt sensitivity; β=-.30 for AI attitudes predicting answer sensitivity
finding.std_deviation: SD=0.8 for prompt d′; SD=1.2 for answer d′

finding.finding_summary: The paper also operationalized task outcome as students’ written explanations of scientific concepts in their own words, excluding direct copy-pastes from ChatGPT. Final written solution accuracy averaged 0.51 (SD=0.25), and success was strongly predicted by receiving more high-level AI answers, better answer-evaluation sensitivity, and asking follow-up questions after low-level answers (model adjusted R2=0.81).
finding.measure: Final written task responses / explanation accuracy
finding.effect_size: β=0.52 for frequency of high-level AI answers; β=0.10 for answer sensitivity; β=0.40 for follow-up after low-level answers

finding.finding_summary: Although this was not a teacher-workload study, it directly examined efficiency in the inquiry process, including whether students could use prompts and responses productively with minimal wasted turns. Students often accepted suggested prompts they had judged inefficient (75.9% of instances) and usually terminated QA cycles without follow-up, indicating inefficient use of AI interaction time.
finding.measure: Prompt usage decisions and number of follow-up turns during QA cycles

paper_profiles.title: VLM@school – Evaluation of AI image understanding on German middle school knowledge
paper_profiles.population: Middle School (grades 8-10 in German school system)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces VLM@school, a benchmark for evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) on German middle-school curriculum content. The authors argue that existing multimodal benchmarks are often English-only, multiple-choice heavy, and insufficiently representative of real classroom tasks, so they build a dataset using textbook and curriculum-aligned material across nine school subjects.

The benchmark contains 486 images and 2,038 open-ended questions spanning arts, biology, geography, history, math, music, physics, religion, and sports. The paper evaluates 13 open-weight VLMs on these questions using LLM-as-a-judge with multiple judges, and separately probes adversarial questions that are intentionally unanswerable from the image alone. The main conclusion is that even strong current VLMs struggle substantially with these middle-school tasks: the best overall score is under 45%, performance varies by subject, and adversarial questions are answered correctly at very low rates. The paper does not study an educational intervention in classrooms; rather, it provides a benchmark and comparative model evaluation to assess current AI capability on school-level science and other subjects in German.

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark includes biology and physics questions that require visual interpretation plus subject knowledge, but the evaluated VLMs perform poorly overall. In the biology and physics domains, best scores are only 48.53% and 47.65% for Qwen2.5VL 32B, while many models are substantially lower (e.g., physics 32.48% for InternVL3 8B). The authors conclude that middle-school science tasks remain difficult for current VLMs when they require combining image evidence with background knowledge.
finding.measure: Accuracy on biology and physics benchmark questions

finding.finding_summary: The math portion is explicitly designed to test image-based calculation and numerical reasoning from middle-school content. Performance is low to moderate, with best domain scores around 34.09% (Qwen2.5VL 32B) and many models far below that (e.g., Ovis2 4B at 9.09%), indicating substantial difficulty with geometric and calculation tasks. The paper notes that models often fail at counting, identifying shapes, and applying formulas correctly.
finding.measure: Accuracy on math benchmark questions

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally studies performance on non-science school subjects as part of a nine-domain benchmark, including arts, history, music, religion, and sports. Results show wide variation by domain but generally modest-to-poor performance, with best scores such as history at 54.36% and religion at 52.92%, and much lower performance in music (best 31.03%). This indicates current VLMs have significant limitations on curriculum-level school knowledge beyond science.
finding.measure: Accuracy across arts, history, music, religion, and sports benchmark questions
finding.study_size: n=1,126 questions (arts n=286; history n=264; music n=166; religion n=206; sports n=154)

finding.finding_summary: A meaningful part of the benchmark requires visual reasoning, cross-modal inference, and following multi-step hints, which map onto durable skills such as reasoning and problem solving. The authors report that models often struggle with explanation-based physics items, reverse lookup in maps, and questions requiring chaining information across modalities, suggesting weak cross-step reasoning. However, the paper evaluates model capability rather than student durable-skill outcomes.
finding.measure: Accuracy on open-ended visual reasoning questions across benchmark domains

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s core contribution is an evaluation benchmark intended to assess whether current AI systems can handle real middle-school curriculum tasks in German. It shows that public benchmark performance does not necessarily translate to this educational setting: model rankings on MMMU and the Open VLM leaderboard do not fully predict performance on VLM@school, and even the strongest open models remain limited. This suggests that benchmark-based claims about readiness for educational deployment may be overstated.
finding.measure: Comparative benchmark performance across VLM@school, MMMU, and Open VLM leaderboard

paper_profiles.title: DrawSim-PD: Simulating Student Science Drawings to Support NGSS-Aligned Teacher Diagnostic Reasoning
paper_profiles.population: K–12 science educators; expert reviewers were former or current K–12 science teachers in graduate science education programs
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a teacher professional development problem in K–12 science education: teachers need practice interpreting student science drawings for diagnostic reasoning, but authentic student work is difficult to collect and share because of privacy constraints. The authors propose DrawSim-PD, a generative AI framework that creates synthetic, NGSS-aligned student-like science drawings with controlled misconceptions, along with first-person student reasoning narratives and teacher-facing diagnostic concept maps.

The system uses capability profiles derived from NGSS performance expectations to specify what a simulated student can and cannot yet do at different performance levels (Emergent, Developing, Proficient, Advanced). These profiles condition multimodal generation so the drawing, narrative, and diagnostic map remain coherent. The paper also releases a 10,000-artifact corpus spanning 100 NGSS topics across K–12 science domains.

To validate the approach, the authors conducted an expert feasibility study with six K–12 science teachers enrolled in graduate science education programs. Across 480 artifact evaluations, reviewers found strong NGSS alignment and generally high plausibility, especially in middle grades, though they noted weaknesses at the K–2 and 9–12 extremes and described some generated misconceptions as somewhat mechanical. The study concludes that DrawSim-PD shows promise as open infrastructure for teacher calibration and visual assessment research, but it does not test learning gains or teacher performance outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims DrawSim-PD can support scalable teacher calibration and professional development by generating privacy-compliant student-like artifacts and diagnostic concept maps. In an expert feasibility study, teachers found the multimodal outputs useful for interpreting student thinking, but the study did not measure workload reduction directly.
finding.measure: Expert judgments of utility for diagnostic reasoning and professional learning

finding.finding_summary: The framework is positioned as open research infrastructure to address privacy barriers in visual assessment research and teacher PD. The paper argues that synthetic data generation could circumvent FERPA-related constraints and enable broader access to calibration sets, but it does not evaluate policy or institutional outcomes empirically.
finding.measure: Expert feasibility evaluation and corpus release as research infrastructure

paper_profiles.title: Shots and Boosters: Exploring the Use of Combined Prebunking Interventions to Raise Critical Thinking and Create Long-Term Protection Against Misinformation
paper_profiles.venue: ACM Workshop on Human-AI Interaction for Augmented Reasoning (AIREASONING-2025-01)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper addresses the problem of misinformation exposure and argues that debunking alone is insufficient because false claims spread quickly and can have lasting effects before corrections arrive. The authors focus on prebunking approaches, especially nudging and inoculation, as complementary strategies for strengthening users’ critical thinking and media literacy.

Rather than reporting a user study, the paper surveys prior HCI and media-literacy work and then proposes an AI-driven design concept for an interactive training game. The concept has two stages: an inoculation stage where users practice judging misleading posts with an AI tutor that critiques their reasoning, and a booster stage where the system delivers brief personalized nudges to reinforce learned strategies over time.

The paper is conceptual and does not evaluate the proposed system empirically. Its main conclusion is that AI can support both immediate reflective prompts and longer-term personalized reinforcement, but the idea remains a design proposal for future development rather than tested evidence. It is aimed at general online media users rather than a specific K-12 population, and it does not involve U.S. middle school science or scientific reasoning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not report an empirical intervention effect on critical thinking; instead, it proposes a conceptual AI-driven prebunking design intended to strengthen critical reasoning and media literacy over time. No sample, outcome measure, effect size, or confidence interval is reported because the paper is not an evaluation study.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Changes to the TN Middle Grades Science Curriculum According to NGSS
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper explains how Tennessee’s middle grades science curriculum would change under the Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS). Rather than testing a classroom intervention, it compares existing Tennessee Grade Level Expectations with the corresponding NGSS disciplinary core ideas and argues, using cognitive-developmental theory and science education policy, that some standards are better suited to earlier grades, some to high school, and some newly added in middle school.

The article’s central purpose is curriculum mapping. It describes posters/guidemaps created by a STEM fellow to show alignments between Tennessee standards and NGSS, and it discusses why concrete, experiential topics are moved to grades 5-6 while more abstract content is shifted to high school. It also highlights new middle-grade emphases in earth science and physical science, such as geological time, natural hazards, synthetic materials, and thermal energy transfer. The paper is best understood as a policy/curriculum rationale piece for educators and administrators involved in standards revision rather than as an empirical study of AI or instructional technology.

The context is Tennessee middle grades science (grades 6-8) and the broader implementation of NGSS. The authors draw on prior research, national assessment data, and developmental theory to justify the relocation and addition of standards. No direct student outcome data, experimental comparison, or evaluation of a specific tool is reported. The main conclusion is that NGSS better aligns science content with students’ developmental readiness and should support deeper understanding, modeling, and authentic inquiry.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that adopting NGSS would reorganize Tennessee middle grades science standards by relocating some content to elementary or high school and adding new middle-grade standards. It presents this as a curriculum-policy improvement intended to better align content with developmental readiness and improve standards coherence, but it does not provide empirical policy outcome data.
finding.measure: Curriculum standards alignment / relocation of Tennessee GLEs to NGSS grade bands

paper_profiles.title: Annotating Implicit Reasoning in Arguments with Causal Links
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of representing and collecting implicit reasoning in argumentative text. The authors argue that existing approaches to argument mining often encode hidden knowledge as either free-text commonsense facts or unstructured explanations, which makes it difficult to explicitly capture the causal reasoning that links a claim to its supporting premise.

To address this, the paper proposes a semi-structured annotation scheme inspired by the Argument from Consequences scheme. The scheme decomposes an argument into an action entity, an outcome entity, and implicit causal knowledge, connected by cause/suppress relations. The authors operationalize this through a two-phase crowdsourcing process on Amazon Mechanical Turk: first, annotators frame the semi-structured implicit reasoning for claim-premise pairs; second, other annotators filter for outcome validity and quality. The source data come from the IBM-Rank-30K argumentation corpus, restricted to six debatable topics and support-stance arguments.

The study is methodological rather than educational or intervention-based. It evaluates the feasibility, coverage, and quality of the annotation scheme, reporting that Phase 1 produced high coverage but many annotations were filtered out in Phase 2, and that expert review found only 45 of 100 sampled annotations to be high quality. The main conclusion is that the causal template can elicit many candidate implicit reasonings, but additional quality-control methods are needed to reliably obtain high-quality structured implicit reasoning at scale.

paper_profiles.title: What is essential is visible to the eye: Saliency in primary school ranking and its effect on academic achievements
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether students’ relative class rank affects later academic outcomes, and whether rank effects are driven by the rank that is actually visible to students versus an “invisible” rank based on standardized test scores. The authors argue that prior rank literature is vulnerable to omitted-variable bias because rank constructed from test scores can still reflect peer-ability composition and other higher-order ability peer effects.

To address this, they exploit Italian administrative data in which students receive teacher-assigned class grades that are salient and reported to students, as well as standardized test scores that are unreported at the time the rank is formed. They construct a visible rank from grades and an invisible rank from test scores, then compare how each predicts later standardized achievement. The core strategy uses large Italian cohorts observed in grades 5, 8, and 10, plus a companion cohort for placebo checks using grade-2 test scores. They also incorporate student fixed effects and flexible controls for class score distributions to better separate rank salience from underlying ability.

The main conclusion is that visible rank has a substantial positive effect on later academic performance, while the invisible rank becomes small and statistically insignificant once the preferred controls are included. Being ranked at the top rather than the bottom of a primary-school class is associated with gains of about 8.5 percentile points in middle school and 7.7 percentile points in high school. The paper also finds that rank effects are stronger than in prior work using standard identification strategies, that class quality matters much more than rank, and that higher visible rank improves self-esteem, school perception, and aspirations/attitudes measured in a student questionnaire.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds a sizable positive effect of visible class rank in primary school on later academic achievement. In the preferred specification, ranking at the top of class versus the bottom is associated with gains of 8.5 percentile points in grade 8 and 7.7 percentile points in grade 10 on national standardized tests; the invisible rank based on unreported test scores is close to zero and not significant once controls are added.
finding.measure: National standardized test percentile scores in grades 8 and 10
finding.study_size: n=387,614 total across two cohorts after selection (205,123 in 2018 cohort; 182,491 in 2019 cohort)

finding.finding_summary: Using the 2018 student questionnaire, the authors find that higher visible rank improves students’ school perceptions, self-esteem, and perceived recognition by peers, and also increases interest in the subjects studied. These associations are interpreted as evidence for a perception channel linking saliency of rank to later outcomes, although no single standardized effect size is reported in the text provided.
finding.measure: Student questionnaire responses on self-esteem, perceived recognition by peers, school perception, and interest in subjects (6-point Likert scale)

paper_profiles.title: GREX-PLUS Science Book v1
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This document is a science-book style mission concept paper for GREX-PLUS (Galaxy Reionization EXplorer and PLanetary Universe Spectrometer), a proposed cryogenic space telescope intended for launch in the 2030s. Rather than reporting an educational intervention or school-based experiment, it lays out the astronomical science cases that the mission would enable, including galaxy formation, cosmic reionization, supernovae, exoplanet atmospheres, organic molecules, and planetary science targets.

The paper describes the instrument suite (a wide-field near-infrared camera and a high-resolution mid-infrared spectrometer), the survey strategies, and the kinds of observations needed to address these science questions. It argues that the mission’s deep/wide 2-8 µm imaging and 10-18 µm high-resolution spectroscopy would complement and extend JWST, Spitzer, and ground-based facilities, with special strengths for detecting very high-redshift galaxies and resolving molecular lines that are difficult from the ground.

Because the paper is an astronomy mission white paper and not a study of AI in education, it has no educational population, no classroom intervention, and no school-level empirical outcomes. Its conclusions are about scientific capability and mission value, emphasizing the potential for legacy data and breakthroughs in astrophysics and planetary science.

paper_profiles.title: The Frontiers of Nuclear Science: A Long Range Plan
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This document is a community-authored long-range planning report from the U.S. Nuclear Science Advisory Committee (NSAC), not an empirical education study. It surveys the state of nuclear science, summarizes major recent discoveries, and lays out future priorities for U.S. nuclear physics research and infrastructure over the next decade. The report discusses advances in quantum chromodynamics, nuclear structure, nuclear astrophysics, neutrino physics, and experimental facilities such as CEBAF, RHIC, FRIB, DUSEL, and a future Electron-Ion Collider.

The paper’s approach is advisory and programmatic: it synthesizes expert consensus from town meetings, white papers, and a working group process to recommend investments in facilities, theory, and workforce development. It includes a short education section emphasizing outreach, undergraduate involvement, and preparation of future nuclear scientists, but it does not evaluate a specific AI intervention, educational technology, or classroom-based science learning program.

Because the document is a policy/planning report rather than a study of students or teachers, it does not provide empirical evidence about learning outcomes, including scientific reasoning outcomes for U.S. middle school grades 6 to 8. No exact AI tool names or student-facing/teacher-facing intervention details are reported in the text provided.

paper_profiles.title: Contributions from Cognitive Research to Mathematics and Science Education
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the Workshop on Research in Science and Mathematics Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This invited talk argues that mathematics and science education should draw more deeply on cognitive science, especially constructivism, expert-novice research, and models of problem solving. The paper does not report a single intervention trial; instead, it synthesizes then-current cognitive research and uses physics examples to motivate instructional principles such as multiple representations, explicit linking of concepts, extended context, comparison/contrast, and multiple-pass learning.

The context is higher education and teacher professional discourse rather than a K-12 classroom study. Gerace emphasizes that learners actively construct knowledge, that misconceptions and surface-feature problem solving are common, and that instruction should be designed as a communication process that models the receiver and elicits evidence of understanding, not just answers. The overall conclusion is that educators should use cognitive research to design more interactive, conceptually rich teaching that helps students build expert-like knowledge structures and better problem-solving habits.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that scientific and mathematical learning should be improved by instructional practices derived from cognitive research, but it does not present direct experimental evidence from this talk. The central claim is that learners must actively construct knowledge, and that conceptually focused instruction can improve problem solving and conceptual understanding; no effect size, CI, or sample size is reported because this is a conceptual review/talk rather than an empirical study.
finding.measure: Conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance discussed through cognitive research examples

finding.finding_summary: The talk strongly emphasizes metacognition, reflection, self-monitoring, and judgment as key components of expert performance. Gerace describes problem solving as involving understanding, planning, executing, and then reflection/evaluation, and argues that instructional designs should cultivate these durable skills; however, the paper itself does not report new quantitative data.
finding.measure: Metacognitive processes, reflection/evaluation, self-monitoring, judgment

finding.finding_summary: The paper identifies motivation, self-confidence, persistence, and reward structure as important to becoming a self-motivated learner and to sustaining problem solving. It argues that activities allowing practice of component skills can build confidence and self-motivation, but provides no direct empirical estimates in this paper.
finding.measure: Motivation, self-confidence, persistence, self-motivation

paper_profiles.title: AI literacy in K-12: a systematic literature review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a systematic literature review of AI literacy in K-12 education worldwide. The authors searched Scopus for peer-reviewed publications on AI literacy or AI education at the primary/secondary school level, excluding work limited to computer-based learning or intelligent tutoring systems, and ultimately reviewed 179 documents published across journals, conferences, and one book chapter.

The review organizes the literature into two broad categories: learning experiences and theoretical perspectives for implementing AI literacy. Learning experiences include efforts to help students recognize AI, understand how AI works, use AI tools, and consider AI’s societal implications; theoretical perspectives include curriculum design, subject integration, student perspectives, teacher training, support resources, and gender diversity. The paper concludes that AI literacy at the K-12 level is still emerging, that many studies focus on technical or applied activities without rigorous assessment of learning outcomes, and that the U.S. and China are leading broader curriculum-implementation efforts.

Importantly for the retrieved-study inventory question, this paper is not itself a U.S. middle school science intervention study. It is a secondary review that mentions several studies and initiatives, including some U.S.-affiliated work, but it does not report a direct U.S. middle school science scientific-reasoning experiment as the paper’s own unit of analysis. No actual U.S. middle school science source is extracted as a primary study from this paper because the paper does not present one as a standalone retrieved study with the requested intervention/outcome details.

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that the U.S. is among the countries leading broader AI literacy implementation schemes, especially through AI4K12 and related curriculum-design efforts. However, it also concludes that AI is still not widely offered in most U.S. K-12 schools and that implementation remains uneven and early-stage.
finding.measure: System-level review of AI literacy initiatives, curricula, and implementation schemes in K-12
finding.study_size: 179 documents reviewed; country-level synthesis, not a single primary sample

paper_profiles.title: Teacher’s Perceptions of Using an Artificial Intelligence-Based Educational Tool for Scientific Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines K-12 STEM teachers’ perceptions of an artificial intelligence-enhanced scaffolding system (AISS) designed to support scientific writing, especially argumentative writing, through GPT-2–generated expert modeling and feedback. The authors’ central question is not whether the tool improved student achievement in a classroom experiment, but how teachers experienced the tool after using it themselves and what concerns they had about its classroom adoption.

The study was conducted at a higher education institution in the southeastern United States with nine in-service teachers enrolled in a doctoral program; participants taught elementary, middle, or high school STEM subjects. Teachers completed a scientific writing task using the AISS, then participated in interviews and researchers analyzed their responses qualitatively. The tool provided individualized sentence and paragraph generation based on user input, and teachers generally viewed it as superior scaffolding that could support reasoning, argumentation, evidence-based writing, and self-directed learning.

The main conclusions are that teachers reacted positively to the idea of AI as a scaffolding source, but also expressed concerns about transparency, validity, and the possible reduction of teachers’ roles. The paper argues that hands-on exposure to AI can improve teacher receptiveness and that such systems may be useful for middle and high school students, but it does not report student outcome data or an experimental comparison of scientific reasoning performance. As a result, the paper is best understood as an educator-perception/implementation study rather than evidence of learning effects in U.S. middle school science classrooms.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers perceived the AI-based scaffolding as supportive of higher-order thinking, including reasoning, argumentation, and self-directed learning. In the qualitative interviews, participants said the system helped them reflect on their argument process and select evidence to justify claims, but no numerical learning gains were reported (n=9 teachers).
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes about reasoning, argumentation skills, higher-order thinking, and self-directed learning during an AI-supported scientific writing task

finding.finding_summary: The study found that teachers viewed the AI-generated scaffolds as useful for scientific writing, sentence structure, paragraph sequencing, and evidence-based writing. Participants described the generated text as a useful expert model, but the paper reports perceptions rather than writing-score outcomes or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes about scientific writing, sentence structure, paragraph sequencing, and evidence-based writing

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported increased receptiveness and interest after hands-on interaction with the AI tool, and they characterized the experience as engaging and impressive. This is a qualitative perception finding only; the paper does not provide survey scores or other quantified motivation/engagement measures.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of interest, receptiveness, and engagement with AI-based scaffolding

finding.finding_summary: Participants emphasized that the system produced immediate support and individualized scaffolding, suggesting it could reduce some instructional burden and provide rapid feedback. However, the paper does not measure actual teacher workload, time savings, or productivity effects.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes about immediate feedback and individualized scaffolding

paper_profiles.title: AutoTutor and Family: A Review of 17 Years of Natural Language Tutoring
paper_profiles.population: Undergraduate; Adult; Middle School (secondary mentions only, not a U.S. middle school science study)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative review of 17 years of research on AutoTutor and related systems in the AutoTutor family. Its goal is to synthesize the rationale, design principles, and empirical findings behind natural-language tutoring systems, especially those using deep reasoning questions, conversational scaffolding, pedagogical agents, affect-sensitive adaptation, and metacognitive support.

The review spans multiple domains and learner populations, including computer literacy, conceptual physics, biology, critical thinking, reading comprehension, and self-regulated learning. The authors summarize prior studies showing that AutoTutor-style tutoring often improves learning relative to static text or no-instruction controls, with reported gains around 0.5σ to 0.8σ in some domains, but the paper itself is not an original intervention study. It includes a few references to middle-school readers and a seventh-grade algebra tutoring corpus used to inspire tutoring dialogue, but these are not U.S. middle school science studies and do not constitute the paper’s primary focus.

For the specific retrieval question about U.S. middle school science and scientific reasoning, this source does not appear to report an actual U.S. middle school science study. Instead, it is a broad review that mentions science-related systems (especially physics and scientific inquiry tools) and one biology tutoring system, but the relevant empirical results summarized are largely from undergraduate, adult, or mixed/other settings. The paper should therefore be treated as a review source with no directly extracted U.S. middle school science intervention evidence.

finding.finding_summary: The review summarizes prior AutoTutor-family studies that used deep reasoning questions and scientific inquiry-like tasks, reporting learning gains in some contexts. However, these findings come from heterogeneous prior studies rather than a single U.S. middle school science study, and the paper does not provide a middle-school-science-specific effect estimate.
finding.measure: Learning tests / posttests on conceptual understanding and scientific inquiry-related skills reported across reviewed studies

paper_profiles.title: Students’ perceptions of using ChatGPT in a physics class as a virtual tutor
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how undergraduate students perceive and trust ChatGPT when it is used as a virtual tutor in an introductory physics course. The study asks whether ChatGPT can answer physics questions accurately, whether student trust varies with answer accuracy, and whether trust is associated with students’ perceived usefulness, ease of use, and intention to use the tool in the future.

The intervention was a ChatGPT-assisted makeup exam assignment embedded in a 16-week college physics class at a public university in the southern United States. Forty students completed the activity; they asked ChatGPT physics questions related to an exam on light and radioactivity, then evaluated and discussed ChatGPT’s responses. The study also collected survey data and student drawings to probe perceptions of ChatGPT, including anthropomorphic misconceptions.

Results showed that ChatGPT answered the physics questions with 85% accuracy overall, but students often trusted its answers even when they were wrong. Trust levels were associated with perceived ease of use and intention to use, and students who trusted ChatGPT more were more likely to perceive it as a robot/machine and as a know-it-all or magic-like system. The paper concludes that GenAI can support learning but can also reinforce misconceptions if students lack AI literacy, and it argues for explicit instruction in critical evaluation, prompt engineering, and AI literacy.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT answered student physics questions with 85% overall accuracy (307/362 correct; 55/362 incorrect) in an introductory physics class (n=40). However, students frequently accepted answers regardless of correctness, and additional prompting sometimes caused ChatGPT to change correct answers to incorrect ones and vice versa, indicating uneven support for scientific problem solving rather than robust scientific reasoning performance.
finding.measure: Accuracy of ChatGPT responses to physics exam questions; student agreement/trust in those responses

finding.finding_summary: Students’ trust and perceptions of ChatGPT varied significantly by answer accuracy and by trust group, with the Trust group agreeing with ChatGPT 100% of the time and reporting higher perceived ease of use and higher intention to use. The paper reports significant differences in perception by trust level (MANOVA: F(6,70)=2.478, p=0.031, η2=0.175), but these are attitudinal rather than achievement effects.
finding.measure: Perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, intention to use, and trust in ChatGPT

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined student trust calibration, critical evaluation of AI output, and misconceptions about AI, all of which map to durable skills such as critical thinking and metacognition. Students often failed to critically evaluate incorrect answers and many displayed anthropomorphic misconceptions (e.g., perceiving ChatGPT as a human-like or magic-like system), suggesting weak AI literacy and judgment.
finding.measure: Trust calibration, agreement with AI answers, and qualitative coding of student drawings for misconceptions

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s core task was a physics course assignment rather than a direct assessment of general course achievement. ChatGPT was used as a makeup-exam tutor for questions on light and radioactivity, but the paper does not report pre/post gains in physics achievement; instead it reports how students interacted with and judged the tool during the assignment.
finding.measure: Physics exam makeup-assignment task performance and related interaction logs

paper_profiles.title: A Review on Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.population: Not a primary empirical study; review spans multiple populations including K-12, higher education, and adult learners
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative review of artificial intelligence (AI) in education. It surveys major application areas such as adaptive learning, teaching evaluation, virtual classrooms, smart campuses, and intelligent tutoring robots, and discusses potential benefits and challenges of AI integration in teaching and learning.

The paper is not a primary study and does not test a single intervention in a defined sample. Instead, it synthesizes prior literature from multiple contexts, including elementary, middle school, secondary, and higher education, as well as teacher-facing administrative uses. The review argues that AI can support personalized learning, improve assessment efficiency, and enhance classroom management, while also warning about ethical, equity, infrastructure, and teacher-preparation issues.

Because this is a broad review, it does not provide a U.S. middle school science study or a scientific reasoning intervention in a middle school science setting. It mentions science-related virtual labs and one middle-school math study (ALEKS) as examples, but these are not U.S. middle school science scientific-reasoning sources. The article's contribution is therefore conceptual and integrative rather than empirical for the target sub-question.

paper_profiles.title: AI as a Teaching Partner: Early Lessons from Classroom Codesign with Secondary Teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report describes a seven-week classroom co-design pilot of Colleague AI Classroom, a generative-AI platform implemented with 21 in-service teachers across five Washington State schools and districts. The project asked how teachers design and implement AI-assisted classroom tools, how teacher judgment and AI competency shape student-AI interactions and instructional outcomes, and what supports make AI integration work in practice.

The platform included four features: Teaching Aide (student-facing conversational AI), Assessment & AI Grading (teacher-facing rubric generation and AI-assisted feedback/grading), AI Tutor, and Student Growth Insights (teacher-facing analytics). Teachers used the tools in real classrooms with more than 600 students in grades 6-12, then completed surveys, planning/reflection forms, interviews, meetings, and the research team examined platform logs. The report finds that AI was most effective when teachers carefully scaffolded use, framed it as a thought partner, and retained final instructional and grading authority.

Across the pilot, teachers reported that student-AI conversations and AI-generated formative feedback were more useful when tasks were aligned to specific instructional goals, kept short and structured for younger students, and supported by active teacher monitoring. The report emphasizes that prior teacher AI experience and confidence shaped implementation quality, and that the main value of the system was in reducing workload and improving feedback cycles rather than replacing teacher judgment. The document is exploratory, based largely on teacher self-report and usage logs, and explicitly calls for future work linking AI activity to actual student artifacts and learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that Colleague AI reduced time spent on drafting rubrics, generating feedback, and scanning student-AI conversations for misconceptions. Platform logs showed high AI grading coverage (median 92.2% of submitted work) across 58 assessments, indicating substantial automation of routine feedback tasks.
finding.measure: Teacher survey responses, platform usage logs, reported turnaround and workload reduction

finding.finding_summary: Teachers generally reported that AI-supported conversations helped engage students, with 35% saying the Teaching Aide helped most students learn and 62% saying some students learned. Engagement was higher when teachers framed the tool well, monitored use, and used concise, developmentally appropriate prompts; however, results varied substantially by classroom and grade band.
finding.measure: Teacher exit tickets and survey ratings of engagement/learning during Teaching Aide conversations
finding.study_size: n=18 teachers for Teaching Aide phase

finding.finding_summary: The report describes AI-supported conversations and AI feedback as helping students practice inquiry, revise work, and engage in evidence-based reasoning, especially when teachers tied activities to clear goals such as seminar prep, proof sketches, or revision cycles. These claims are based on teacher reports rather than direct student outcome testing.
finding.measure: Teacher observations of inquiry, revision, and reasoning during AI-assisted activities
finding.study_size: n=18 teachers (Teaching Aide); n=19 teachers (Assessment phase)

finding.finding_summary: The report includes subject-specific examples outside literacy, math, and science, such as Spanish and engineering. Teachers reported that AI supported ACTFL-aligned proficiency feedback in Spanish and helped with brainstorming and prewriting in English, but these were descriptive implementation claims rather than formal outcome measures.
finding.measure: Teacher-described subject-specific instructional uses and perceived usefulness

paper_profiles.title: How to QuantCrit: Applying Critical Race Theory to Quantitative Data in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book is a conceptual and methodological guide to QuantCrit, or the application of Critical Race Theory to quantitative data and methods in education. Rather than reporting an empirical study, it explains why quantitative methods are not neutral, traces the racist and eugenic histories of statistical reasoning, and argues that quantitative work should be explicitly oriented toward racial justice and equity.

The book develops the core tenets of QuantCrit: centrality of racism, numbers are not neutral, categories are not natural, data cannot speak for themselves, and a justice/equity orientation. It also situates QuantCrit within broader critical quantitative traditions, distinguishes it from quantitative criticalism, and offers examples and positional reflections from the authors’ own research and training. The intended audience is researchers, data users, and graduate students in education and education-related disciplines; the book does not present a study of students, schools, or an intervention.

Because the text is theoretical rather than empirical, it does not evaluate an AI tool, science curriculum, or scientific reasoning outcomes in a middle school U.S. setting. It instead serves as a methods and praxis resource for using quantitative data in more racially just ways.

paper_profiles.title: Comparative Analysis of Multicriteria Decision Making Methods for Postgraduate Student Selection
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of selecting postgraduate students when applicant evaluation must consider multiple criteria simultaneously. The authors frame student selection as a multicriteria decision-making problem and compare three methods—Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP), Weighted Product (WP), and TOPSIS—using real data from the Defense Sciences Institute of Turkish Military Academy.

The study is not an intervention study in an educational-technology sense, but rather a methodological comparison of ranking approaches for admissions decisions. Decision criteria included APPEE grade, English exam grade, interview grade, graduation degree, graduation school, and duration since graduation, with subcriteria for interview and reference letter. The paper computes scores for 31 previously admitted postgraduate students and compares each method's rankings against the students' cumulative grade point average (CGPA) as a benchmark.

The main finding is that AHP produced the smallest total deviation from CGPA, suggesting it aligned most closely with historical student performance. TOPSIS performed worst by the paper's deviation metric, and WP was intermediate. The authors conclude that AHP may be the most appropriate method for future postgraduate admissions at the Defense Sciences Institute, and they suggest further work could test additional criteria and multiple performance measures.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that AHP is the most appropriate multicriteria decision-making method for postgraduate student selection at the Defense Sciences Institute. Using 31 enrolled students as the comparison set, AHP had the lowest total deviation from CGPA (5.307) compared with WP (6.693) and TOPSIS (8.540), indicating the method best matched historical admissions outcomes.
finding.measure: Total deviation between method-generated student rankings/scores and normalized CGPA used as the benchmark

finding.finding_summary: The paper examines postgraduate student selection, not student learning outcomes directly. It shows that the decision method chosen for admissions can rank applicants differently, with AHP yielding the closest alignment to subsequent CGPA performance among the compared methods.
finding.measure: Applicant ranking/scores for postgraduate admissions compared with CGPA benchmark

paper_profiles.title: Thirty-First International Conference on Learning: The Converging Challenges for Inclusive Education: Intercultural Competences and Digital Literacies in Global Contexts
paper_profiles.venue: Conference proceedings / program book (Common Ground Research Networks, International Conference on Learning)
paper_profiles.population: Mixed / not a single empirical study population
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This document is a conference program/book for the 31st International Conference on Learning, held in Utrecht, Netherlands, in July 2024. It includes welcome letters, conference themes, plenary speaker bios, and a list of presentations, rather than a single empirical study. The overall conference theme emphasizes inclusive education, digital literacies, intercultural competences, and learning across contexts.

Within the program, one listed presentation concerns cyber-social learning and educational technology, and another concerns teachers’ knowledge and attitudes about inclusion of hard-of-hearing students in elementary schools in the United States and Saudi Arabia. However, the provided text does not include a full study report with methods, sample sizes, interventions, or outcomes beyond brief abstract-like descriptions. No U.S. middle school science study on AI tools and scientific reasoning is identifiable in the supplied text; the only science-related plenary is a talk on computational thinking and modeling in science education, not an empirical middle school science study.

paper_profiles.title: How to QuantCrit: Applying Critical Race Theory to Quantitative Data in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book is a methodological guide rather than an empirical study. It explains how QuantCrit—Quantitative Critical Race Theory—can be used to analyze educational data in racially just ways, with a strong emphasis on the historical ties between quantitative methods and eugenics, racism, and white supremacy in the United States.

The book walks readers through the origins of critical race theory, the development of critical quantitative methodologies, and the formalization of QuantCrit as a framework. It elaborates five core tenets: the centrality of racism, numbers are not neutral, categories are neither natural nor given, data cannot speak for themselves, and a social justice/equity orientation. The authors position the book as a practical resource for researchers and data users, not as a report of a specific intervention or experiment.

Although the text discusses education broadly and references applications across K-12 and higher education, it does not present a study of artificial intelligence tools, middle school science education, or scientific reasoning outcomes. It is best understood as conceptual/positionality-oriented scholarly book content that synthesizes prior literature and offers guidance for equitable quantitative research practice.

paper_profiles.title: School Virus Infection Simulator for Customizing School Schedules During COVID-19
paper_profiles.population: School-aged students (simulation of elementary/middle/high school settings; not limited to U.S. middle school science)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces the School-Virus-Infection-Simulator (SVIS), a simulation tool intended for teachers and education policymakers to explore how different school schedules and classroom configurations may affect COVID-19 transmission. The main question is not about learning outcomes, but about how ventilation, classroom type, and scheduling choices change the modeled maximum number of simultaneously infected students and the share of face-to-face instruction.

The simulator uses an agent-based extension of the susceptible-exposed-infectious-removed framework and a Wells-Riley-based infection probability model. The authors test scenarios involving self-contained versus departmentalized classrooms, different classroom ventilation rates, and a range of schedule patterns including UNESCO-style hybrid schedules. The paper argues that higher ventilation reduces infection risk, but that schedule design can be even more important and can behave differently depending on classroom structure.

The context is school reopening during the COVID-19 pandemic, with parameters motivated by published estimates rather than a direct field study. The paper does not focus on any U.S. middle school science population, scientific reasoning instruction, or student learning intervention. Instead, it is a modeling study for school operations and public health decision-making. Because it is an arXiv preprint and not an empirical education study, it should be treated as grey literature.

finding.finding_summary: The simulator is designed to help teachers and education policymakers plan schedules that reduce infection spread while maintaining face-to-face instruction. In the modeled scenarios, increasing classroom ventilation reduced the maximum number of simultaneously infected students, and certain schedule designs further reduced infection risk relative to other schedules.
finding.measure: Modeled maximum number of students infected simultaneously; percentage of face-to-face lessons

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents SVIS as a decision-support tool for school scheduling and reopening policy during COVID-19. Its main contribution is institutional: enabling policymakers to compare scheduling options, classroom types, and ventilation scenarios when planning school operations.
finding.measure: Simulation-based school scheduling comparisons for decision-making

paper_profiles.title: Integrated Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) Education through Active Experience of Designing Technical Toys in Vietnamese Schools
paper_profiles.venue: British Journal of Education, Society & Behavioural Science
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how STEM education might be integrated into Vietnamese middle school technology instruction through creative, experiential activities. The authors argue that, in Vietnam, middle school STEM integration had not yet been systematically implemented and that students often lacked practical, problem-solving experience. They therefore propose a framework for designing technical toys as a way to connect science, technology, engineering, and mathematics content in a concrete learning task.

The paper is primarily conceptual and descriptive, outlining a 5-step procedure for teachers and a corresponding 5-step student process for technical toy design. It presents an illustrative example in which 8th-grade students design a mini-racing car, showing how technology, math, and physics competencies can be integrated into one project. The article argues that this approach can foster active learning, creativity, problem solving, and subject integration, but it does not report an empirical comparison, outcome data, or statistical effects.

The study context is Vietnamese middle schools, not the United States, and the intervention is a teacher-designed, student hands-on technical toy project rather than an AI tool. Because it is a qualitative, practice-oriented article with no controlled evaluation and no reported scientific reasoning outcomes, it provides no evidence of effects beyond the authors' instructional claims and illustrative example.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not report an empirical test of scientific reasoning outcomes. It proposes a STEM integration model and describes a mini-racing-car design activity for 8th graders, but provides no measured gains, effect sizes, or comparator condition for scientific reasoning.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The authors claim the technical-toy design activity can increase students' motivation, interest, enthusiasm, and pride in their products, but these claims are not backed by quantitative measurement. The discussion is based on instructional rationale and prior literature rather than direct outcome data from this study.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The article centrally emphasizes creativity, problem solving, collaboration, and critical thinking as intended benefits of the integrated STEM activity. However, these are proposed instructional outcomes rather than empirically measured effects, so no effect size or sample-based estimate is reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Designing AI Systems that Augment Human Performed vs. Demonstrated Critical Thinking
paper_profiles.venue: 2025 ACM Workshop on Human-AI Interaction for Augmented Reasoning (AIREASONING-2025-01)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper argues that research on generative AI and critical thinking often conflates two different constructs: performed critical thinking, meaning independent reasoning done without AI assistance, and demonstrated critical thinking, meaning reasoning products or processes carried out with AI support. The authors review prior work on critical thinking measurement and explain why evaluating only AI-assisted outputs can overstate whether a person's own reasoning ability has improved.

The paper is conceptual rather than empirical. It does not test an intervention, collect participant data, or study a school-based population. Instead, it synthesizes definitions from education and psychology, relates them to human-AI collaboration, and proposes a framework for designing AI systems that either support demonstrated critical thinking or intentionally scaffold performed critical thinking.

The main conclusion is that many current AI systems may improve the quality of final outputs without necessarily improving independent reasoning skill. The authors call for future research designs that separately measure independent and AI-assisted critical thinking and suggest that educational and training-oriented interaction patterns may better support long-term skill development.

finding.finding_summary: This is a conceptual position paper, not an empirical study, so it does not report original effect sizes or participant outcomes. Its central claim is that generative AI may improve demonstrated critical thinking in AI-assisted outputs without improving performed critical thinking, and may even reduce independent reasoning through overreliance.
finding.measure: Conceptual distinction and literature-based discussion of critical thinking evaluation

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing science instruction in the elementary schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This short article is an editorial-style description of collaborative efforts to improve elementary school science teaching and learning, with a focus on inquiry-based instruction around flight concepts. The authors frame the piece around long-standing concerns about U.S. science education and declining student interest, citing national reports and TIMSS results as context rather than presenting a formal research question.

The main example is a local Penn State–State College Area School District partnership (“flight team”) that worked on enhancing the Air and Aviation unit in 3rd- and 4th-grade classrooms. The work included teacher collaboration, a wind-tunnel demonstration, student-designed airfoil testing, a video project, and an online Faculty Forum for sharing curriculum resources, but the article does not report a controlled evaluation, sample size, or quantitative outcomes for K-12 students. Instead, it emphasizes the professional learning of teachers and teacher candidates as they engaged with inquiry-based science and reflected on teaching science as inquiry.

The paper’s conclusions are essentially advocacy-oriented: collaborative university-school partnerships can support richer elementary science instruction, and these kinds of projects may help teachers become more comfortable and enthusiastic about science. The article is not a U.S. middle school science study and does not present an artificial intelligence tool or any scientific reasoning outcome in a middle-school setting.

finding.finding_summary: The article describes inquiry-oriented activities in which prospective teachers and elementary students asked testable questions, collected data, examined patterns, and constructed evidence-based explanations in a flight unit. However, this is a descriptive editorial with no quantitative evaluation, no student outcome data, and no reported effect size or sample size for scientific reasoning gains.
finding.measure: Participation in scientific inquiry activities; no formal scientific reasoning measure reported

paper_profiles.title: From Propositional Logic to Plausible Reasoning: A Uniqueness Theorem
paper_profiles.venue: arXiv preprint / submitted to International Journal of Approximate Reasoning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a formal logic/mathematics manuscript rather than an empirical education study. It asks what minimal logical requirements on a plausibility function would uniquely determine probability theory as an extension of classical propositional logic, in the spirit of Cox’s Theorem.

The paper proposes four requirements: invariance under logical equivalence, invariance under introduction of new definitional symbols, invariance to irrelevant added information, and preservation of the implication ordering. From these, it proves that plausibility values are order-isomorphic to rational probabilities and that the plausibility of a query given a premise is exactly the ratio of satisfying truth assignments, recovering the classical definition of probability.

No students, schools, classrooms, science instruction, artificial intelligence tool, or scientific reasoning intervention are studied. The manuscript is theoretical and contains no empirical research design, sample, comparator, or outcome data relevant to K-12 education. As a result, there are no U.S. middle school science studies to inventory from this source.

paper_profiles.title: Experience gravity in the classroom using the rubber sheet: an educational proposal from the collaboration between University and School
paper_profiles.venue: Edizioni Efesto / open-access eBook (educational proposal article)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents an educational proposal for teaching general relativity and gravity concepts in high school through a rubber-sheet analogy (RSA) activity. The authors describe a low-cost DIY space-time simulator, a set of eight instructional cards, and a co-design process developed with Italian high school teachers and university staff to make the activity classroom-ready and easy to replicate.

The paper reports preliminary classroom/outreach use of the RSA in Italy, including public outreach events, classroom testing with more than 200 high school students, and a teacher-training course with 25 teachers. The authors administered pre- and post-questionnaires to students and report a marked improvement in understanding of the topics addressed, but the detailed results are stated to be forthcoming in a future paper. The work is primarily a design and implementation report with qualitative feedback and limited preliminary evaluation, not a controlled study.
