For the specific retrieval question about AI tools and scientific reasoning in U.S. middle school science education, this source is not an AI study, not U.S.-based, and not middle school. It should be excluded from any U.S. middle-school-AI inventory. It is instead a high school physics/science education proposal centered on general relativity and outreach/teacher support materials.

finding.finding_summary: The authors report that pre- and post-questionnaires administered to more than 200 high school students showed a remarkable improvement in their knowledge and comprehension of gravity and general relativity topics after the rubber-sheet activity. No statistical test, effect size, or confidence interval is reported in the paper, and the detailed results are deferred to a future paper.
finding.measure: Pre- and post-questionnaires on understanding/comprehension of gravity and general relativity topics

paper_profiles.title: The Illusion of Understanding: How Middle-Schoolers Fail to Regulate Inquiry with ChatGPT in a Science Task
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether middle-school students can use ChatGPT in scientifically oriented inquiry tasks in ways that support meaningful learning. The authors focus on a question-asking (QA) cycle: identifying good versus poor prompts, evaluating AI answers, and deciding whether to continue asking follow-up questions or stop. The central concern is that generative AI may create an illusion of understanding, where students feel informed but do not actually regulate their inquiry well.

The study recruited 73 French middle school students from four schools in Nouvelle-Aquitaine; after exclusions, the final sample was 63 students aged 14–15. Students completed six validated science investigation tasks using ChatGPT 3.5, with randomized efficient versus inefficient prompt suggestions. The design was observational/correlational rather than experimental because the main analyses examined students’ sensitivity to prompt quality, answer quality, and follow-up behavior, and related these measures to self-reported metacognition, AI attitudes, and prior knowledge. The paper reports that students were often unable to distinguish good from poor prompts or answers, rarely asked follow-up questions, and frequently ended inquiry prematurely.

Task performance was only moderate overall, and higher self-reported AI familiarity and prior domain confidence were associated with worse regulation and evaluation. By contrast, metacognitive regulation and more skeptical perceptions of AI were associated with better QA behavior. The authors conclude that middle-school students need explicit AI literacy and metacognitive scaffolding to use ChatGPT productively for science inquiry, and they argue that current LLMs do not adequately support the regulatory demands of learning.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined students' ability to use ChatGPT for science investigation tasks and to produce conceptually accurate explanations of scientific ideas. Although students had unrestricted access to ChatGPT, the average task success rate was only M=0.51 (SD=0.25) across six problems (n=63), indicating only moderate scientific understanding overall; better QA behaviors were associated with higher success.
finding.measure: Science investigation task success rate / quality of written scientific explanations

finding.finding_summary: Students showed weak self-regulation during AI-mediated inquiry: only 14 students asked any follow-up questions, and follow-up occurred on just 22 questions across six tasks. Students frequently terminated inquiry prematurely even after receiving low-quality answers, showing limited persistence in the QA cycle.
finding.measure: Follow-up question frequency; premature termination of inquiry cycles

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally studied metacognitive regulation, prompt discrimination, and answer evaluation as durable skills in AI-mediated inquiry. Students performed near chance on prompt discrimination (Md′=0.19, SD=0.8; t=1.77, p=0.08) and answer evaluation (Md′=0.07, SD=1.2; t=-0.45, p=0.65), indicating a general inability to reliably judge prompt or answer quality. Better metacognitive regulation predicted better prompt discrimination (β=.3, p=.022).
finding.measure: Signal detection sensitivity (d′) for prompt discrimination and AI answer evaluation; metacognitive questionnaire scores

finding.finding_summary: The study also tracked efficiency of the inquiry process, showing that students often relied on suggested prompts and did not use the QA cycle efficiently. Students used suggested prompts at least once in 94.1% of cases, and low-quality answers were often accepted as useful, suggesting inefficient interaction patterns that likely reduced the productivity of the learning session.
finding.measure: Prompt usage patterns; answer ratings; number of QA turns

paper_profiles.title: Rising Stargirls: Benefits of a Creative Arts-Based Approach to Astronomy Education for Middle-School Girls from Underrepresented Groups
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates whether participation in Rising Stargirls, a creative arts-based astronomy outreach program, is associated with changes in middle-school girls’ science engagement and science identity. The authors frame the work as an informal science education intervention aimed at girls from underrepresented groups, especially girls who may not have access to formal astronomy courses in school.

The intervention consists of after-school, summer, and virtual workshops that combine astronomy content with arts-based activities such as free writing, visual art, theater, and creative reflection. The paper analyzes anonymous program-improvement survey data collected from six workshops run between 2015 and 2023: three in-person workshops in the United States and three virtual workshops reaching participants across multiple U.S. states and, in 2023, five countries outside the United States. Survey items asked about talking to family/friends about science, liking science classes or being excited for science classes, believing one can do well in science, and seeing oneself as a scientist/science person.

Results are based on pre/post self-report comparisons and show positive shifts overall in engagement and science identity across both in-person and virtual workshops. Because the study uses retrospective or program-improvement survey data without a control group, it supports an association rather than causal inference. The paper concludes that integrating creativity and the arts into astronomy education may help strengthen middle-school girls’ engagement with science and their science identity.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies participants’ science-related identity and engagement in the context of astronomy/science workshops, but it does not measure scientific reasoning with a test of reasoning skills or content knowledge. The closest direct science outcome is self-reported science engagement and self-concept; across six workshops, these responses increased after the intervention, but this is not a scientific-reasoning measure in the strict sense.
finding.measure: not_reported
finding.study_size: n=126 total workshop participants across six workshops; survey response counts varied by item (e.g., in-person total NB/NA=26/24, virtual total NB/NA=66/66)

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported higher engagement and stronger science identity after the workshops. Across all in-person workshops, talking to family and friends about science increased (Hake’s gain g=0.2344; dAw=0.4268, NB/NA=26/24) and seeing oneself as a science person increased (g=0.2582; dAw=0.4463, NB/NA=25/26). Across all virtual workshops, the gains were larger: talking about science g=0.4906 and dAw=1.0700 (NB/NA=66/66), and seeing oneself as a science person g=0.3377 and dAw=0.6235 (NB/NA=66/66).
finding.measure: Self-report Likert survey items on science engagement and science identity
finding.study_size: n=126 total; in-person combined NB/NA ranges from 24-26; virtual combined NB/NA=66/66

finding.finding_summary: The study includes one activity and survey-adjacent discussion of curiosity, creativity, imagination, and critical thinking, but the central empirical outcomes are not durable skills in a formal sense. Still, the arts-based workshop is presented as supporting broader scientific thinking, and the authors report positive pre/post shifts in related self-report items that plausibly reflect reflective and engagement-oriented durable skills.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Students’ perceptions of using ChatGPT in a physics class as a virtual tutor
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how undergraduate students perceived ChatGPT when it was used as a virtual tutor in an introductory physics class. The authors focus on three questions: how accurately ChatGPT answered physics problems, whether students’ trust in ChatGPT tracked the correctness of its answers, and how trust shaped students’ perceptions of usefulness, ease of use, and intention to use the tool in the future.

The study was conducted in a 16-week physics course at a public university in the southern United States with 40 participating students. Students first completed a multiple-choice exam on light, radioactivity, and related concepts, then used ChatGPT for up to 10 incorrect items in a make-up exam assignment over about 1.5 weeks, following a structured chat prompt sequence but also with room for additional questioning. The authors combined quantitative analysis of ChatGPT accuracy, trust group differences, and survey scales with qualitative analysis of student drawings to infer anthropomorphic misconceptions.

Overall, ChatGPT answered 85% of the physics questions correctly, but many students still trusted its answers uncritically, including incorrect ones. Trust was associated with higher perceived ease of use and greater intention to use ChatGPT again. The drawing analysis suggested many students viewed ChatGPT as a robot or machine, and some attributed super-intelligence or magic-like capabilities to it. The paper concludes that while ChatGPT may be useful as a tutoring aid, educators should teach AI literacy, critical evaluation of outputs, and prompt engineering, and should be cautious about anthropomorphic design cues that may increase blind trust.

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively examines students using ChatGPT to answer physics questions in an introductory physics context, with performance measured by correctness on exam-style multiple-choice items about light and radioactivity. ChatGPT answered 307 of 362 questions correctly (85%) overall, but students often accepted both correct and incorrect answers, indicating limited support for accurate scientific reasoning and a risk of reinforcing misconceptions.
finding.measure: Correctness of ChatGPT responses to physics exam questions (multiple-choice items on light, radioactivity, and related concepts)
finding.study_size: n=40 students; 362 ChatGPT questions across 46 unique items

finding.finding_summary: Students’ trust and perceptions of ChatGPT were measured with Likert-scale survey subscales for perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and intention to use. Trust groups differed significantly in perception, with the Trust group rating ChatGPT easier to use than the Partial Trust group and showing a higher intention to use it in the future; however, these are perceptions rather than learning gains.
finding.measure: Survey ratings of perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and future intention to use ChatGPT
finding.effect_size: η2=0.175 (MANOVA for perception by trust group)

finding.finding_summary: A central finding is that many students trusted ChatGPT regardless of accuracy, revealing limited critical evaluation and AI literacy. The authors also report that trust levels were associated with different perceptions of ChatGPT, and they explicitly recommend teaching critical thinking, warranted judgment, and prompt engineering to help students evaluate AI outputs.
finding.measure: Trust in ChatGPT, agreement with answers, and qualitative drawing analysis of anthropomorphic misconceptions

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on physics problem-solving in an undergraduate course, but it does not measure broader physics achievement beyond ChatGPT accuracy on exam questions and student perceptions of the tutoring process. The key substantive result is that ChatGPT performed with 85% accuracy on the assigned physics items, with some instability when students asked follow-up questions.
finding.measure: ChatGPT accuracy on physics exam items and student responses in the make-up assignment

paper_profiles.title: AI literacy in K-12: a systematic literature review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how AI literacy is being integrated into K-12 education worldwide. Using a systematic literature review approach, the authors searched Scopus and screened 750 records down to 179 peer-reviewed documents related to AI literacy/education in primary and secondary schooling, excluding work on computer-based learning and intelligent tutoring systems that did not focus on learning about AI itself.

The review organizes the literature into two broad categories: learning experiences and theoretical perspectives. Learning experiences include activities that help students recognize AI, understand how AI works, use AI tools, and think critically about AI’s social/ethical implications. Theoretical perspectives include curriculum design, AI as a school subject, student perspectives, teacher training, support resources, and gender diversity. The paper concludes that AI education in K-12 is still immature, with few studies that rigorously assess learning outcomes, and that more clearly defined competency frameworks, curriculum integration, and teacher co-design are needed.

For implementation, the review highlights country-level initiatives, especially in the U.S., China, Germany, Singapore, and Canada, but notes that the U.S. is not widely implementing AI in most K-12 schools despite active work such as AI4K12. The authors also emphasize that AI literacy should be integrated across disciplinary subjects rather than necessarily added as a standalone subject, and that ethical, social, and security concerns should be addressed alongside technical content. Because this is a review rather than an intervention study, it reports no primary effect sizes or causal outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The review finds substantial policy and curriculum activity around AI literacy in K-12, especially in the U.S. and China, but also notes that implementation remains limited and uneven in schools. In the U.S., AI4K12 and MIT-related efforts are described as influential, yet AI is still not widely offered in most K-12 schools.
finding.measure: Systematic review of curriculum/implementation literature and country-level initiatives

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI literacy can support critical thinking and broader decision-making by helping students understand how AI works, its limits, and its ethical implications. However, this is a synthesis-level claim rather than a directly tested outcome, and the review notes that few studies rigorously assess whether these competencies are actually learned.
finding.measure: Narrative synthesis of AI literacy goals and reported learning experience aims

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that many AI literacy proposals aim to increase student motivation, engagement, and interest through hands-on, contextualized, and playful activities. It also notes that some studies examine students’ intentions and interest in learning AI, but the review does not report pooled quantitative effects.
finding.measure: Student interest, motivation, and behavioral intention as reported across included studies

paper_profiles.title: AutoTutor and Family: A Review of 17 Years of Natural Language Tutoring
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.population: Undergraduate; Middle School (adjacent studies only); High School (adjacent studies only); Adult
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review synthesizes 17 years of research on AutoTutor and related natural-language tutoring systems. The paper asks what design features of dialog-based AI tutors support learning, how those features evolved over time, and what the evidence shows across domains such as computer literacy, physics, biology, critical thinking, reading comprehension, affect-sensitive tutoring, and self-regulated learning support.

The intervention family is centered on automated conversational tutoring: students answer deep reasoning questions, receive pumps, hints, prompts, corrections, and summaries, and interact with animated pedagogical agents. The review describes the tutoring architecture, semantic analysis methods, affect detection, collaborative lecturing, and learning progression models, then summarizes empirical results from prior studies rather than reporting a new primary experiment.

The population represented in the reviewed evidence is mixed and mostly not K-12 U.S. middle school science. Relevant adjacent studies include undergraduate and adult learners, high school physics learners, and one biology tutor aligned to Tennessee Biology I. The paper notes that AutoTutor/related systems often produced learning gains versus textbook or control conditions, with reported effects around 0.5σ in some physics/computer literacy studies, 0.72σ in Guru biology, 0.79σ in a small DeepTutor study, and 1.4σ in Operation ARA versus no instruction. It also highlights moderating findings: low-knowledge students tended to benefit more from supportive affective tutoring, while high-knowledge students sometimes did not.

For the specific retrieval focus on implementation, measurement quality, subgroup findings, and safety issues in U.S. middle school science, this paper does not provide a direct U.S. middle school science study. It does, however, provide adjacent implementation details for physics and biology tutoring systems, including dialog structure, some session length information, and a few assessment descriptions, but not detailed fidelity, training dosage, usage logs, or validity/reliability evidence for a middle-school scientific reasoning measure. No substantive hallucination, bias, dependency, or misuse safety analysis is reported in the paper.

finding.finding_summary: Across the AutoTutor family, the review reports consistent learning gains on science-related reasoning tasks, especially physics and biology. In the WHY2/AutoTutor physics studies, learning gains were about 0.5σ over textbook controls, with one pretest/posttest study reporting 0.61σ over a no-material control and 1.22σ over a textbook-reading condition; a small DeepTutor study (n=30) reported 0.79σ gains for a 1-hour session with macro-adaptivity, and Guru biology produced about 0.72σ on a biology posttest versus classroom instruction only.
finding.measure: Physics concept tests (4 essay questions and 40 multiple-choice items, many adapted from the Force Concept Inventory); biology posttest; pretest/posttest learning measures for conceptual understanding and deep reasoning
finding.effect_size: 0.5σ to 1.22σ depending on condition; 0.79σ in DeepTutor study; 0.72σ in Guru biology

finding.finding_summary: The review emphasizes critical thinking, metacognition, and self-regulated learning as major targets of the AutoTutor family. SEEK aimed to improve scientific inquiry and critical thinking skills but did not significantly improve finding relevant information after a 1-hour intervention, whereas Operation ARA reported about 1.4σ gains on a scientific research skills test versus no-instruction controls after 8–12 hours of play-based tutoring.
finding.measure: Scientific research skills test; scientific inquiry / critical thinking skill tasks; information evaluation and synthesis tasks
finding.effect_size: 1.4σ for Operation ARA; no significant gain for SEEK

finding.finding_summary: Affect-sensitive tutoring often improved learning for low-knowledge students but not for high-knowledge students. In the Supportive AutoTutor study, low-knowledge learners showed a 0.71σ gain on posttest scores relative to standard AutoTutor on a second session when difficulty was greater, while high-knowledge students did not benefit and sometimes learned less; GazeTutor increased attention and produced 0.26σ overall gains (p<.178) and 0.45σ gains on deep learning (p<.035).
finding.measure: Posttest scores; attention to tutor; deep learning outcomes; affect classification from discourse, facial expressions, posture, and gaze

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that iSTART improved reading comprehension for both college students and middle-schoolers, with effects differing by reader skill. Less-skilled readers improved on single-sentence content questions, while more skilled readers improved on bridging questions that connect multiple sentences; the review does not provide a single pooled effect size for these outcomes.
finding.measure: Reading comprehension questions; paraphrasing, bridging, predicting, and elaborating strategy tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes limited evidence that some AutoTutor-family systems were efficient in the sense of supporting learning in relatively short sessions or with targeted adaptive delivery. For example, DeepTutor’s macro-adaptive study reported 0.79σ gains in a 1-hour session, and the review notes that automated tutoring can approximate expert tutoring gains while scaling instruction, but it does not provide direct teacher workload or productivity outcomes.
finding.measure: Training duration and learning gain relative to control; system scalability claims

paper_profiles.title: AI Grand Challenges for Education
paper_profiles.population: Not a human-subject study; conceptual education technology article referencing learners across K-12, higher education, and lifelong learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article is a conceptual agenda piece arguing that artificial intelligence can transform education by addressing five grand challenges: mentors for every learner, learning 21st century skills, using interaction data to support learning, universal access to global classrooms, and lifelong/lifewide learning. Rather than reporting a single empirical study, it synthesizes prior AI-in-education and learning-sciences work to outline where AI systems can support personalized feedback, collaborative learning, real-time assessment, and large-scale learning analytics.

The paper emphasizes that AI-based instructional systems can model learner knowledge, emotion, motivation, and collaboration; adapt instruction; and provide richer feedback than traditional classroom approaches. It discusses technologies such as intelligent tutoring systems, user modeling, educational data mining, and agents, and it argues that these tools may improve science learning, 21st-century skills, and access to learning. However, it does not present new data from an intervention, and it does not report a U.S. middle school science study, dosage, fidelity, subgroup effects, or safety outcomes from a specific implementation.

For the retrieved sub-question, this source is only adjacent: it mentions middle school science generally and scientific reasoning conceptually, but it does not provide direct evidence from U.S. middle school science classrooms. It also does not report measurement validity/reliability evidence for scientific reasoning measures, usage logs, training, or teacher mediation in an empirical trial. No direct U.S. middle school science AI source is present in the provided text, so those requested implementation and safety details are not reported here.

paper_profiles.title: Facilitating student engagement through the flipped learning approach in K-12: A systematic review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how flipped learning affects student engagement in K-12 settings and what contextual, methodological, and technological features characterize the field. Rather than testing a single intervention, it systematically reviews 107 empirical studies published between 2012 and 2018 across seven databases, coding study characteristics, measures of engagement, theoretical framing, and technologies used.

The review finds that flipped learning in K-12 is reported to support engagement across behavioral, affective, and cognitive dimensions, with the most common benefits being increased peer interaction, enjoyment, participation, teacher interaction, and confidence. It also shows that the evidence base is dominated by North American and Asian studies, especially U.S. studies, with most research in high school STEM contexts and relatively little in elementary or middle school settings. Most studies used multiple measures such as surveys, interviews, observations, and ability tests, but many lacked clear definitions of engagement, strong theoretical grounding, or detailed descriptions of the intervention.

In terms of implementation, the review notes frequent use of teacher-made videos, quizzes, and LMS platforms such as Edmodo, Google Classroom, and Moodle. It also highlights common limitations: small samples, short study durations, limited reporting of fidelity and intervention detail, and uneven measurement quality. The paper is a synthesis of engagement-focused flipped learning research, not a direct study of scientific reasoning in U.S. middle school science, so it provides only adjacent evidence rather than a direct source on that sub-question.

finding.finding_summary: Across 107 K-12 flipped-learning studies, the review found consistent positive associations with student engagement. Overall, 87 studies (81%) reported behavioral engagement, 79 (74%) affective engagement, and 77 (72%) cognitive engagement; 61 studies (57%) reported all three dimensions. The most common engagement indicators were increased peer interaction (n=50), enjoyment (n=42), participation/involvement (n=39), increased interaction with teachers (n=37), and confidence (n=33).
finding.measure: Surveys, interviews, observations, focus groups, and counts of engagement behaviors

finding.finding_summary: The review reports frequent evidence of collaboration, communication, self-regulation, and responsibility as outcomes of flipped learning. Studies commonly noted students learning from peers, increasing questions and curiosity, taking ownership of learning, and becoming more independent; for example, increased peer interaction was reported in 47% of studies and participation/involvement in 36%.
finding.measure: Survey responses, interviews, classroom observations, and qualitative coding of study findings

finding.finding_summary: The review suggests flipped learning can improve classroom time use and teacher access to students. Teachers reported having more time for individual or small-group support, more vibrant class time, and better visibility into student understanding; however, these were synthesized descriptive findings rather than pooled effects. The review also notes that teacher-made videos, quizzes, and LMS use may require additional preparation time and professional development.
finding.measure: Teacher and student reports; classroom observations; descriptions of classroom organization

paper_profiles.title: A Review on Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative review of artificial intelligence (AI) in education. It synthesizes prior literature on major AI-enabled education applications, including adaptive learning systems, automated teaching evaluation, virtual classrooms and laboratories, smart campuses, and intelligent tutoring robots. The authors aim to describe how AI is being used in educational settings, what benefits it may offer, and what challenges it raises.

The review argues that AI can support personalized learning, improve teacher efficiency, enhance classroom and campus management, and expand access through remote or adaptive instruction. It also notes that AI may improve learning quality and teaching effectiveness, but the paper is not an empirical study of a specific intervention. Instead, it summarizes existing examples and prior studies across educational levels and contexts, many outside the United States and outside middle school science.

For the user’s sub-question, this source does not report a direct U.S. middle school science study of an AI tool. It does mention AI-supported virtual laboratories and science learning generally, but only as adjacent examples from other contexts (including tertiary biology, physics, chemistry, and VR science labs). It also raises general safety and ethics concerns about data privacy, responsibility, fairness, and the risk of cognitive overload in VR science learning, but it provides no dosage, fidelity, usage-log, subgroup, or measurement-validity details for a U.S. middle school science AI intervention.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not present a direct empirical test of scientific reasoning in U.S. middle school science. It only reviews adjacent science-learning literature, noting that virtual laboratories can support science learning and practical ability, but also citing evidence that immersive VR science labs may increase presence while reducing learning due to cognitive overload.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The review claims AI-adaptive and intelligent tutoring systems can increase student enthusiasm, initiative, creativity, and autonomous learning/self-regulation, but these claims are synthesized from cited studies rather than newly estimated here. No pooled effect size or direct measurement is reported in this paper.
finding.measure: student motivation, autonomy, self-regulation, engagement

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI tools may help develop learning-related durable skills such as creativity, practical ability, and independent learning, mainly through adaptive learning and educational robots. However, these are narrative conclusions from prior literature rather than directly measured outcomes in the review.
finding.measure: creativity, practical ability, independent learning

finding.finding_summary: A central claim of the review is that AI improves operational efficiency by automating scoring, homework correction, attendance, and other routine tasks. The paper highlights that image recognition and automated assessment can reduce teacher workload and errors, but it does not provide a new empirical estimate in this article.
finding.measure: teacher workload, grading/scoring efficiency, attendance and management efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The review presents AI as supporting smart-campus development, resource allocation, campus safety, and education equity through remote personalized instruction and data-driven management. These are conceptual/narrative claims supported by cited examples, not a direct causal evaluation in this paper.
finding.measure: campus safety, resource allocation, access/equity, institutional management

paper_profiles.title: Perceptions and Barriers to Adopting Artificial Intelligence in K-12 Education: A Survey of Educators in Fifty States
paper_profiles.venue: IntechOpen chapter (Reimagining Education – The Role of E-Learning, Creativity, and Technology in the Post-Pandemic Era)
paper_profiles.population: K-12 educators in the United States and Puerto Rico
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter reports a nationwide survey study examining K-12 educators’ perceptions of artificial intelligence (AI), their readiness to adopt AI, and the barriers they face in doing so. The paper is framed around a practical implementation question: what policies, training, resources, and infrastructure are needed for AI integration in U.S. schools? The authors also situate the work within broader STEM/AI-in-education discussions and emphasize the importance of teacher preparedness, equity of access, and ethical use.

Using a Qualtrics survey distributed through social media and approved by the Lindenwood University IRB, the researchers collected responses from 4,528 educators across all 50 states and Puerto Rico. The instrument asked about district AI policies, technology comfort, teacher-prep training, openness to new technologies, AI tools used, access to internet/hardware/software, and perceptions of AI. Analyses were descriptive and subgroup-based (e.g., age, gender, grade level, region), showing generally positive attitudes toward AI but notable inequities in access, training, and comfort. The chapter concludes that schools and districts should expand AI and technology training, improve infrastructure, and develop clearer policies on ethical and responsible AI use, including privacy and bias concerns.

The paper is not an intervention or student outcome study; it is primarily an educator survey about adoption conditions and perceived barriers. It contains implementation-oriented recommendations for integrated STEM and mentions possible uses of AI in science classrooms, but it does not evaluate an AI tool’s effect on scientific reasoning or any other student achievement outcome. No direct U.S. middle school science AI source on scientific reasoning was identified in this paper; adjacent discussion is conceptual only.

finding.finding_summary: Educators reported generally favorable perceptions of AI and a strong need for district- and system-level support for implementation. In the sample of 4,528 educators, 64.07% reported district AI policies, 82.53% reported policies for ethical/responsible technology use, and 75.26% believed AI implementation would require substantial resources, indicating institutional readiness gaps rather than direct effects on student outcomes.
finding.measure: Survey responses on district AI policies, ethical technology policies, and perceived resources needed for AI implementation

finding.finding_summary: The chapter emphasizes that AI can reduce teacher workload by automating administrative tasks such as attendance, record keeping, assignment checking, grading, and assessment, but this is presented as a general claim rather than an evaluated intervention effect. The survey data show many educators are open to AI and concerned about training and infrastructure needed to use such tools efficiently.
finding.measure: Survey perceptions of AI usefulness for classroom and administrative tasks; descriptive usage of AI tools

finding.finding_summary: Educators’ comfort with technology and openness to learning new technologies varied by age, grade level, and region. For example, 40.77% reported being somewhat comfortable and 16.13% extremely comfortable with technology, while 56.74% were open to learning new technology, suggesting generally positive readiness but uneven confidence across subgroups.
finding.measure: Survey items on comfort with technology and openness to learning new technologies

finding.finding_summary: The chapter argues that AI can support skills such as problem-solving, collaboration, communication, and creative thinking within integrated STEM, but these are proposed applications rather than measured outcomes. The survey itself mainly assessed educator attitudes and readiness, not student durable-skill development.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of integrated STEM and survey perceptions of AI adoption
